In a recent interview on "In Depth With Graham Bensinger," Winkler — who was fired as director of Hanks’ 1989 movie "Turner & Hooch" after 13 days of filming — addressed the situation that initially ignited the reported rift.
Winkler admitted he was not "suited" to direct the movie, but accepted the job after being handpicked by Disney executive Jeffrey Katzenberg.

I [did] what I thought was my job, and I wanted to do it over again and apparently that p---ed them off."
Winkler said the situation came to a head just 13 days into filming.
SCOTT EASTWOOD SAYS HIS FATHER SENT KEVIN COSTNER HOME FROM SET WHILE FILMING 'A PERFECT WORLD'

title: Hollywood Marine veteran Rob Riggle doubts modern stars would make Jimmy Stewart's WWII sacrifice
summary: Marine veteran Rob Riggle doubts today's Hollywood stars would leave fame to serve like WWII bomber pilot Jimmy Stewart, who enlisted after winning an Academy Award.
story: Actor and comedian Rob Riggle discusses fan outrage over sports games on streaming services, his new Fox Nation special on baseball’s impact on New Yorkers after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, and more on ‘Fox & Friends Weekend.’
Hollywood Marine veteran Rob Riggle has doubts about whether today's stars would be willing to step away from the spotlight to serve in uniform like WWII bomber pilot Jimmy Stewart.
Stewart famously walked away from an Oscar-winning career at its peak to enlist in the U.S. Army Air Corps as a private nine months before the attack on Pearl Harbor.
In the upcoming biopic "Jimmy," Riggle, who is a retired U.S. Marine officer, plays Colonel Terrill, Stewart's squadron commander and mentor.
TOM HANKS PUT 'BAND OF BROTHERS' STARS IN THEIR PLACE DURING BOOT CAMP 'MUTINY', NEAL MCDONOUGH REVEALS

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 56-year-old actor and comedian weighed in on whether modern celebrities would be willing to make the same wartime sacrifice as the late movie icon.
"I would be surprised if anybody made that same choice today, especially an actor of his status," Riggle said.
Hollywood Marine veteran Rob Riggle shared his doubts that today's stars would make Jimmy Stewart's sacrifice. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images; Bettman/Getty Images)

"You got to remember, he won an Academy Award before the war," "The Hangover" star continued. "It wasn't like he was an up-and-coming actor. He was an established Academy Award-winning actor before the war. And then decided to put on the uniform and not in a safe way."

"He wanted to put on the uniform and serve where he could be used best," Riggle added. "And he was a pilot, so he put his hand in the air and went into harm's way. And I don't know if you'd see that today. I mean, I hope you would, but I would be surprised."
Stewart is pictured in front of a military airplane in 1941. (Getty Images)

Stewart joined the military in March 1941, just 28 days after winning the best actor Academy Award for his performance in the classic 1940 film, "The Philadelphia Story." He had tried to enlist in late 1940 prior to winning his Oscar but was initially rejected for being five pounds under the weight requirement for his 6'3" frame. Determined to serve, Stewart actively gained the weight so he could reapply and enlist right after the Academy Awards.

Due to his fame, the military initially tried to keep Stewart, who was a licensed commercial pilot, stateside as a flight instructor and used him for publicity and March of Dimes promotional tours. However, Stewart repeatedly requested overseas combat duty, appealing to his superiors to let him fly rather than serve in public relations.
99-YEAR-OLD WWII VETERAN AWARDED PURPLE HEART AFTER WAITING MORE THAN 80 YEARS

Stewart's persistence eventually paid off, and he was sent to England in late 1943 with the 445th Bombardment Group. He went on to fly 20 official combat missions over Nazi-occupied Europe as a command pilot, squadron commander and wing commander in B-24 Liberator heavy bombers.
Stewart enlisted in the United States Army less than a month after winning an Oscar. (Bettmann Archive)
By the end of WWII in 1945, Stewart had risen from private to full colonel. His combat awards included the Distinguished Flying Cross, the Air Medal and the French Croix de Guerre.
REMEMBERING THE COLLEAGUES WE LOST: A VETERAN'S MEMORIAL DAY REFLECTION
Riggle noted that people may be unaware of the danger that Stewart willingly placed himself in while serving his country.
"I think Jimmy went through a lot harder service than most with the flying over Germany, dropping bombs, having to make those sorties under tremendous stress and loss of his peers," Riggle said.

"But I do think when you decide to serve your country, you're kind of writing a blank check with your life and limb and I think it takes a lot to do that, so I'm so proud of the way he served his country and came back and then found a way out of the darkness of PTSD," he added. "That was pretty amazing."

As a commander, Stewart carried the immense burden of sending young men into brutal anti-aircraft fire and Luftwaffe attacks. During his service, Stewart witnessed heavy losses among his men and carried deep guilt over the lives lost under his command.

Biographers and historians have documented that Stewart suffered from severe psychological trauma, which caused digestive issues, insomnia, nightmares, shakes and sweats. Though Stewart's symptoms indicated that he was experiencing post-traumatic stress disorder, the formal clinical diagnosis of PTSD was not established until 1980.
Stewart starred as George Bailey in the holiday classic "It's A Wonderful Life." (Getty Images)

After returning to Hollywood, Stewart channeled his suppressed trauma into his post-war acting roles, including his performance in 1946's "It's A Wonderful Life," in which he played George Bailey, a banker who was experiencing a mental breakdown, raging at his family and contemplating suicide.
GARY SINISE SAYS HIS MONEY WOULD BE ‘MOVING A LOT FASTER OUT THE DOOR’ IF HE STILL LIVED IN CALIFORNIA
According to historians, portraying darker, more complex characters than in his pre-war Hollywood years enabled Stewart to process his trauma.

In the years following the war, Stewart enjoyed a successful career, built a family and continued his service in the Air Force Reserve for another two decades. Stewart died from a heart attack in 1997 at the age of 89.
Stewart served over two decades in the Air Force Reserve before retiring as a Brigadier General in 1959. (Bettmann Archive)

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Riggle explained that he drew upon his own military experience in the U.S. Marine Corps while portraying Colonel Terrill. Riggle served in the Marines for 23 years, reaching the rank of lieutenant colonel and serving deployments in Af­ghanistan, Albania, Liberia and Kosovo before retiring in 2013.
The actor noted that his service gave a personal understanding of what it means to send young men into harm's way.

"I myself was a lieutenant colonel so I know what it is to be in charge of a group of people," he said. "I was a Marine, but I know what it's like to be responsible and in charge and I know the weight of leadership. So I felt for all the characters in the movie that have that responsibility of leading men and making decisions that could affect their lives or end their lives."
Riggle played Stewart's commander and mentor Colonel Terrill in "Jimmy." (Miki Barlok)

Riggle launched his comedy and acting career in 1997 in New York City while he was still serving on active duty in the Marines. He had a short stint as a cast member on "Saturday Night Live" from 2004 to 2005, and later made his breakthrough as a correspondent for "The Daily Show."

The actor later appeared in numerous sitcoms, including "New Girl," "Arrested Development," "The Office" and "Modern Family," in which he played Ty Burrell's character, Phil Dunphy's arch nemesis, Gil Thorpe.
He has also had roles in hit movies including "The Hangover," "Step Brothers," "The Other Guys," "Dumb and Dumber To" and "Let's Be Cops."
Riggle told Fox News Digital that serving in the Marines gave him the qualities and mindset that he needed to succeed in Hollywood.

"Tenacity, don't quit, never give up, get up and try again," he said. "All those intangible lessons of mental toughness and fortitude, you need to have those if you're gonna be in Hollywood or any life in the arts, really."

"Because people are going to reject you, people are gonna deny you, people are not gonna see it the way you see it," Riggle continued. "You've got to be able to take the blows and keep going forward. And I think that's what the Marines gave me with those intangibles."
Riggle also said that his military background has helped keep fame and Hollywood success in perspective.
Riggle served in the Marines for 23 years before retiring in 2013. (Kyle Rivas/Getty Images)
"When you're a Marine, Uncle Sam doesn't care who you are," he said. "He still expects you to go do your job and every day get up and do it."
"I think it's great," Riggle added. "I think that it's very humbling and it's a good reminder. Get up and go do your job."
Riggle shared that he considers his military service to be among his top life achievements.
"It's got to be right up there in the top three, next to my kids," he said.
"There should be some mention of it on my tombstone, let me put it that way," Riggle added with a laugh.

Riggle noted that while Hollywood is generally appreciative of former service members, he believes many civilians still harbor a fundamental misunderstanding about why men and women choose to enlist in the first place.

"I have felt that Hollywood is actually very respectful toward its veterans," Riggle said. "It's been really nice to see. But if there are misconceptions out there, I think some people, again, this is a general statement, but I think people might think that people who join the military, they do it because they don't have any other choices."
"And that's simply not true," he continued. "They've got a tremendous amount of choices. And they choose to serve their country."

"It's an all-volunteer force," he added. "No one's making them do anything. So the people that put their hand in the air have made that decision in their mind and that decision is to serve something bigger than themselves. And I think it's quite honorable."
KJ Apa as Jimmy Stewart and Riggle as Colonel Terrill are pictured in "Jimmy." (Courtesy of Burns Co.)

Directed by Aaron Burns and starring "Riverdale" alum KJ Apa as Stewart, "Jimmy" follows the actor's transformative journey from Hollywood stardom to World War II combat pilot. The movie also explores his return home as a decorated Colonel who is quietly struggling with PTSD, which was then known as "combat fatigue." Tickets for the movie go on sale today.

"Jimmy" depicts how Stewart was disillusioned and considering quitting acting when director Frank Capra (Max Casella) persuaded him to star as George Bailey in "It's a Wonderful Life" and how playing the role in the holiday classic enabled the actor to heal and reclaim his life.
Riggle told Fox News Digital that he was drawn to the project because it's a "great American story."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I think it's a patriotic story," Riggle said. "I think people know Jimmy, especially younger generations, know him from his acting. I really wanted people — or I'm glad to be part of the story that's being told, about his service to his country."
"I hold it to high esteem,"he continued. "So I thought his journey was fantastic, it was amazing, and it was a true American journey."
"I think he's a hero," Riggle added.
KJ Apa as Jimmy Stewart and Max Casella as Frank Capra in "Jimmy." (Courtesy of Burns Co. )
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Riggle expressed his hope that audiences who watch "Jimmy" and may be unfamiliar with his military service may come to see him in a new light.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"I hope they remember the man, Jimmy Stewart," Riggle said. "Most people just remember him from 'It's a Wonderful Life.' Every Christmas they see him, and they're like, ‘Oh yeah, I love this movie.’ And there's so much more to the man."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"And I hope they remember that there are people out there — we see so much news about the bad guys," he continued. "There's a lot more stories of good guys, you're just probably not seeing enough of them. And this is a story about a really great guy who did what he thought was right, followed his heart, followed his conscience, and did what he thought he needed to do, and we're all better for it."

title: Prince Harry's rumored Diana film 'might feel like another betrayal' to Prince William as rift grows: expert
summary: Prince Harry's rumored Princess Diana documentary "might feel like another betrayal" to Prince William, with experts warning unreleased tapes could rock the royals.
story: King Charles confirms Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will not return to royal duties. A letter sent on behalf of the King explains their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and they are now akin to private citizens.
Prince Harry's rumored movie about his late mother, Princess Diana, "might feel like another betrayal" to Prince William as the royal rift between the brothers grows, according to experts.

The Daily Mail pushed a report last week that Harry was returning to the U.K. to create a movie, ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death next year. Harry and William have been estranged for years and their last public joint outing was at King Charles's coronation in May 2023.
Fox News Digital reached out to Archewell for comment, but did not hear back.

Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube’s "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital that Harry and Meghan Markle potentially using the tragic death of Diana for publicity would "infuriate" William.
Prince Harry is reportedly creating a movie based on Princess Diana, and Prince William might feel like it's a betrayal, according to experts. (Getty Images)

"If Meghan were involved creatively, it would inevitably make the project more controversial because Harry has repeatedly drawn parallels between Meghan and Diana," she began. "Those comparisons are particularly sensitive because William knew Diana in a way Meghan never could. Meghan never met Diana. If the documentary began using Diana’s experiences to reinforce Harry and Meghan’s existing narrative about themselves, I think that would be where it becomes too much for William."
PRINCE WILLIAM LIKELY 'LIVID' OVER MEGHAN MARKLE'S 'TASTELESS' PHOTOS AT PRINCESS DIANA'S HOME: EXPERT

Schofield continued, "In fact, I am hearing that The Diana Award fundraising dinner that Prince Harry was expected to attend later this month was cancelled when Prince William was notified that Meghan planned to attend and had a list of superficial 'asks' regarding her presence there. Meghan using a Diana-related event as a PR opportunity for herself would infuriate the heir."

"There is a difference between telling Diana’s story and using Diana’s story to validate your own or elevate yourself."
Adding: "That is why I think watching his brother commercialize their mother almost 30 years after her death could feel vulgar to Prince William and might feel like another betrayal."
Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!", pointed out that William and Harry previously collaborated on a documentary about their late mother in 2017.
"Meghan using a Diana-related event as a PR opportunity for herself would infuriate the heir."

"But obviously, a lot has happened since then, and the brothers aren't speaking, much less partnering on a project," he said. "'Diana, The Unheard Truth' is a three-part documentary based on never-before-released tapes, and William sees it as a posthumous invasion of their mother's privacy. How could it not be?"

title: Dolly Parton 'could not bear negative things' and kept her cancer diagnosis from fans and family
summary: Stella Parton reveals that Dolly Parton kept her cancer diagnosis secret because she "did not want people sad" or her fans and family worried.
story: Country music star Bill Anderson joins ‘America’s Newsroom’ to remember longtime friend Dolly Parton after her death at age 80 after a brief battle with cancer. Dolly Parton's sister is sharing why the legendary singer kept her cancer diagnosis a secret.

"Well, Dolly did not want anybody to tell that, because Dolly could not bear negative things, and she would not have wanted her fans worried about it," she shared. "She didn’t want a lot of the family worried about it. Some of us knew, the ones that were closer, but not every relative."

title: Skillet's John Cooper says woke activists have 'big hearts' but are 'hurting themselves'
summary: Skillet musician John Cooper gets candid about about how wokeness can harm people and explains why he doesn't believe in cancel culture.
story: John Cooper of Skillet told Fox News Digital that he doesn’t think any style of music has "inherent evil," and he believes God gave everyone creative expression.
Skillet frontman John Cooper believes people labeled "woke" are often motivated by good intentions — but warned their approach can ultimately "hurt society."

"I think it’s really worth mentioning that people that we would call woke, the things that we find really problematic, I think it's worth mentioning that most of those people really have big hearts," Cooper said during a recent appearance on the "Unashamed with the Robertson Family" podcast. "They want justice. They want the world to be better."
"They’re just going about it in a way that they don’t know is wrong, and it’s actually hurting them," he continued. "It’s hurting everybody. It hurts society."

He said that inner cities in particular are "getting so much worse," saying, "I look at the things that the politicians that say they want to help the poor, they want to help the marginalized, they want to help people of color, whatever it may be, and all they do is keep hurting them more and more and more."

The musician ultimately attributed his disagreement with those views to his Christian faith.

"What they’re doing is not true, and it’s not based on the Bible," Cooper said. "It goes against the way God tells us how to live. "I am a huge believer in freedom of speech," Cooper said. "I hate cancel culture. I don’t want anybody to be canceled because I’ve never said, ‘So-and-so rock artist sings a song against Jesus and I want him pulled down from Spotify.’"

title: Prince George follows Prince William's footsteps at Eton in a changing royal world: experts

"A new successful chapter for the future heir to the throne. His great-grandmother would be tickled pink," British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital. (Matt Porteous / Kensington Palace)

"I think Prince William and Catherine have been incredibly thoughtful in allowing Prince George to be a child before he has to be a king. "Eton is a significant new chapter, but I suspect their priority remains the same," Schofield continued. "George should understand who he is without allowing that title to become his entire identity. story: The driveway in front of Nicolas Cage's Malibu home collapsed on Tuesday, creating a sinkhole. (Video courtesy of ABC7 Los Angeles)
Nicolas Cage's beachfront home was damaged after the driveway collapsed following days of rough surf.

The driveway in front of the Oscar-winning actor's oceanfront home collapsed, creating a sinkhole. Fox 11 reported that the Los Angeles County Fire Department said it was caused by coastal erosion spurred by a hurricane that formed in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Marie, generating big waves and high tides.
Video taken of the home shows a 30 by 30 foot hole in front of the home with the waves and the beams holding up his home visible underneath.

"The City’s Building Safety Division and Southern California Gas Company are working to assess the situation," they wrote. "At this time, the City red tagged five homes (prohibited entry). Pamela Anderson paid a steep price to beat hepatitis C.
After living with the disease for years, the 59-year-old actress said she drained her bank account to pay for an early treatment that insurance didn’t yet cover.

Anderson opened up about her battle with hepatitis C and the shame she carried after her diagnosis in the late '90s while accepting amfAR’s Award of Courage on Sunday in Venice. The nonprofit, which works to end the HIV/AIDS epidemic, also supports hepatitis C research and advocacy.

Anderson went public with her diagnosis in 2002 and claimed she contracted the disease while sharing needles with her ex-husband, Tommy Lee. The Mötley Crüe drummer has denied Anderson's claim.
When a cure eventually became available, Anderson said getting access required a major financial sacrifice.

"Ten blurry years later, there was a cure. I was lucky," she said. "I was offered it in its early stages, and it took everything I had in my bank to pay for it. It wasn't covered by insurance yet, and I felt tremendous guilt that others weren't granted the same access."

title: Prince Harry finds way to live ‘half-in, half-out’ life Queen Elizabeth refused to endorse: experts
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan's U.K. return with their children echoes the "half-in, half-out" proposal Queen Elizabeth II rejected at Sandringham.
story: Hugo Vickers, author of "Queen Elizabeth II: A Personal History," details how the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's exit and Oprah interview added strain during the late monarch's final years.
Prince Harry may have finally found a way to live the life that his grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, refused to endorse.

On Sept. 8, 2022, Britain's longest-reigning monarch died after 70 years on the throne. She was 96. On Aug. 26 this year, Harry and his wife, Meghan Markle, returned to the U.K., where their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, will attend school.

As the Sussexes settle into their new life in Britain, with details about their private home and their children's school closely guarded, royal experts told Fox News Digital that the arrangement recalls the "half-in, half-out" proposal the late queen rejected.
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK MOVE PUTS FRESH SPOTLIGHT ON THEIR EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS AGAINST ROYAL FAMILY

From left: Queen Elizabeth II, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex watch a flypast to mark the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace on July 10, 2018, in London, England. The couple stepped back as senior royals in 2020. They returned to the United Kingdom before Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet started school in September 2026. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Harry may feel vindicated because, superficially, he has created something resembling the freedom he originally wanted," Kinsey Schofield, host of the YouTube show "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. "But I think calling it a victory misunderstands what the queen rejected."

"I see absolutely no reason to believe she would have changed her mind," Schofield said. "Queen Elizabeth spent 70 years protecting the distinction between the crown and the individual. It seems unlikely that one of the defining judgements of her final years would suddenly have become negotiable."

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, Duke and Duchess of Sussex, leave a service of thanksgiving for the reign of Queen Elizabeth II at St. Paul's Cathedral in London on June 3, 2022, during Platinum Jubilee celebrations marking the monarch's 70 years of service. (Matt Dunham - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

While the Sussexes have returned to the U.K. for an extended stay, they won't resume their roles as working royals. They will live in a private, non-royal residence outside London while maintaining their California home and a property in Portugal. People magazine reported that Meghan is in early talks for a role in the Netflix drama "The Gentlemen."
WATCH: PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE CAUSED QUEEN STRESS IN FINAL YEARS: AUTHOR

On Monday, the Lord Chamberlain, the most senior official in the royal household, sent a letter to senior officials in the government and military, as well as lord lieutenants, the king's personal representatives around the country.
The letter drew a firm line around the Sussexes’ homecoming, reaffirming that the couple will not resume official duties.

"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of The Sovereign, and are no longer working Members of The Royal Family," a letter sent on behalf of King Charles III read, Fox News can confirm. "This position, distinct from the State and Royal duties undertaken by the working Royal Family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected."

"It follows that there is no change to the current status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex," the letter added. "Their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and are not used. The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity. In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests."
A letter sent on behalf of King Charles on Monday reaffirmed that Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will not resume official duties. (Isabel Infantes//POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals in 2020 after describing intense scrutiny from the British press and saying they lacked support from the palace.

"Following conversations with the duke, the queen has written confirming that in stepping away from the work of the royal family it is not possible to continue with the responsibilities and duties that come with a life of public service," a statement from Buckingham Palace read at the time.

From left: Queen Elizabeth II, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex watch a flypast to mark the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace on July 10, 2018, in London, England. The couple stepped back as senior royals in 2020. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
In response, the couple issued a statement of their own, saying: "We can all live a life of service. Service is universal."
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex depart Canada House in London, on Jan. 7, 2020. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital the queen drew a firm line before the couple's departure, insisting the Sussexes could not be "half in, half out" as working royals.

"Her position was simply stated as ‘all in or all out,’" Fordwich said. "While King Charles has maintained that position, he is likely to be more open to private reconciliation and family gatherings, especially if Harry refrains from further public attacks on the family. Prince William, however, remains resistant to any formal restoration of royal duties for Harry."

Prince William, Prince of Wales and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex attend the Committal Service for Queen Elizabeth II at St. George's Chapel, Windsor Castle on Sept. 19, 2022, in Windsor, England. (Getty Images)
In 2020, Harry attended the Sandringham Summit at Queen Elizabeth II's Norfolk estate, where senior royals determined the terms of his and Meghan's departure from royal life.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex sits in a car as she attends Queen Elizabeth's state funeral and burial in London on Sept. 19, 2022. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

According to People magazine, it was there that the late queen made her position clear. After lengthy discussions, Harry was told there would be no "half-in, half-out" role for the Sussexes. They could not remain working royals while also pursuing independent, income-generating ventures.

In his memoir "Spare," Harry recalled the Sandringham meeting and wrote that he believed the royals would consider five options for the Sussexes. "Option Five" called for a full departure. After about an hour, the queen's private secretary — nicknamed "The Bee" by Harry — distributed drafts of a statement announcing "Option Five." Harry wrote that he was stunned.

From left: Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Queen Elizabeth II attend the Queen's Young Leaders Awards Ceremony at Buckingham Palace in London on June 26, 2018. (John Stillwell/WPA Pool/Getty Images)
"Wait. I'm confused," he wrote. "You've already drafted a statement? Before any discussion? Announcing Option Five? In other words, the fix was in this whole time? This summit was just for show?"
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, arrives at Westminster Abbey ahead of the State Funeral of Queen Elizabeth II in London on Sept. 19, 2022. (Christopher Furlong/Getty Images)
Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital he believes the palace made a mistake by rejecting the proposal outright.

"In my view, the queen was very badly advised by her representatives over the ‘half in, half out’ policy," he said. "I cannot see any reason in this day and age why it could not work. It shows a level of hypocrisy. Harry and Meghan could have remained in the royal fold without costs to the public purse. And yet, this was deemed unacceptable."
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, and Queen Elizabeth II attend Day 1 of Royal Ascot at Ascot Racecourse in Ascot, England, on June 19, 2018. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
Schofield argued the queen had good reason to reject the proposal.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Sandringham House, the royal family's estate in Norfolk, England. (Radcliffe/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images/Getty Images)
"The queen had already learned the dangers of ‘half in, half out’ long before Harry and Meghan proposed it," she explained.

"Prince Edward and Duchess Sophie attempted to maintain commercial careers alongside royal duties, with Edward running his television company and Sophie working in public relations. The arrangement became increasingly uncomfortable for the institution, especially as their professional lives generated headlines that risked trading on their royal connections. Ultimately, they abandoned those careers and became full-time working royals."

Duchess Sophie and Prince Edward depart Soufriere by boat on Day 6 of their Platinum Jubilee royal tour of the Caribbean on April 27, 2022, in Soufriere, Saint Lucia. (Stuart C. Wilson - Pool/Getty Images)

"That experience demonstrated exactly why the lines need to be clear," Schofield continued. "You are either representing the Crown and accepting the restrictions that come with that privilege, or you are pursuing a private, commercial life. Trying to do both inevitably raises questions about royal status, access and whether relationships are being leveraged for personal gain."
Prince Harry told the BBC in 2025 that he's ready for reconciliation. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

Schofield argued senior royals dedicate themselves fully to serving the crown and supporting the monarch as a united front. She said it would have been "unfair" to relax those restrictions for the Sussexes while allowing them to benefit from their royal status. In the queen's eyes, commercial freedom was "incompatible" with royal service.

"The queen might have wanted more family connection with Harry and Meghan, but she wouldn’t have compromised the constitutional aspects of such an arrangement," Fordwich said. "She would also have been deeply wary of the commercial conflicts it could create. It would have set a precedent for other royals wanting to have it both ways."
Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Harry attend the annual Chelsea Flower Show at Royal Hospital Chelsea on May 18, 2015, in London, England. (Julian Simmonds - WPA Pool / Getty Images)
Before Harry and Meghan returned to Britain, Simon Vigar, author of "The Four Wives of Windsor," told Fox News Digital that a "hybrid" model was inevitable.

"[The Sussexes] thought they could have a hybrid role of having a business life and a private life, while also spending a few months in the U.K. supporting the queen," he shared. "Harry believed that was an option, which was whipped away from him."
WATCH: PRINCE HARRY BELIEVED ROYAL FAMILY COULD HAVE ALLOWED A ‘HYBRID’ ROLE: AUTHOR

After stepping back from royal duties, the Sussexes signed lucrative deals with Netflix and Spotify and publicly aired their grievances in interviews, documentaries and Harry's memoir, further straining his relationship with the royal family.
Queen Elizabeth sits with Prince William and Prince Harry in the royal box at Guards Polo Club, Smiths Lawn, Windsor. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
In 2025, Harry told the BBC he was ready for reconciliation and eager to spend more time with his father, who is being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, relocated to California in 2020. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
According to a source close to the Sussexes, Meghan will continue leading her As Ever company from the U.K., while Harry will spend more time working with his U.K.-based charities.
In July, the Sussexes privately met with the king at his Highgrove estate. It was the first time Archie and Lilibet had seen their grandfather since the late queen’s Platinum Jubilee in 2022.
Highgrove House, the king's private residence, in Doughton, Gloucestershire. (Neil Bennett/Mirrorpix/Getty Images)
Schofield questioned whether Harry has any regrets about his grandmother's final years.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Catherine, Princess of Wales, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex leave after escorting Queen Elizabeth II's coffin to Westminster Hall from Buckingham Palace for her lying in state on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. (Emilio Morenatti - WPA Pool/Getty Images)
"Harry says he loved his grandmother, and has spoken very warmly about their relationship," she said.

"But some of his choices during her final years became part of an already difficult period for the royal family. Whatever grievances Harry had with the institution, his grandmother was elderly, recently widowed and approaching the end of an entire life of service. title: Julia Louis-Dreyfus reveals ‘tons’ of friction behind the scenes of ‘Seinfeld’
summary: Julia Louis-Dreyfus opened up on the "Friends Keep Secrets" podcast about the arguments and hard work that shaped "Seinfeld" into a phenomenon.
story: FOX Business contributor Katrina Campins, comedian Rich Vos and comedian Charles McBee joined 'Fox News Saturday Night' to discuss how comedy has evolved alongside society's affinity for political correctness.
Julia Louis-Dreyfus didn't mince words about what it took to make "Seinfeld" a television phenomenon.
The actress, who starred as Elaine Benes, revealed there was "tons" of friction behind the scenes as the cast and creators worked to get the groundbreaking comedy just right.
"Well, I mean, it's hard to do anything really well, and it takes a lot of work, and you're gonna butt heads," she explained during an appearance on the "Friends Keep Secrets" podcast.
According to Louis-Dreyfus, creators Larry David and Jerry Seinfeld were "collaborative" with the cast when it came to direction. However, "sometimes there was an argument."

Julia Louis-Dreyfus revealed that there was "tons" of friction behind the scenes while making "Seinfeld." (Joseph Del Valle/NBCU Photo Bank)
Despite the occasional clashes, Louis-Dreyfus believed in what they were creating from the start. Her bigger concern was whether NBC would see the same potential.

title: Christine Taylor was asked to lose 10 pounds after landing Marcia Brady role in 'Brady Bunch Movie'
summary: Christine Taylor revealed she was asked to lose 10 pounds for her role as Marcia Brady in "The Brady Bunch Movie" during the "Office Ladies" podcast.
story: "The Brady Bunch" stars Barry Williams and Christopher Knight share how they’ve stayed connected over 55 years since the show’s debut.
Christine Taylor landed her dream role as Marcia Brady in "The Brady Bunch Movie" – but the part came with a catch.

The "Brady Bunch Movie" star recalled the uncomfortable demand she received after landing the role of Marcia Brady during the "Office Ladies" podcast, revealing she was "embarrassed" but agreed to do it because "that was just how things went" in Hollywood at the time.
Taylor landed the role of Marcia after starring in a live show called "The Real Live Brady Bunch."
The actress had been obsessed with Marcia Brady for years and had seen "every single episode ... backwards and forwards, inside out."
MICHELLE PFEIFFER SAYS SHE FELT 'HUMILIATED' FOLLOWING HER AUDITION FOR HER BREAKTHROUGH ROLE IN 'GREASE 2'
Christine Taylor revealed she was asked to lose 10 pounds after landing the role of Marcia Brady in "The Brady Bunch Movie." (Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"And then out-of-the-blue one day, I mean, out of the blue on my answering machine in 1990, whatever year this was, 92 or 93, I got a message from Sherwood Schwartz calling me, just cold calling me saying, 'I would love to meet with you...'" she recalled.
For Taylor, getting a personal call from "The Brady Bunch" creator was the kind of Hollywood moment she never expected – and one she wished she had preserved.
"It was a pinch me moment that I cannot believe to this day that I still didn't keep my little tape from the answering machine," she added.
But beneath the disbelief, Taylor said she had no doubts about whether she was right for the role.
‘BRADY BUNCH’ STAR SHARES THE SIMPLE WORD THAT SAVED HER FROM HOLLYWOOD TRAPS
Christine Taylor said she was "embarrassed" by the request but agreed because that was common in Hollywood at the time. (Getty Images)
"I knew it in my core that there was nobody who could do it better than me," Taylor remembered.
That confidence appeared to carry her through the casting process, which Taylor remembered as surprisingly straightforward.
"I'm fairly sure that I met with them and that was pretty much it," she recalled. "They didn't tell me I got it, but I never had to go back in and audition solo again."
Instead, Taylor read with different actors who would later portray her siblings – Jan and Cindy.

Christine Taylor also noted that viewers can see her weight fluctuate throughout the movie because of reshoots. (Getty Images)

But Taylor said the role also came with a request that reflected a much different era in Hollywood."...It was a very different time in the industry," Taylor explained of the 90s era. "The one thing that I got, and I was not a super heavy person, but they asked me to lose 10 pounds."
Taylor emphasized that she wasn't heavy at the time, but said dropping the weight felt like just another requirement of getting the job.

"I was like, 'I'll lose 10 pounds,'" she admitted. "Of course I was embarrassed when that ask came my way because, by the way, it would never happen today. And also it just was like, I wasn't the only person ever being asked to lose weight for a role back then. That was just how things went."

"But I was like, 'I'll do it.' And then the joke is over the course of the movie, which if you watch it very closely, I start to put the 10 pounds back on, and you can see it," Taylor recalled. Like I'll come into a scene looking a little rounder. And then like I exit the scene looking a little thinner just because of how they had to reshoot things."
Despite the pressure, Christine Taylor said she enjoyed filming the movie and treated herself to frozen yogurt after wrapping scenes. (Taylor Hill/WireImage)

Whatever pressure Taylor felt to shed weight didn't stop her from enjoying herself once the cameras stopped rolling.

title: King Charles III clarifies Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will not resume royal duties after UK move
summary: Buckingham Palace reaffirmed that Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will not resume royal duties despite their UK return, keeping HRH titles in abeyance.
story: Royal commentator Kinsey Schofield discusses reports that Meghan Markle and Prince Harry are house-hunting in the United Kingdom with a lavish wish list on 'Fox & Friends.'
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle may be back on British soil, but their return home won’t come with a royal reset.

Buckingham Palace has drawn a firm line around the Sussexes’ homecoming, reaffirming that the couple will not resume official duties and that their status remains unchanged from when they stepped back as working royals in 2020.

"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of The Sovereign, and are no longer working Members of The Royal Family," a letter sent on behalf of King Charles III read, Fox News can confirm. "This position, distinct from the State and Royal duties undertaken by the working Royal Family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected."
The letter further underscored that a change in address does not mean a change in royal status.
PRINCE HARRY AND MEGHAN MARKLE FACE RENEWED CRITICISM OVER ‘HALF-IN, HALF-OUT’ ROYAL ROLE: EXPERTS

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle moved back to the U.K. with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, but Buckingham Palace confirmed their royal status has not changed. (Joshua Sammer/Getty Images)

"It follows that there is no change to the current status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex," the letter added. "Their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and are not used. The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity. In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests."
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE'S UK RETURN SIGNALS ‘SPECTACULAR DEFEAT’ AS ROYAL EXPERTS WARN OF WILLIAM SHOWDOWN
A letter sent on behalf of King Charles III stated that the couple will not resume official duties and will continue to use their titles privately. (Jane Barlow/PA Images via Getty Images)

Markle and Prince Harry moved back to the U.K. in late August.

The couple’s children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, have already enrolled at British schools and will start classes sometime in September. The family plans to live at a private, nonroyal residence outside of London, but haven’t said exactly where that will be.

title: Alcohol tied to surprising cancer death pattern in adults under 55, researchers find
summary: Alcohol-attributable cancer deaths in the United States more than doubled from 1990 to 2023, with colorectal cancer surpassing liver cancer in younger men.
story: A University of Miami cancer expert reveals why alcohol is an increasingly important modifiable cancer risk factor, including its potential role in colorectal cancer among younger men.

Annual U.S. cancer deaths tied to alcohol consumption more than doubled over a three-decade period, according to a recent study led by researchers at the Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine.

The findings, published in The Lancet Regional Health — Americas and presented at the American Society of Clinical Oncology Annual Meeting in Chicago, revealed that alcohol-attributable cancer deaths jumped from 11,361 in 1990 to 23,126 in 2023.
Researchers analyzed more than 30 years of data from the Global Burden of Disease study to track the trends.
BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK
While alcohol has long been classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, surveys show that awareness of its link to cancer remains limited.

"The most surprising finding was the breadth of alcohol’s potential impact across cancer types," Chinmay Jani, M.D., corresponding author of the study and chief fellow in hematology and oncology at Sylvester, told Fox News Digital.
The study highlights that liquor may have a different risk profile than wine despite containing similar amounts of alcohol. (iStock)

"Although its relationship with liver cancer is widely recognized, its contribution to cancers such as colorectal, esophageal, breast, pancreatic and prostate cancer is less understood by the public."
CANCER DOCTOR REVEALS 5 HABITS THAT MAY REDUCE DISEASE RISK AND IMPROVE OUTCOMES

The research showed that older adults and men bore the highest overall burden of alcohol-related cancer deaths. Among older men, liver cancer was the primary cause of alcohol-attributable mortality, followed closely by esophageal and colorectal cancers.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Breast cancer was the leading cause of alcohol-related cancer deaths among women overall, the study found.

Among younger adults between the ages of 20 and 54, colorectal cancer emerged as the leading cause of alcohol-attributable cancer deaths in men and the second leading cause in women, surpassing liver cancer in both groups.
Breast cancer was the leading cause of alcohol-related cancer deaths among women overall, the study found. (iStock)

The authors noted that the findings carry significant weight for public health messaging, particularly because general awareness surrounding alcohol's connection to various cancers remains low compared to known risks like tobacco use.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Because no minimum "safe" level of alcohol has been established, researchers said drinking less may help lower long-term cancer risk.
Because the study used existing national data rather than following individuals over time, researchers couldn’t determine each person’s exact drinking habits or account for every lifestyle factor.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

As a result, the findings show a strong association between alcohol use and cancer deaths, but they cannot prove that alcohol directly caused those deaths or establish a specific "safe" drinking limit.
The findings show a strong association between alcohol use and cancer deaths, but they cannot prove that alcohol directly caused those deaths or establish a specific "safe" drinking limit. (iStock)

"What this study makes clear is that alcohol-related cancer risk is not limited to one disease or one group of people," Gilberto Lopes, M.D., senior author and chief of the Division of Medical Oncology at the Miller School, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"As physicians and cancer researchers, we have an opportunity to help patients understand that alcohol is a modifiable risk factor and that even small, informed changes can be part of a broader strategy to reduce cancer risk in our community."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Ground Zero first responder needed major surgery decades after 9/11 exposure: ‘I thought it was over’
summary: Volunteer EMT Mordechai Shedrowitzky shares how Ground Zero dust exposure led to years of hospitalizations, steroids and a rare airway disease diagnosis.
story: Volunteer EMT Mordechai Shedrowitzky and an NYU doctor share how exposure to World Trade Center dust can have serious health consequences decades later.
Those who were present at Ground Zero on Sept. 11, 2001, continue to experience the physical effects of their exposure.
As Lower Manhattan was engulfed in dust and debris from the remnants of both towers, first responders and survivors were forced to breathe in toxic air.

More than 400,000 people were exposed to toxic contaminants, physical-injury risks and stressful conditions in the days, weeks and months following the attacks, according to the World Trade Center Health Program.
SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POSSIBLE LINK BETWEEN 9/11 AND ACCELERATED AGING

As of March 2025, 8,215 people who had enrolled in the WTC Health Program had died, including 5,844 responders, as reported by the CDC. The figures include deaths from all causes; the program does not track whether a member’s death was related to 9/11 exposure.
A responder’s long-term health battle
In an interview with Fox News Digital, Mordechai Shedrowitzky, a volunteer EMT who responded on 9/11, shared how his exposure led to multiple hospitalizations and, ultimately, major surgery.

FDNY firefighters and rescue workers attend to an injured firefighter in the rubble of the World Trade Center in Manhattan, New York, after it was destroyed by planes in a terrorist attack on Sept. 11, 2001. (Getty Images)

Queens-born Shedrowitzky, 51, was living in Brooklyn at the time of the attacks. After helping cover his local area for much of the day, he headed into Lower Manhattan that evening to assist with the response.

"My most vivid memory was actually entering Manhattan from Brooklyn," he said. "As we approached the tunnel, the first thing we noticed was there were no lights, there was no electricity in the area, it [was] pitch black."
FOX NEWS' ERIC SHAWN REVEALS CANCER AND RESPIRATORY ILLNESS FROM 9/11 TOXIC DUST
"When we entered the tunnel, there was a tremendous amount of swirling debris, at speeds that I just can't even imagine."
Once Shedrowitzky and his team arrived at South Street Seaport, where his ambulance was staged with others, he described the debris as "overwhelming."
"I remember the engine actually sputtering at times," he said. "I would imagine that it was taking in a tremendous amount of dust."
Firefighters gather near ground zero after the attack on the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"We were definitely not cognizant of what effect ... the air might have on us. And therefore, we did spend a significant amount of time outside of the ambulances, just commiserating with the people around us."
Shedrowitzky said he "thought it was over" once he left the scene. But years later, he noticed small symptoms that were turning into a big problem.
His pre-existing asthma — which typically flared during seasonal changes and caused coughing that required an inhaler — was worsening each year.
AMERICA'S FIREFIGHTER SHORTAGE HITS CRISIS LEVEL AS EMERGENCY CALLS TRIPLE, PUTTING LIVES AT RISK

"I started to require oral steroids," he said. "I would have wheezing; I would have coughing. It would last longer; it would be more serious ... I wouldn't be able to go to work, wouldn’t be able to take care of my kids. So, the effects were definitely increasing over time."
Shedrowitzky added that his condition was "getting to the point where it was leading to frequent respiratory infections and hospitalizations."
A graphic shows a close-up of dust particles breathed in during the 9/11 terrorist attacks. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
"It took a number of years, many years, for us to realize that what was going on with my health was probably related to 9/11."
In 2019, Shedrowitzky described that his condition got "significantly worse," after experiencing a cough that wouldn’t resolve itself, even after the "highest doses" of steroids and antibiotics.
NAVY VETERANS REUNITE AFTER 30 YEARS FOR 'GRUELING' CROSS-COUNTRY BIKE CHALLENGE HONORING 9/11
Shedrowitzky ultimately was put in touch with the World Trade Center Health Program – a federal program administered by the CDC – where his condition was classified as 9/11-related and was monitored.
It was eventually confirmed that Shedrowitzky had tracheobronchomalacia, a condition in which the walls of the windpipe and major airways weaken and collapse during breathing.
Mordechai Shedrowitzky and Dr. Denise Harrison of NYU Langone's WTC Health Program are pictured on Sept. 8, 2026. (Khloe Quill/Fox News Digital)
"[It] was probably secondary to both the asthma getting worse as well as steroid use over the years to try to treat those symptoms," he said.
In 2024, Shedrowitzky underwent a procedure called a tracheobronchoplasty to structurally reinforce his trachea and main bronchi.
RUDY GIULIANI REVEALS HE HAD 'SPIRITUAL EXPERIENCE' WHILE IN PNEUMONIA-RELATED COMA
Two years after the procedure, he said he is feeling "much better," although he still experiences occasional infections. He hopes to return to work as a physical therapist soon.
"Even a couple of months ago, I wouldn't have been able to speak for more than a very short time," Shedrowitzky said.
"It took a number of years, many years, for us to realize that what was going on with my health was probably related to 9/11."
As a father of six, Shedrowitzky – who is now also a grandfather of two – said his condition made it difficult for him to spend time with his children as they were growing up.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Things as simple as lifting my children, even speaking to them," he said. "The amount of time that I spent in the hospital and its effect on them was quite significant."
"Now, they're older, but my ability to spend time, interact with them ... has been greatly improved."
Treating 9/11-related illnesses
Dr. Denise Harrison, medical director of the NYU Grossman School of Medicine WTC Health Program Clinical Center of Excellence, has been involved in post-9/11 healthcare since 2002.
The program has since grown to provide screening, monitoring and treatment for people experiencing health effects related to their 9/11 exposure.
The doctor noted that the dust on 9/11 was "highly alkaline," which can be "very irritating" to the airways.
People rush away from the collapsing World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001, after two hijacked airplanes hit the twin towers in New York City in a terrorist attack. (Getty Images)

"Usually, the larger size dust gets deposited in the upper airways and the smaller size dust gets deposited in the lower airways," she told Fox News Digital. "Because of the overwhelming nature of the disaster, a significant number of large particles got deposited into the lower airways as well. So, this is not just the airways, but also the digestive tract, in the esophagus."

Harrison said patients often report sinus problems, asthma and COPD. These conditions can occur alongside other "aerodigestive" issues, including gastroesophageal reflux disease, which may complicate diagnosis and treatment.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Other 9/11-related conditions may also be interlinked.
"We have patients with asthma and PTSD who might perceive their asthma symptoms differently than the patients without PTSD, so that requires a combination of providers," the doctor said.
The dust on 9/11 was "highly alkaline," which can be "very irritating" to the airways, the doctor noted. (iStock)
Shedrowitzky urged other first responders who are experiencing health issues to not wait to get help and to confirm that what they’re experiencing may be linked to 9/11.
"Continue to be monitored so that potential issues can be picked up early," he advised.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If we can look back and see the quality of life that it's robbing you of, it might push you to contact the World Trade Center Health Program, get the help that you need."
NYU Langone's WTC Health Program 9/11 exhibit is on display. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
As of March 31, 2025, the WTC Health Program had more than 130,000 currently enrolled members.
The program, which is authorized through 2090, operates branches across multiple health systems, including NYU Langone Health, Mount Sinai, Northwell, Stony Brook and Rutgers.

Harrison reiterated that the health effects of 9/11 exposure remain "persistent," and can be exacerbated by the environment and other illnesses. Experts predict that the fallout will continue for decades to come.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Symptoms are still ongoing and research is still ongoing," she said, urging the public and responders to "have patience."
"While it might not directly benefit them or may provide some benefits now, it could be more beneficial in the future and help the overall response to disasters."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Weight regain after obesity drugs tied to higher odds of suicidal thoughts in observational study
summary: Weight-loss drug users who regained weight had 4.2 times higher odds of suicidal ideation, according to a study analyzing data from over 27,000 adults.
story: Bonnie Mitchell, a licensed professional clinical counselor in California, said that while a new study shows a correlation between weight-loss drug use and self-reported mental health symptoms, it cannot prove causation.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Adults who reported using prescription weight-loss medication in the last year had higher rates of depression, mental-health counseling, suicidal thoughts and suicide-related behaviors compared to people who did not take the drugs, according to an observational study.
The research, conducted at Asan Medical Center in South Korea, analyzed data from 27,741 adults (10,908 men and 16,833 women).
Of these participants, 846 had been taking prescription medications for weight control during the previous year, while 26,895 did not take them.
OZEMPIC USERS MAY BE MAKING A MAJOR WEIGHT-LOSS MISTAKE, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS
The weight-loss drug users were 1.9 times more likely to experience depression and twice as likely to seek mental health counseling.
They were also 2.7 times more likely to have suicidal thoughts and 1.7 times more likely to make a suicide attempt.

Adults who reported using prescription weight-loss medication in the last year had higher rates of depression, mental-health counseling, suicidal thoughts and suicide-related behaviors compared to people who did not take the drugs, according to an observational study. (iStock)
The associations were stronger among those using the medications who gained or regained weight.

"The tendency for depression and suicide-related indicators to increase as weight rebounds after using weight-loss drugs may reflect not only the neuropsychiatric effects of the drugs themselves, but also a complex interplay of psychological and social factors associated with failed weight control," the research team wrote in the study.
PATIENTS TAKING WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS OFTEN MAKE 5 CRITICAL MISTAKES, DOCTOR WARNS
The findings were published in the Korean Journal of Family Practice on Aug. 23.
Bonnie Mitchell, a licensed professional clinical counselor in California, noted that this was an observational, cross-sectional study.
The associations were stronger among those using the medications who gained or regained weight. (iStock)

"It shows a correlation between weight-loss drug use and self-reported mental health symptoms, but it cannot prove causation," she told Fox News Digital. "It does not demonstrate that weight-loss medications directly induce depression or suicidal thoughts."
The data was collected between 2013 and 2022.

"During most of this period, modern GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists used for weight loss (such as high-dose semaglutide/Wegovy or tirzepatide/Zepbound/Mounjaro) were either not yet on the market or had very limited real world uptake in South Korea," Mitchell said.
WHEN IS A MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS TOO SEVERE FOR TELEHEALTH? WARNING SIGNS FAMILIES SHOULDN'T IGNORE
"The study sample captures older anti-obesity agents historically prescribed in South Korea during that decade, including phentermine, diethylpropion, phendimetrazine, topiramate and orlistat."
Central nervous system stimulants – including phentermine-based drugs – have been shown to carry risks of anxiety, mood changes and insomnia, the counselor noted.
Weight regain or perceived "failure" in weight management can trigger profound guilt, shame, helplessness and psychological distress, according to a mental health counselor. (iStock)
"The study highlighted a striking sub finding that found users who gained weight despite taking the medication had 4.2 times higher odds of suicidal ideation compared to non-users," Mitchell noted.
Weight regain or perceived "failure" in weight management can trigger profound guilt, shame, helplessness and psychological distress, according to the expert.

"Individuals with severe obesity have higher baseline rates of depression, anxiety and body dysmorphia," Mitchell said. "A cross-sectional survey cannot separate pre-existing mental health struggles from new symptoms that arose after starting a medication."
"Any active suicidal thoughts require immediate emergency medical care."

More research is needed to determine whether weight-loss medications themselves affect mental health, or whether depression and other symptoms are related to factors such as obesity or difficulties losing weight.
The researchers also need to determine whether mental health risks differ between specific weight-loss drugs.
NEW WEIGHT-LOSS COMPOUND MELTS FAT WITHOUT CURBING APPETITE — AND PRESERVES MUSCLE

"Even though GLP-1 clinical trials show low absolute risk, the FDA’s product labels for chronic weight management drugs (like Wegovy and Zepbound) include warnings to monitor for mood changes," Mitchell noted.

She recommends that a physician conducts a baseline mental health history before prescribing new weight-loss medications, evaluating past or current depression, bipolar disorder, or history of suicidal ideation or behavior.

More research is needed to determine whether weight-loss medications themselves affect mental health, or whether depression and other symptoms are related to factors such as obesity or difficulties losing weight. (iStock)
"Individuals with severe obesity have higher baseline rates of depression, anxiety and body dysmorphia."

"Doctors can inform patients and caregivers about potential mood changes so they know what to watch for," Mitchell said. "The next important step for ongoing monitoring would be to schedule check-ins at 4- to 8-week intervals during dose escalation, to evaluate both physiological progress and psychological well-being."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Patients should contact their healthcare provider immediately if they notice new or worsening depressive symptoms, including the following.

Persistent low mood, unexplained sadness or severe fatigueAnhedonia (loss of interest in activities once enjoyed)Increased anxiety, agitation, panic attacks or extreme restlessnessSleep disturbance or insomniaNew or worsening thoughts of self-harm or suicideMarked changes in behavior or personality, reported by friends or family

"Any active suicidal thoughts require immediate emergency medical care," Mitchell advised.
"If a patient develops emergent depression or suicidal ideation during treatment, clinicians should discontinue the weight-loss medication and connect the patient with psychiatric support."
Eli Lilly, manufacturer of the tirzepatide weight-loss medication Zepbound, explicitly mentions "depression or thoughts of suicide" in its safety information.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"You should pay attention to changes in your mood, behaviors, feelings or thoughts," the website reads.
It further advises patients to contact a healthcare provider if mental health changes are "new, worse or worry you."
An expert recommends that a physician conducts a baseline mental health history before prescribing new weight-loss medications. (iStock)
On Lilly's medical-information site, the company says that after reviewing clinical trials and medical reports, "no increased risk" of suicidal ideation or psychiatric adverse effects was identified.

Novo Nordisk, manufacturer of the semaglutide weight-loss medication Wegovy, states in its trials that less than 1% of participants experienced suicidal ideation or behavior during treatment. It also says there was "no difference between semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo."
