title: Georgia woman celebrates 112th birthday, reveals her secret to a long life
summary: Mabel Dunbar of Fayetteville, Georgia, turned 112 and says religious faith and close family ties are the secrets behind her remarkable longevity.
story: Dr. Jessica Gray explains several factors contributing to the increase in U.S. life expectancy, including decreased drug overdoses and improved cancer survival rates.
A Georgia woman who just celebrated her 112th birthday credits her longevity to staying close to her family and embracing her strong religious faith.

Mabel Dunbar, of Fayetteville, Georgia, was born in Jamaica in 1914. She is the mother of one, grandmother of four and a great-grandmother, and was honored by loved ones on her birthday Sept. 5 with a custom berry cake, flowers and a crown, FOX 5 Atlanta reported.
"God is love and I love my families," Dunbar said at her party. "I love all my families and strangers."
HOW A 93-YEAR-OLD SOCCER REFEREE CREDITS WARTIME RATIONS AND DISCIPLINE FOR HIS LONGEVITY
Fayetteville resident Mabel Dunbar reflects on reaching her 112th birthday milestone surrounded by loved ones at her metro Atlanta home on September 5, 2026. (FOX 5 Atlanta)
Those who know her describe Dunbar as "deeply religious, pleasant and talkative," according to FOX 5.

She spent her life serving others and remaining active, the station reported. Until recently, Dunbar still enjoyed cooking and made breakfast for herself every morning. She also enjoyed sharing stories with visitors.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
After moving to Florida to live with her daughter in 1994, Dunbar relocated to Fayetteville in August 2025 to live with her granddaughter and grandson-in-law.
Family remains an important part of Dunbar’s daily life, according to FOX 5.

"Treat them the best you can, because they are important," Dunbar said of younger generations, specifically her grandchildren. "You need them when you can't help yourself like me. These good people are on me all the time, and I'm happy to see them when they come."
A custom berry cake decorated for Mabel Dunbar’s 112th birthday milestone sits ready for family festivities in Fayetteville on September 5, 2026. (FOX 5 Atlanta)
Leading oncologist and University of Pennsylvania bioethicist Dr. Ezekiel Emanuel has identified several principles for living longer and reducing disease risk.

They include prioritizing an active social life, staying mentally active with new hobbies and opportunities to learn, limiting processed and sugary foods and drinks without being overly restrictive, engaging in moderate exercise and getting proper sleep, Fox News Digital previously reported.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Emanuel also recommends avoiding obviously dangerous activities and behaviors.
Religious involvement has also been associated with greater longevity, research has suggested.
Generations of family gather around 112-year-old Mabel Dunbar at her Fayetteville home to celebrate her long life and Jamaican heritage. (FOX 5 Atlanta)

In a 2016 study published in JAMA Internal Medicine, researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health examined religious service attendance and health outcomes among 74,534 women over 16 years.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
They found that women who attended religious services more than once a week had a 33% lower risk of dying during the follow-up period compared with women who never attended religious services.
Family members place a sparkling birthday crown on 112-year-old Mabel Dunbar during a milestone celebration at her Fayetteville home. (FOX 5 Atlanta)

Weekly attendance was associated with a 26% lower risk, while attendance less than once a week was associated with a 13% lower risk. Regular attendees also tended to smoke less, experience fewer depressive symptoms and have stronger social support, the researchers reported in 2016.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The world’s oldest documented living person is Ethel Caterham, of England, who turned 117 in August.
Caterham previously told The Associated Press that she credited her long life to "never arguing with anyone," adding, "I listen, and I do what I like."
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Why couples should flirt with each other every day — plus the ‘red flag’ to avoid
summary: A relationship expert says flirting boosts self-esteem and confidence, but couples in long-term relationships often lose the "muscle memory" of playfulness.
story: Clinical sexologist Mindy DeSeta, PhD, shares how flirting can release dopamine and oxytocin, reduce stress and help people feel more confident, attractive and connected.
Flirting may do more than spark romantic interest — experts say it can also benefit emotional well-being, as long as it stays within appropriate boundaries.

Mindy DeSeta, Ph.D., a clinical sexologist and mental health counselor in Miami, Florida, defined flirting as a "one-on-one interpersonal experience," delivering a message that someone is interested in learning more about another person.
Flirting in general "feels good," the expert told Fox News Digital, adding that there are both emotional and physiological effects.
COMMON MARRIAGE HABIT COULD QUIETLY KILL YOUR SEX LIFE, EXPERT WARNS
Flirting may activate brain chemicals involved in pleasure, reward and social bonding, DeSeta said. It can also lower the stress hormone cortisol.

"It builds confidence, it's a positive social interaction that improves self-esteem," she went on. "What I also hear is that people want to flirt in general because it makes them feel attractive and desired … That's a normal human feeling."
Flirting may activate brain chemicals involved in pleasure, reward and social bonding, experts said. (iStock)
DeSeta said she views flirting as a signal of attraction and believes it should remain between romantic partners or people pursuing a romantic relationship.
"It’s really hard to be platonic because it does release that bonding hormone," she said.
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT
For those who feel the need to flirt with someone who is not their partner, the expert suggested this could be a "red flag" for what’s happening in the relationship.
"As a sexologist, I'm a huge believer that we must date and flirt with our partner every day," DeSeta said.
Feeling the need to flirt with people outside your relationship may be a "red flag." (iStock)
It's normal for relationships to sometimes need a "reboot," she said.

"In one marriage, you're going to get many, many marriages… You'll find people getting stale or very hollow in their relationship, and that's when you will start looking outside to get those needs met, especially in flirting, because it's something that's very easy to do."
HOW OFTEN ARE MARRIED PEOPLE HAVING SEX? WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT THE INTIMACY STANDARD IN AMERICA
If flirting begins to extend beyond the relationship — from a coffee-shop barista to a colleague at the office — DeSeta advised stopping "immediately" and redirecting that energy toward the partner.

"Be vulnerable and go in with, ‘I miss this about us. I want to bring this back into our relationship,’" she said. "And don't forget to share, ‘This is what would make me feel attractive and desired by you.’"
When flirting fades

Anna Elton, Ph.D., a licensed marriage and family therapist and clinical sexologist in Massachusetts, said couples struggling with intimacy often miss the fun they shared at the beginning of their relationships.
"There’s a time and place for flirting, and you have to be in the right headspace."
As couples devote more attention to schedules, errands, bills and childcare, other aspects of the relationship can get pushed aside, Elton said.
Affection, physical touch, flirting and playfulness may become less frequent, making room for "stress, conflict and growing resentment."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Body changes, aging and stress can also affect how confident or desirable people feel, Elton noted.
"When couples have been together for a long time, I ask them, ‘So, how do you flirt with your partner? How do you let them know about your erotic intentions?’ And they say, ‘Oh, we don’t flirt.’"
Creating a "new language of flirting" can help couples reconnect and spark intimacy, Elton said.
Creating a "new language of flirting" can help spice up the relationship and spark moments of intimacy, experts say. (iStock)
Bringing back the spark
Elton suggested small ways to rebuild connection, including a 20-second hug or a six-second kiss.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Small acts of self-care, such as applying lotion or following a skincare routine, can also help people "feel more connected with themselves," she said.
DeSeta cautioned, however, that flirting may not always be welcomed by a partner, depending on timing and mood.
Pay attention to body language indicating your partner will be accepting of flirtatious advances. (iStock)

"I’ve heard from my couples, ‘They were trying to flirt with me when I was unloading the dishwasher,’" she noted as an example. "There’s a time and place for flirting, and you have to be in the right headspace."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Maybe when someone's in a stressed mood, they're really focused on work, or they're just doing a task that does not make them feel sexy — this is not the right time."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Positive signals from a partner, such as leaning in, making eye contact and smiling, can indicate that flirting is welcome.
Still, partners should communicate about when flirting feels appropriate, DeSeta added.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Your daily coffee habit could be taking a toll on your bones, new study suggests
summary: A Flinders University study links high coffee consumption to lower bone density in postmenopausal women, while tea's catechins may promote bone health.
story: Dr. Alexa Fiffick, a board-certified family medicine physician and founder of Concierge Medicine of Westlake in Cleveland, Ohio, speaks about a new study linking hormone replacement therapy to lower dementia risk.
If you’re a woman who regularly reaches for coffee throughout the day, you may want to think twice about that next cup — or consider switching to tea.

Researchers at Flinders University reported in a study published in the journal Nutrients that high coffee consumption may be associated with lower bone mineral density (BMD) in older, postmenopausal women.

The scientists analyzed coffee and tea consumption among 9,704 women age 65 and older over a 10-year period. During that time, they also measured participants’ BMD at the femoral neck and hip, areas where osteoporosis-related fractures commonly occur.
The researchers found that drinking tea was associated with higher total hip BMD, while drinking more than five cups of coffee per day was associated with lower BMD.
COFFEE MAY HAVE POWERFUL EFFECT ON LIVER HEALTH, MAJOR STUDY SUGGESTS
Drinking more than five cups of coffee per day was associated with lower bone mineral density in older women, according to the study. (iStock)
Moderate coffee consumption — about two to three cups a day — was not associated with negative effects on bone health.

The study also identified differences based on other health and lifestyle factors. Coffee consumption was associated with lower femoral neck BMD among women with higher alcohol intake, while the positive association between tea and bone density was more pronounced among women with obesity.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
The researchers wrote that osteoporosis, which is characterized by low BMD, "is a major global public health concern affecting individuals across all ages, genders and ethnicities."
About one in three women and one in five men age 50 and older worldwide experience osteoporosis-related fractures, according to the study.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Women face a particularly high risk because they generally have lower bone mass and experience accelerated bone loss after menopause.

In the U.S., the number of adults age 50 and older with low BMD in the hip or spine is projected to increase by 17.2 million by 2030, adding to the healthcare costs and long-term disability associated with osteoporosis-related fractures, the researchers noted.
Coffee lovers may not need to give up their daily brew, researchers said, but consuming more than five cups per day could be linked to lower bone density. (iStock)

The scientists wrote that they studied the relationship between coffee and tea and bone health because dietary factors play a "crucial role in the prevention of noncommunicable disease and may influence bone health," and these are two of the most widely consumed beverages globally.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Study co-author Ryan Liu told ScienceDaily "compounds called catechins, abundant in tea, may promote bone formation and slow bone breakdown."

"Coffee’s caffeine content, by contrast, has been shown in laboratory studies to interfere with calcium absorption and bone metabolism, though these effects are small and can be offset by adding milk," Liu said.
Older women who drank tea had higher bone density in the hip than those who did not, according to a study. (iStock)

"Our results don't mean you need to give up coffee or start drinking tea by the gallon," Liu added. "But they do suggest that moderate tea consumption could be one simple way to support bone health and that very high coffee intake might not be ideal, especially for women who drink alcohol."

"This study offers an interesting look at how everyday beverages might relate to bone health, but the findings should be interpreted with caution," Lisa Young, registered dietitian and adjunct professor of nutrition at New York University, told Fox News Digital.
"Because it followed women over time without assigning them to drink coffee or tea, it can only show associations, not prove that coffee weakens bones or that tea strengthens them."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The study had limitations, including differences in participants’ lifestyles, its focus on bone density rather than fractures and relatively small effects seen mainly in older women, Young noted.
Symptoms of osteoporosis and early bone loss include back pain, loss of height over time and stooped posture, according to the Mayo Clinic.
"The bottom line for the public is reassuring: Moderate coffee intake appears fine, and there is no need to switch drinks for the sake of your bones," Young said.
"The most proven ways to protect bone health remain getting enough calcium and vitamin D, staying physically active and avoiding smoking and excess alcohol," she added.
"With that said, I do make a case for moderate amounts of coffee for good health. Too much of anything is never a good thing."
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Quiet quitting’ could silently destroy your marriage — 4 ways to bring the spark back
summary: From flirting and dating to spending quality time without phones, experts share how small daily gestures can reverse quiet quitting in a marriage.
story: James Sexton explains how emotional withdrawal develops between couples and why renewed attention, affection and mindfulness can reveal whether both partners remain invested.
Much like the workplace term that means doing the bare minimum, "quiet quitting" could also happen in marriage, sometimes gradually.

The informal term, which is not a clinical diagnosis, refers to spouses who remain together while reducing their emotional effort, communication or involvement in the relationship, according to experts.
New York City divorce lawyer James Sexton described what "quiet quitting" can look like at home and at work.
"I'm not going to go through the dramatic gesture of ending this thing," Sexton said. "I'm just going to stop. I'm going to stop paying attention. I'm going to stop participating."
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT

Silently pulling away from the relationship may seem to be easier than going through the "trauma" of divorce, Sexton told Fox News Digital, and the person avoids looking like the "bad guy" for ending the relationship.
"Very often, you actually receive more sympathy because you're perceived as the victim of the breakup as opposed to the perpetrator," he added.
A mature couple looking despondent after having a fight with one another at home (iStock)
A lack of effort in a relationship can be a bigger warning sign than frequent conflict, according to Sexton.
"When people are fighting, it kind of means there’s still skin in the game," he said. "The opposite of love is not hate … it’s indifference."
NEARLY 1 IN 3 MARRIED AMERICANS AREN'T HAVING SEX — EXPERT REVEALS HOW TO BRING BACK THE SPARK
Dr. Mindy DeSeta, a clinical sexologist and licensed mental health counselor in Miami, said some couples seek help after about 30 years of marriage, when the demands of family life have eased.

"The kids are gone, or they're hitting that retirement age, so they don't have the life distractions, and they're realizing, ‘Wow. I actually quiet quit my relationship when my kids were toddlers,’" she told Fox News Digital.
Some couples realize they've been out of their marriage since their children were young, an expert said. (iStock)
DeSeta identified four relationship principles, including the following:
Learning how to discuss physical and sexual intimacy
Focusing on teamwork
Staying autonomous
"Learning and earning" your partner through constant dating
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Couples experiencing quiet quitting may continue to function well as a team, managing the household and other responsibilities while becoming emotionally disconnected.
DeSeta said this disconnection can develop gradually as spouses begin living increasingly separate lives.
"Quiet quitting" your relationship can show up in subtle signs like taking interests in different things or going to bed at separate times. (iStock)

"When you stop spending the evenings together … you each are kind of doing your own thing. Your shows are different. You're going to bed at different times. … You may have different friend groups. You're working out at different times," she said.
4 tips to turn it around
Both experts shared tips for addressing emotional disconnection between romantic partners.
Reconnection often requires small, active steps that restart the momentum, rather than making grand gestures, Sexton suggested.
"Every single person in your life is not permanently gifted to you. They're loaned."
The divorce lawyer encouraged revisiting the simple acts and gestures that both partners enjoyed early in the relationship.
His suggestions included sending sweet "good morning" texts, writing a note complimenting a partner or sharing a song that sparked a romantic memory.

"It costs nothing, takes 30 seconds to do it," he said. "What does it cost to write an email with a list of 10 things I like about you? These are not only things we welcome receiving under any circumstances, but they're actually reminders."
Oftentimes, quiet quitting looks like zoning out during moments of quality time, DeSeta said.
If one partner scrolls on a phone while watching a movie together, the device can become "the third member of the relationship," signaling where that partner’s attention lies, the expert cautioned.
"When you're on your phone, you're just actually saying, ‘I'm choosing to do this versus spending this quality time with you,’" an expert said. (iStock)
"When you're on your phone, you're actually saying, ‘I'm choosing to do this versus spending quality time with you,'" she added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In addition to paying attention during one-on-one activities, the act of asking personal questions — as simple as "how was your day?" — can also help to restore a connection, DeSeta said.
Instead of leading with a complaint about the relationship, Sexton suggested using a positive approach.
For example, instead of saying, "We never spend time with each other anymore," try calling back a positive memory and suggest recreating it.
Communicating positively is more likely to receive a positive response, experts advise. (iStock)

"Focusing on what we need to work on is harder than focusing on what it is that we really like about this person, what drew us to them to begin with," he said. "Chances are, they might feel far away from who they were at the beginning of the relationship.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"And maybe our job in a relationship is to try to remind each other of the 'you' and the 'me' before we became the 'we.'"
Making an active effort to flirt with a partner can boost your mood while signaling continued romantic interest, according to DeSeta.
"Let your partner know that you are there to earn them every day," she said, emphasizing the importance of continuing to learn about and pursue a partner throughout the relationship.
The relationship expert emphasized the importance of consistently "learning and earning" your partner. (iStock)

"Let them know in the most subtle ways every single day that you care about them, that you're thinking about them. And if you do that, you kind of break this cycle of the quiet quitting, and, eventually, it starts coming back to you."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Sexton reminded couples that their time together is limited, so illness or tragedy should not be the catalyst for renewed effort.

"Every single person in your life is not permanently gifted to you. They're loaned," he said. "There’s a finite number of times that you're going to be with this person, see this person, tell this person that you love them."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Scientists discover new tick-borne virus after testing thousands of patients with mysterious illnesses
summary: The Asian longhorned tick nairovirus caused flu-like illness and thrombocytopenia in over 10% of tick-bitten patients studied in a China lab.
story: Dr. Sharon Nachman, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Stony Brook Children’s Hospital in New York, shares what to know about the newly discovered Asian longhorned tick nairovirus.
Scientists in China have identified a previously unknown tick-borne virus that can cause flu-like illness, fatigue and gastrointestinal symptoms, according to a new study.

The newly discovered virus, the Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), which is part of the orthonairovirus group, has also been found to cause thrombocytopenia (reduced blood platelet counts) and laboratory evidence of liver-cell injury or inflammation.

Since 2009, Chinese researchers have been tracking patients with unusual illnesses, including severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), according to Dr. Sharon Nachman, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Stony Brook Children’s Hospital in New York.
NO CURE, NO VACCINE: EXPERTS WARN OF RARE BOURBON VIRUS AFTER FIRST NY CASE
"Thrombocytopenia is low platelet count, so those patients bled, and it had about a 30% mortality, which is quite high," she told Fox News Digital. "So, they kept following those patients."
Many of the cases were linked to Dabie bandavirus (DBV), a tick-borne hemorrhagic fever, but it was not the most common virus.

The newly discovered virus, the Asian longhorned tick nairovirus, which is part of the orthonairovirus group, has also been found to cause thrombocytopenia (reduced blood platelet counts) and laboratory evidence of liver-cell injury or inflammation. (Getty Images)
After extensive testing of blood samples and viral fragments, researchers identified the new virus, ALTNV, which is genetically distinct from DBV.
Researchers from the State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity in Beijing identified the virus in 10.4% of 3,163 patients who had been bitten by ticks.
HANTAVIRUS IN THE US: WHERE THE RARE, SOMETIMES DEADLY DISEASE HAS BEEN FOUND
Patients who had both ALTNV and DBV were more likely to have respiratory issues and kidney complications. Seven (18.4%) of these patients died during the course of the study.

"The cocirculation of ALTNV and DBV in the same areas, coupled with their shared tick vector, underscores the need for improved differential diagnosis between infections with these viruses in regions where SFTS is endemic," the authors concluded.
Because tick-borne viral symptoms can overlap with many infections, a doctor emphasized the importance of identifying the specific virus. (iStock)
The findings were published this week in the New England Journal of Medicine.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The big picture is that ticks carry lots of viruses," Nachman said. "We're getting smarter at identifying those viruses. And when one blood sample is negative, it's important to say, 'Maybe there was a new virus there, and let's look for it.'"
Symptoms and treatment
Illness from ALTNV can initially resemble the flu, causing fever, muscle aches, fatigue and sometimes respiratory symptoms.

Although an ALTNV infection can cause low platelet counts, the study did not link the virus alone to severe bleeding or deaths. The fatal cases involved patients who were also infected with DBV, which causes severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome.
Illness from ALTNV can initially resemble the flu, causing fever, muscle aches, fatigue and sometimes respiratory symptoms. (iStock)
Because tick-borne viral symptoms can overlap with many infections, Nachman emphasized the importance of identifying the specific virus.
"Effective antivirals exist for flu, but not for many tick-borne viruses, including the newly identified one," she said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

For most patients, supportive care is given to help manage symptoms, "but it's also about being smart and not giving patients the wrong medication," Nachman noted. "And we certainly don't want to use antibiotics because those only work for bacteria, not for viruses."
Preventing tick bites
Nachman shared the best practices she recommends to families looking to avoid tick bites.
"Wear the right clothing, meaning long pants, tucking them into your socks, and use tick repellents on your skin if you're an adult or on your clothing if you're a young child," she advised.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
It’s also important to be on the lookout for ticks on the skin.

"The longer the tick is on your skin, the more it's engorged, the more it’s likely to pass an infection to you," Nachman said. "So, removing them after you've gone hiking or walking on the beach will be really important."
People who are bitten by ticks should remove them as soon as possible. (iStock)
While the Asian longhorn tick is not yet seen in the U.S., Nachman noted there are "lots and lots of other ticks, and those ticks carry other diseases."
"I don't want to say one tick is worse than another tick. It's rather all about the diseases they carry and who you are," she said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"So, if you're a healthy adult, and you get babesiosis, you often get better without any medications. But if you're an immune-compromised adult, you're going to be quite sick.
"It’s not really about the ticks. It’s about the patient. Who are you? What's your underlying illness if you have any? How old are you, and how healthy are you?"
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Common cholesterol drug linked to lower dementia risk when started early
summary: A massive study found that starting statins within a year of a type 2 diabetes diagnosis was linked to a 15% lower risk of dementia over a decade.
story: A geriatrician explains why starting statins soon after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis may be linked to lower dementia risk, particularly vascular dementia, while stressing that a recent study does not prove causation.
Starting statin therapy shortly after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis may not only protect the heart — it may also be linked to a lower dementia risk.

A large study presented at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Munich on Aug. 30 found that adults who began taking a statin within one year of their type 2 diabetes diagnosis had a 15% lower relative risk of developing dementia over 10 years compared to those who did not take the medication within five years.
Even for those who delayed starting a statin for one to five years, there was still a 10% lower relative risk, according to the findings, which were published in The Lancet Regional Health – Europe.
3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS
A statin is a prescription medication that lowers "bad" LDL cholesterol and helps reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke.

Researchers conducted the study by tracking health data from 132,585 patients in Denmark who were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2006 and 2019 and had no prior history of statin use or dementia.
A statin is a prescription medication that lowers "bad" LDL cholesterol and helps reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke. (iStock)
During a median follow-up of 7.1 years, the team analyzed how the timing of statin treatment impacted overall dementia rates.

Dr. Liron Sinvani, a geriatrician and director for research and innovation at the Northwell Institute for Healthy Aging in New York, said this was a "well-designed, large-scale observational study that adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that statins may help protect brain health."
GAME-CHANGING CHOLESTEROL PILL WINS FDA APPROVAL AFTER CUTTING LDL NEARLY 60%
She noted that while a 15% reduction is a modest improvement, it remains "very significant."
People with type 2 diabetes have an increased risk of cognitive decline and heart disease, consistent with previous research.

Starting a statin within one year of a type 2 diabetes diagnosis was associated with a 15% lower relative risk of developing dementia over 10 years, while delaying treatment reduced the benefit to 10%. (iStock)
Although guidelines generally recommend statins for many adults ages 40 to 75 with diabetes, statin treatment is not always started soon after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis.

The study also examined whether the timing of treatment was linked to dementia risk. People who started statins within a year of their diagnosis had a lower risk than those who did not begin treatment.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"The message here is that maybe waiting is actually not the right approach," Sinvani said, supporting earlier consideration of statin therapy in routine diabetes care.
The expert said she found the results "especially compelling" because the benefit was driven by a lower risk of vascular dementia rather than Alzheimer's disease.
"The message here is that maybe waiting is actually not the right approach."

"And that makes biological sense, because we know statins lower cholesterol, reduces inflammation and protects blood vessels," she added, pointing out that these same mechanisms prevent vascular damage to the brain.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Statin therapy should be viewed as one piece of a broader health strategy alongside exercising regularly, adhering to a healthy diet and staying socially connected, according to the expert.
Because this was an observational study rather than a randomized controlled trial, the findings show a strong association but do not prove a direct causal link. (iStock)
Almost half of dementia cases may be preventable or delayable by addressing modifiable risk factors, according to the Lancet Commission.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The study did have limitations. Because it was observational rather than a randomized clinical trial, the researchers could not definitively state that statins directly prevent dementia.
As Sinvani cautioned, "This is not proof that statins prevent dementia, but I think it's an important step in this literature."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The doctor encouraged people with type 2 diabetes who are not taking a statin to ask their doctor whether the medication is appropriate for them."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Trump administration proposes ending 60-day grace period after job loss for H-1B, other visa holders
summary: USCIS and DHS propose eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders who lose their jobs, requiring foreign workers to leave immediately.
story: A federal judge in Boston ruled against the Trump administration's $100,000 fee for H-1B visas, deeming it an unauthorized tax. The fee, which was significantly increased from a typical $2,000 to $5,000, aimed to prioritize U.S. citizens in the workforce. The administration is appealing the decision.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) are preparing to propose a rule that would eliminate an existing grace period for visa holders who can't find a job, according to an unpublished document posted to the Federal Register.

Under current immigration laws, holders of certain visas, particularly H-1B visas, which are non-immigration visas that allow employers to sponsor skilled workers with Bachelor's degrees or higher, get a 60-day grace period to find a new job if they lose the employment tied to their visa.
The new rule proposal would eliminate that grace period, according to the document.
FEDERAL JUDGE STRIKES DOWN TRUMP’S $100K H-1B VISA FEE, RULING IT AN UNCONSTITUTIONAL TAX

"This proposal restores a direct relationship between an alien’s nonimmigrant status and the specific employment or activity that formed the basis of his or her admission or grant of status in the United States and reduces administrative burden," the document reads.

People wait inside a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services office. The Trump administration is preparing to propose a new rule rescinding the 60-day grace period allotted to non-immigrant visa holders with visas tied to employment if they no longer work at the place of employment tied to their visa. (John Moore/Getty Images)
A noncitizen would have to immediately leave the U.S. if no longer working for an employer linked to a visa status if the rule were to be implemented.
US STATE DEPARTMENT HAS YANKED MORE THAN 175K VISAS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SO FAR

"DHS believes that restoring the expectation that aliens depart the United States upon cessation of the employment or activity upon which the alien’s status was based, would better promote program integrity and be more consistent with statutory purpose," the rule proposal reads.

The agency also claimed that eliminating the grace period would greatly reduce administrative burden "as the process of determining when the up to 60-day grace period may apply, reviewing the information submitted, and determining whether to shorten or eliminate the grace period may be time consuming and complex for the agency and confusing or unpredictable for the petitioner, alien and the alien’s dependents."
AMERICA’S BROKEN LEGAL IMMIGRATION SYSTEM IS REPLACING US WORKERS BY DESIGN

Before 2017, the document states, there was no 60-day grace period. But in 2016, DHS established the grace period in a rule that came into effec Jan. 17, 2017, three days before President Donald Trump first took office.

President Donald Trump signed two executive orders Sept. 19, 2025, establishing the Trump Gold Card and introducing a $100,000 fee for H-1B visas. The Trump Gold Card is a visa program that allows foreign nationals permanent residency and a pathway to U.S. citizenship for a $1 million investment in the United States. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
DHS also wrote that the rule's elimination would favor U.S. workers because employers who previously filled jobs with foreign workers would have less foreign-born labor to choose from.

"DHS assumes that almost all these entities would offer the same jobs to equally qualified U.S. workers, go through the I-129 petition process to sponsor nonimmigrant workers, or reassign the work to other current employees. DHS acknowledges that some of these petitioners may incur a temporary loss of productivity due to labor turnover," the rule proposal reads.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks during a news conference at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The unpublished rule is scheduled to publish Friday, Sept. 11, 2026, according to the Federal Register. It will then be subject to a two-month period of public comment before becoming law.
Fox News Digital contacted DHS and the White House for further comment.

title: Outgoing Rep Chip Roy says the GOP has already 'delivered significantly,' but must 'finish the job'
summary: Outgoing House Republican Chip Roy of Texas said that while Republicans have "delivered significantly," they still must "finish the job."
story: During an interview with Fox News Digital on Sept. 9, 2026, outgoing Rep. Chip Roy of Texas gave his analysis of the GOP ahead of the midterm elections.

Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas — who lost the Lone Star State GOP attorney general primary runoff in May and will depart the U.S. House of Representatives when his current term expires — said Republicans have "delivered significantly" but "need to finish the job."

"Well, we've done so much that frankly, it kinda gets lost in a lot of the noise," Roy told Fox News Digital during an interview on Wednesday, pointing to issues such as tax provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed by President Donald Trump last year.
The Texan pointed to the nation's border as the "biggest example" of Republicans' achievements, saying that "we've literally shut down the flow across the border" through enforcing the law.

He also pointed to the passage of the "Laken Riley Act," a measure named after the 22-year-old woman murdered in 2024 by Jose Ibarra, a man who, according to a 2024 statement by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), had previously been "arrested by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP)" after illegally entering the U.S., but was "paroled and released for further processing."
Roy said Republicans "need to unite with a singular vision about where we wanna take the country if we wanna be... rewarded in November... and then frankly looking ahead to 2028."
TEXAS MAGA BATTLE ENDS WITH MIDDLETON VICTORY AS CHIP ROY FALLS SHORT IN AG RACE
Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, talks with reporters outside the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on July 16, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
"Have we done everything we should do? No," Roy said, claiming that "Congress has fallen short" regarding some of what they "should do."
But he still believes the GOP could potentially retain their majorities in both congressional chambers during the midterms.
"I think right now Republicans are staring at barely holding onto the Senate and slightly losing the House, but I still think we can win the House," he said.

The House is now only scheduled to work for several days next week before a lengthy break until after the Nov. 3 elections. Roy indicated that Republicans should get back to work after the midterms "to do our part to finish the job."

"Obviously I'm not campaigning. So I'm thinking a lot about what we could do with another reconciliation package or what we might be able to do in the lame duck or in January, when I'm not in office," he noted.
FENTANYL DEATHS COULD NOW COST DRUG DEALERS THEIR LIVES UNDER NEW GOP PROPOSAL

In a Sunday post on X, Roy wrote, "Government does not fund anything. It takes money from people under force of law and distributes it to other people very inefficiently and usually tyrannically. Child care is unaffordable because government (& corporate cronyism) has made life unaffordable. Stay out."

The New York Times reported last week that the Trump administration is moving to enable some married people with a stay-at-home parent situation to receive a childcare subsidy from a federal program that was meant to help parents who work.

The proposal "creates the option for a new category of care, parent-based child care, that will allow one married parent to receive C.C.D.F. [Child Care and Development Fund] assistance to care for their own child, while a spouse works at least 35 hours per week," the outlet reported, citing a draft document.

Roy said during the interview on Wednesday, "I just don't believe that it's good for the human soul to have the government coming in with a grant and making you dependent on government. I just don't philosophically think that that's freedom. I think freedom, non-dependence, independence is what makes America great."

A White House official said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital on Thursday that the Trump administration "has not announced any such proposal. Until and unless it does, any discussion about potential policies is baseless speculation."
CHIP ROY FIELDS PROPOSAL TO BLOCK PAY AND POWER FOR LONGTIME LAWMAKERS
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

As for whether he has any interest in running for office again, Roy said the matter is "up to God" and to Texans, adding that he has "a calling for service" and his current focus is on attempting to "solve the big problems for" Americans.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Republican sounds alarm on rising Dem star: 'This guy’s going to be a problem'
summary: Mike Collins claims Jon Ossoff is using the Georgia Senate race as a Democratic Party springboard for a 2028 presidential run as a DSA candidate.
story: Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., told Fox News Digital that he believed Sen. Jon Ossoff’s bid for re-election in Georgia was the first step on his way to a 2028 presidential bid, and that he was the only one who could stop the Democratic star’s rise.

DALLAS — There’s a rising star in the Democratic Party that is generating buzz for a possible presidential run, but one Republican argues he’s the only thing standing in the way of a future "DSA candidate" in 2028.

Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., is running to unseat Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., in one of the most closely watched contests of this midterm election cycle. Ossoff has sought to nationalize their battle, focusing more on President Donald Trump and leaning into viral clips on social media to sell his message.

But Collins told Fox News Digital during the GOP’s midterm convention that Ossoff’s intentions extended beyond a second term representing the Peach State. Instead, Collins charged that Ossoff is eyeing the White House and using this cycle as a springboard to get there.
TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATE SURVIVES GRUELING RUNOFF, ADVANCES TO HIGH-STAKES SENATE RACE
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks to members of the media during the opening of the Democratic Party of Georgia's South DeKalb Field Office on May 23, 2026. (Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"This guy is nothing but a trust fund kid who's never had a real job in his life," Collins said. "And at the end of the day, and I think the whole puzzle has been put together now, you can put the pieces of this thing so easy."

"He caters to that far-left base, and at the end of the day, we've got to stop him in Georgia," he continued. "If we don't stop him in Georgia, this guy's going to be a problem for the entire country in 2028."

Those puzzle pieces were scattered throughout his voting record, which Collins said aligned over 90% of the time with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., through his support of progressives, like former Maine Senate Democratic nominee Graham Platner and Michigan Senate Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, and because the bulk of his campaign donations are from out-of-state.
'JESUS WAS A RADICAL': PROGRESSIVES INVOKE CHRIST TO SELL LEFT-WING AGENDA ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL
Collins contended that the final piece was when the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) opened their first permanent field office in Atlanta last month. The organization has not endorsed Ossoff.
"That just tells you, yes, Jon Ossoff is really running for president," Collins said. "He's going to be the DSA candidate. He uses Georgia as a platform to raise money."
Ossoff’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
OBAMA STRATEGIST TURNS ON RISING DEM STAR OVER VIRAL TRUMP ATTACK: 'GRATUITOUS AND UNNECESSARY'
Republican Senate candidate Rep. Mike Collins speaks to supporters at a primary night event on May 19, 2026, in Jackson, Georgia. (Jason Allen/Getty Images)

He has previously thrown cold water on the notion that he was chasing the White House and told MSNOW last month, "I have zero interest in running for president in 2028, and, frankly, zero interest in the 2028 fantasy football right now."

The first-term senator is considered one of the most vulnerable incumbents on the Democrats’ Senate map this cycle, running in a state that Trump won in 2024 over former Vice President Kamala Harris by nearly three points.

Still, he has gained national attention over the summer for his speeches on the campaign trail, particularly when he needled Trump in a viral social media clip bringing into question his relationship with his executive assistant, Natalie Harp.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"He doesn't want to do the job," Ossoff said. "He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar."

That remark stoked a news cycle and earned him accolades from the likes of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who noted that Ossoff was one of the top communicators on the trail when it came to targeting Trump.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Zohran Mamdani urged to skip New York City's 9/11 memorial: 'Vile antisemite'
summary: Rep. Mike Lawler demands Zohran Mamdani skip the 9/11 memorial, citing the NYC mayor's ties to terror sympathizers and antisemitic rhetoric.
story: Reps. Mike Lawler and August Pfluger spoke with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.
DALLAS – A House Republican representing the New York City suburbs is calling on Mayor Zohran Mamdani to skip the Sept. 11 memorial in downtown Manhattan.

"From my vantage point, I don't think he should be there, and I think most New Yorkers agree that he should not be there," Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., told Fox News and Fox News Digital. "Certainly, the 9/11 families and the first responders believe he should not be there."

Political rancor is threatening to cast a long shadow over this year's Sept. 11 remembrance events, marking 25 years since the tragedy that rocked the United States. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's past rhetoric and links to terror sympathizers are spurring intense backlash ahead of the city's events memorializing the World Trade Center attacks, with Republicans and people whose lives were changed by the attacks demanding he not show his face.
MAMDANI FACES GROWING 9/11 BACKLASH AS OLD POST RESURFACES AHEAD OF GROUND ZERO CEREMONY: 'IS THIS REAL?'
Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks to the media regarding the attempted bombing at a right-wing protest in front of Gracie Mansion on March 8, 2026, in New York City. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

"I think Mayor Mamdani has proven himself to be a vile antisemite. I think he has associated with people who believe America deserved 9/11, and it's not just Hasan Piker. If you go look at many of the people that support his administration, they agree with that rhetoric. They agree with that philosophy," Lawler said.
An online petition led by family members of people killed on Sept. 11 — signed by over 100,000 people — has called on Mamdani to skip the memorial.
9/11 FAMILIES PUSH TO BAN MAMDANI FROM 25TH ANNIVERSARY REMEMBRANCE OVER 'HOSTILE' RECORD

"Mr. Mamdani has praised Brooklyn Imam Siraj Wahhaj, who has been linked to radical Islam, was named as an alleged co-conspirator in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, and served as a character witness for the 'Blind Sheikh,' who was convicted in 1995 of plotting terror attacks against the United States," the petition said. "Mr. Mamdani has endorsed candidates such as Aber Kawas, who described 9/11 as an attack 'a couple of people did in the context of U.S. capitalism, racism, white supremacy, and Islamophobia,' and who also expressed sympathy for Ahmed Ferhani, who pleaded guilty to plotting to blow up a Manhattan synagogue."

Mamdani and other socialist candidates' association with far-left activist Hasan Piker has also seen intense scrutiny over Piker's past comments that the United States "deserved" the attacks, remarks that he promptly walked back at the time but continue to haunt him and his political circle. Mamdani himself has also condemned the comment.
A firefighter walks through the rubble of the World Trade Center as an American flag hangs from a traffic light post on Sept. 11, 2001, in New York. (Doug Kanter/AFP via Getty Images)

Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital that Mamdani should not attend Sept. 11 memorial events "until he can... actually call out terror groups around the world for what they want to do to this country, and that includes Hamas."
Hamas was not responsible for the Sept. 11 attacks, for which al Qaeda took credit, but Hamas has recently been front-and-center for perpetuating the Oct. 7, 2023, terror attack in Israel.

"These people are really a cancer to the freedoms that we fought for, and they do not represent the American values that our founders set up and that we have had for 250 years," Pfluger said of Mamdani and his allies.
MAMDANI DROPS MASSIVE 9/11 RECORDS TROVE AS OLD CLAIMS ABOUT GROUND ZERO COME UNDER FIRE

Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., speaks with local law enforcement about the rise of antisemitism in New York City during a campaign endorsement event at Haverstraw Elks Lodge No. 877 in Haverstraw, New York. (Kyle Mazza/CNP)
Both he and Lawler spoke with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the 2026 GOP midterm convention in Dallas.

Mamdani's office recently launched an online portal allowing city residents to access roughly 170,000 pages of local government records on Sept. 11, which appear to show city officials misled the public about air quality following the attacks.

Fox News Digital reached out to the New York City mayor's office for comment.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: For 'horrible moment,' Bush White House thought US military shot down Flight 93
summary: Condoleezza Rice recalled the tense moment she and George W. Bush believed Flight 93 had been shot down while coordinating responses in a bunker.
story: Former President George W. Bush recounted the "horrible moment" on 9/11 where the White House thought the U.S. military had shot down Flight 93.
Former President George W. Bush discussed his memories of 9/11 with his former secretary of state, Condoleezza Rice, ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks this week.

Bush and Rice said they both remember sitting in a bunker in the hours after the attacks, coordinating the U.S. domestic response. Rice recounted how they were working to ground civilian flights across the country and said at one point they thought the U.S. military had shot down United Airlines Flight 93.

"I do want to say one thing to Gen. [Daniel] Caine, because something in what you said, our paths crossed in a strange way. So you mentioned that you heard that as the president, you have to understand the hard decisions that this man had to make, just like that. And one of them was what would happen if a plane was not properly identifying itself, because every plane had become a missile," Rice said.
FLIGHT 93 HERO'S DAD WARNS 'ENEMIES FROM WITHIN' AIM TO DESTROY AMERICA AT THE BALLOT BOX
President George W. Bush discusses creating the Department of Homeland Security following 9/11. (Getty Images)

"And so we were trying to land, I remember Norm Mineta, the transportation secretary, trying to land planes on a legal pad, yellow pad, legal pad. But you'd given the order through the vice president that should a plane not squawk properly, it should be shot down. Gen. Caine, we thought initially, standing in that bunker, that Flight 93 had been shot down," she continued.
9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD'
"Yeah, I thought it was the same thing," Bush said.
Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice joins "Special Report" for an interview on June 26, 2025. (Fox News/Special Report)

"And there was this horrible moment where the vice president kept trying to get confirmation as to what had happened. And for about 10 minutes we thought we'd shot down a civilian aircraft. And that always, to me, represented just how hard the decisions were that you had to take under a lot of pressure," Rice said.
The event, called, "A Legacy of Service: America at the 25th Anniversary of 9/11," saw Bush host many members of his 2001 administration in Texas.

President George W. Bush, first lady Laura Bush, Vice President Dick Cheney and his wife Lynne Cheney participate in a moment of silence on the south lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., Sept. 11, 2005, to honor the fourth anniversary of the terrorist attacks. (Brooks Kraft LLC/Corbis via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

As part of the 25th anniversary commemoration, Bush painted 16 works of art that "reflect on the courage, sacrifice, and resilience that emerged from one of the most defining moments in American history," that will be displayed at Freedom Hall at the Bush Museum through September.
Fox News' Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: 9/11 hero’s memory preserved through massive effort to ‘do good’ for vets, first responders: ‘His legacy’
summary: Tunnel to Towers' 343 Homes Initiative honors Stephen Siller and the 9/11 firefighters with mortgage-free homes for fallen first responders' families.
story: Tunnel to Towers Foundation CEO Frank Siller shares the inspiration behind his new memoir, 'Let Us Do Good.' Siller reflects on the sacrifice of his FDNY firefighter brother, Stephen Siller, and how their parents' lessons of service guided their family's mission.

On one of the darkest days in America’s history, New York City firefighter Stephen Siller strapped on his gear and ran through the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel to the collapsing Twin Towers, ultimately giving his life to save those caught in the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. Two and a half decades later, Tunnel to Towers, founded by Siller’s family, has continued his legacy through its commitment to "do good" for veterans and first responders and their families across the country.

Since its founding, inspired by Siller and his favorite quote, "While we have time, let us do good," Tunnel to Towers has provided more than 1,700 mortgage-free homes to the families of fallen service members and first responders, as well as to disabled veterans and first responders. The organization has also delivered housing assistance and support services to more than 20,000 homeless veterans and holds hundreds of events nationwide to honor America’s heroes and preserve the memory of those who lost their lives for future generations.

Tunnel to Towers CEO Frank Siller, the brother of the 34-year-old firefighter who gave his life on Sept. 11, previously warned in 2020 that America was "very close to forgetting the impact 9/11 had on our nation." Now, with anti-American sentiment on the rise and some online commentators belittling the Sept. 11 attacks or even justifying them, many worry the legacy of those who lost their lives, including the 343 members of the New York City Fire Department who made the ultimate sacrifice, will be forgotten.
Siller, however, has vowed that "Tunnel to Towers will never let that happen."
9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS
The Tunnel to Towers Foundation was started in honor of  FDNY firefighter Stephen Siller, who died responding to the attacks. (Tunnel to Towers Foundation)

The Tunnel to Towers 9/11 Institute has helped to educate students from kindergarten through 12th grade on the "extraordinary heroism and goodness of everyday people" on Sept. 11, "while demonstrating the strength and resilience of America’s spirit." Its mobile 9/11 exhibit has traveled to nearly all 50 states as well as Canada.

This year, Tunnel to Towers launched its "Steel Across America" display, in which a 16,000-pound steel beam pulled from the wreckage of the World Trade Center traveled more than 10,500 miles to 35 stops across 21 states and the District of Columbia, culminating in New York City.
NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS

Frank Siller, CEO of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, stands near a piece of World Trade Center steel that will be featured during the foundation's effort to honor and remember the victims of the 9/11 attacks as the 25th anniversary approaches. (Courtesy: Tunnel to Towers Foundation)

To mark the 25th anniversary, Tunnel to Towers also launched its 343 Homes Initiative this year to honor the 343 New York firefighters who died on Sept. 11. According to the group, this initiative will deliver 343 mortgage-free homes to the families of fallen service members and fallen first responders as well as to catastrophically injured service members across the country.

This initiative builds on Tunnel to Towers' "In the Line of Duty Programs," which have provided more than 1,700 mortgage-free homes to the families of fallen service members and first responders, as well as to catastrophically injured veterans and first responders. More than 220 of those homes have been custom "Smart Homes," modified to be fully accessible to catastrophically injured veterans and first responders.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

A firefighter walks through the rubble of the twin towers of the World Trade Center as an American flag hangs from a traffic light post on September 11, 2001, in New York. (DOUG KANTER/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In a recent Fox News opinion piece, Siller put it simply: "Stephen’s life and heroic death serve as a reminder to us all to live life to the fullest and to spend our time here on earth doing good—this is his legacy."
Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Supreme Court again blocks Missouri from using Trump-backed congressional maps
summary: The Supreme Court blocked Missouri's Republican-backed congressional map for a second time as a contempt hearing looms for Denny Hoskins this week.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
The Supreme Court turned back another effort to use Missouri congressional maps supported by President Donald Trump.
"The application for stay presented to Justice [Brett] Kavanaugh and by him referred to the Court is granted," Thursday's ruling read.
The court's brief order was unsigned and gave no explanation, as is common when the justices handle emergency matters. No justice publicly dissented from the decision.
While the Missouri Supreme Court’s ruling paved the way for use of the old maps, the state’s Aug. 4 primary was already held under the new maps.
MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP
Facade of the Supreme Court. (Valerie Plesch/picture alliance via Getty Images)

"After repeated legal victories defending Missouri’s fair and lawful map, this 11th-hour ruling pulls the rug out from under voters who already cast their primary ballots," RNC Election Integrity Communications Director Ally Triolo wrote in a statement. "Changing the rules mid-election is reckless and wrong."

The court’s decision came after U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark ordered Missouri to use the new map, conflicting with a unanimous ruling by the Missouri Supreme Court that said the districts had not legally taken effect and that the state’s older map should be used unless voters approve the changes.
Following the U.S. Supreme Court's stay, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said his office is directing local election authorities to use the 2022 congressional map.
MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING

"Following the United States Supreme Court's stay, the only governing court order in effect is from the Missouri Supreme Court. In accordance with that order, my Office is directing local election authorities to use the 2022 congressional map," Hoskins said in a statement.
Republican state officials have argued it would violate voters' federal rights to switch districts before the general election.

The Missouri Supreme Court also ordered Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to appear at a contempt hearing Thursday, after he instructed local election officials to use the new districts. A federal judge declined to halt that hearing before the Supreme Court issued its order.

The redrawn map was approved by Missouri Republicans in 2025. It dismantles the Kansas City-based 5th Congressional District held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo., by shifting portions of the seat into neighboring districts and extending the remainder into heavily Republican areas.
The way the map was designed gave Republicans a strong chance of winning seven of Missouri’s eight House seats, compared with the current six-to-two Republican advantage.

Opponents of the map, including the group People Not Politicians, submitted hundreds of thousands of petition signatures seeking a statewide referendum. The Missouri Supreme Court ordered that referendum to appear on the November ballot, meaning voters will decide whether the redrawn map can be used in future elections.

The Missouri Supreme Court has ordered Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to appear at a contempt hearing Thursday, after he instructed local election officials to use the new districts. A federal judge declined to halt that hearing before the Supreme Court issued its order. (Nick Wagner/The Kansas City Star/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Republicans currently hold a 219-214 majority in the House, including one independent who caucuses with the GOP.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Mamdani, touting RI socialist’s victory, answers question of ‘What is the Democratic Party?’
summary: David Morales' rent control platform powered his upset of Providence's incumbent mayor, and Zohran Mamdani says it signals a national shift.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani says Rhode Island State Rep. David Morales’ Providence mayoral primary victory as evidence voters support rent stabilization policies.

Democratic socialist David Morales’ victory in Rhode Island's mayoral primary Wednesday night got the attention of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who says it is evidence of where the party as a whole is headed as November's midterm elections draw near.

"I think it comes back to what I’ve said before, which is what is the Democratic Party, if not its voters?" Mamdani asked during a Thursday morning news conference on the first day of school in his city.

"We’re seeing that the voters across this country are eager for not only a change, but also for a vision of something that we are fighting for," Mamdani added. "And, you know, I've spoken a lot about childcare this morning. I've often couched it as the second driver of the cost of living crisis. The first driver is housing."
MAMDANI CLAIMS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS CAN WIN ‘ANYWHERE’ AS DEMOCRATS FEUD OVER PARTY’S FUTURE
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has promised to enact a four-year rent freeze on rent-stabilized units in New York City. (Yuki Iwamura-Pool/Getty Images)

Mamdani was hailing a new free education program for 2,000 needy families, as Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul unveiled a pledge for $425 million more in next year’s state budget to expand early childhood programs, including services for families with disabilities.

At the end of Thursday's news conference, Mamdani responded to a question about Morales, a 27-year-old state representative and Democratic socialist who defeated one-term Providence Mayor Brett Smiley, 47, in the Democratic primary.

Republicans hold no seats on the Providence City Council, and Democrats make up a majority of registered voters in the city. Former Vice President Kamala Harris beat President Donald Trump in the city by 51 points in 2024.
Mamdani hailed Morales’ campaign for rent stabilization and affordability in the deep-blue city.
MAMDANI RIPPED OVER RECORD-HIGH NYC RENTS WITH CRITICS POINTING TO POLICY THEY SAY IS FUELING CRISIS

title: Bush revives ‘Islam is peace’ message with fresh focus on post-9/11 mosque visit
summary: George W. Bush recalled visiting a mosque six days after 9/11, declaring "Islam is peace" to protect Muslim Americans facing harassment across the country.
story: George W. Bush recalled visiting a mosque six days after 9/11, declaring "Islam is peace" to protect Muslim Americans facing harassment in the wake of the attacks.

DALLAS – As the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches, former President George W. Bush reflected on his decision to visit a mosque six days after the attacks, saying he wanted Muslim Americans to know they were not to blame for the terrorism.

"This decision, shortly thereafter, was to go to a mosque," Bush said on Wednesday evening. "I did so because I was deeply concerned about stories of women in coverings being harassed at shopping centers, particularly in Michigan."

Bush revisited his 9/11 response during a conversation with former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice at "A Legacy of Service: America at the 25th Anniversary of 9/11," held at his presidential center in Dallas.

The mosque visit became a prominent part of Bush’s response to the attacks as he sought to distinguish Islam and Muslim Americans from the terrorists responsible for 9/11. Six days after the attacks, Bush visited the Islamic Center of Washington, where he declared, "Islam is peace."
REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS
President George W. Bush speaks during the rededication ceremony of the Islamic Center on June 27, 2007, in Washington, D.C.

"It became clear to me that if this was an ideological struggle, which is what I viewed it as, and we forego one of the most important parts of our ideology, which is the freedom to worship the way you want to worship," said Bush.

"I want you to talk about a couple of those events. You talked about going to the Islamic Center and trying to make sure that our Muslim American citizens knew that we didn't blame them for what had happened," said Rice.
9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS
Former President Bush and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice sat down to reflect on the legacy and meaning of 9/11. (Fox News Digital)
"I also made it clear that Islam was a religion of peace, not a religion of war, and that these people subverted their religion," Bush added.
Bush visited the Islamic Center of Washington on Sept. 17, where he sought to draw a sharp distinction between Islam and the terrorists responsible for killing nearly 3,000 Americans.

He met with Muslim leaders and specifically raised concerns about Muslim women who wore head coverings, saying he had been told some were afraid to leave their homes or go shopping because they feared being intimidated.
"That should not and that will not stand in America," he said in 2001.
ABDUL EL-SAYED HITS BACK AT ISRAEL QUESTIONS, SUGGESTS HIS NAME AND FAITH ARE BEHIND PRESS SCRUTINY
President George W. Bush meets with Islamic community and religious leaders during a tour of the Islamic Center of Washington, D.C., Sept. 17, 2001. (Getty Images)

Bush’s remarks come as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches and as the attacks and their aftermath have returned to the political spotlight.

title: Trump dangles $5,000 checks as debt surges — but only if GOP can clear major midterm hurdle
summary: President Donald Trump's $5,000 dividend pledge could cost roughly $1.2 trillion, with JD Vance suggesting wealthy Americans may be excluded.
story: The president is claiming that he will disburse over $1 trillion in payments to citizens if Republicans retain control of Congress.

President Donald Trump vowed to issue Americans a $5,000 "dividend" that could cost the federal government more than $1 trillion — but it's contingent on Republicans retaining control of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections.

Trump made the pledge Wednesday night during his nearly two-hour speech at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas, promising to issue the payment to every adult citizen if the GOP wins both the House and Senate in November.

"Here is my promise: If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000," Trump said.
FOLLOW FOX NEWS DIGITAL’S COVERAGE OF THE GOP’S 2026 MIDTERM CONVENTION
Trump’s proposed $5,000 payments could cost roughly $1.2 trillion, adding to the federal government’s spending and borrowing. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images)

The president's proposal comes as the national debt hovers just north of $40 trillion and the federal government recorded a budget deficit of roughly $1.8 trillion in fiscal year 2025, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
The payments could cost approximately $1.2 trillion, based on the roughly 240 million adult citizens in the United States, potentially adding significantly to the government’s eye-watering borrowing.

It's unclear where the money would come from, but the motivation behind the idea is crystal clear — Trump wants to incentivize voters who are feeling a pocketbook squeeze to keep his party in power so his agenda is not brought to a screeching halt should one of the congressional chambers flip blue in this year's midterms.
Vice President JD Vance suggested after Trump's speech that wealthy Americans could be excluded from the payments, potentially reducing the plan’s overall cost.
"What the president is talking about is fundamentally a dividend for American workers," Vance told Fox News.
He also defended the proposal's funding by pointing to the administration’s tariff revenue.

"We’re taking an extraordinary amount of revenue because the president of the United States is standing up to both foreign companies but also foreign countries who have been taking advantage of America’s workers," Vance said.

Treasury data shows the government collected a record $34.2 billion in customs duties in a single month. Since January, those collections totaled approximately $208.5 billion, still far below the estimated $1.2 trillion cost of Trump’s proposed $5,000 payments.
However, those figures reflect gross tariff collections and do not account for refunds tied to tariffs that were later struck down by the Supreme Court.
The administration has since returned billions of dollars to importers, meaning the amount ultimately available to the government could be lower.

"If you keep us in power and allow us to continue to do these things, then you’re going to share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we are creating in the United States of America," Vance added.
'WE WERE RIGHT': HE TOOK TRUMP'S TARIFFS TO THE SUPREME COURT AND WON
The White House has not provided specific eligibility requirements or a detailed funding proposal.
Trump said the dividend would be similar to a cash distribution from a successful company to its shareholders and indicated that the money would need to be spent in the United States.
President Donald Trump pledged to issue a $5,000 "dividend" to every adult citizen if Republicans win control of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
The proposal would require approval from Congress before any payments could be issued. Trump does not have the unilateral authority to distribute the checks.
Trump has previously floated other direct-payment proposals, including a $2,000 tariff dividend and a plan to return a portion of government savings to taxpayers. Neither proposal has become law.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The president’s latest pledge came as he urged voters to treat the midterm elections as a referendum on his administration.
"If the Republicans win, you win with us," Trump said. "Now all we have to do is win."
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Charlie Kirk continues to inspire Republicans as party rallies for midterm battle: 'Have courage'
summary: Republicans at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas reflect on Charlie Kirk's assassination one year after the Turning Point USA founder was killed at a college event.
story: Republicans in Dallas remembered the legacy of Charlie Kirk during the GOP midterm convention.

DALLAS, Texas – A year after the shocking assassination of conservative titan and Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk, Republicans gathered at the GOP's midterm convention shared the profound ways in which the young leader and family man impacted their lives.

"Charlie Kirk is a wonderful man, and he is very much missed," Marsha Landry of Texas told Fox News Digital during an interview at the American Airlines Center, where the Republican Party is rallying to try to keep control of the House and Senate in November. "He was making a lot of progress in this country, especially among the youth. I know personally some of our children have really started paying attention."
Jacquez Jones, a young convention attendee, said Kirk's legacy lives on.
REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR

Charlie Kirk throws hats to the crowd after arriving at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah, on Sept. 10, 2025. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking at his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

"It's a daily reminder that we have to have courage to go out there and spread the message, not only of just conservatism, but our faith as well," he said. "And so on this anniversary, I look back at not only what Charlie Kirk was able to accomplish, but the things that even in his passing he's still able to do."

On this day last year, Kirk, 31, was speaking at Turning Point's "American Comeback Tour" event at the Utah Valley University (UVU) in Orem, Utah, just after noon, when he was shot in the neck. He was pronounced dead at a local hospital shortly thereafter.

The suspect in the killing, then-22-year-old Tyler Robinson, is accused of firing one shot from a rooftop overlooking the quad where Kirk was speaking. A shocked crowd scattered as Kirk was rushed away from the scene.
Kirk, who was a father, left behind his wife Erika and two young children.
ERIKA KIRK REFLECTS ON FIRST YEAR OF GRIEF AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION IN NYT ESSAY
Conservative activist Charlie Kirk is pictured with his wife Erika Kirk on stage at an event earlier this year in Phoenix. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images)

"I think it's an extremely somber reminder of what we have in this country, that free speech is not free, that somebody died for that right, and Charlie Kirk [was] somebody who was brave enough to go out there on the college campuses and talk about conservatism and prove to the American people and the young generation that the conservative policies still work," Jones said.
Another Republican convention-goer, Mike Hurst of Mississippi, described what he remembers after first hearing the news that Kirk had been killed.

"It was one of the most gut-wrenching feelings I've ever seen, and of course, I went online, I saw the video, and to this day I'm still shocked that that could happen in our country," Hurst said, adding that we need more people like Kirk who encourage civil dialogue instead of political violence.
ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN ALLEGEDLY CONFESSED IN TEXTS, APOLOGIZED AND DESCRIBED MOTIVE, AGENT TESTIFIES

Robinson allegedly fled the rooftop, ditched his rifle in a wooded area across the street from the UVU campus, and fled the scene. A statewide manhunt persisted until the following night at around 10 p.m. when Robinson surrendered to authorities in St. George, Utah, about four hours south of the UVU campus.
The American Airlines Center, as preparations are underway for the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, on September 7, 2026. (Jessica Koscielniak, Reuters)
His parents reportedly convinced him to turn himself in.

Pre-trial proceedings in Robinson's case are ongoing after a protracted battle regarding media access to the courtroom, and motions attempting to remove the death penalty as a possible sentence should Robinson be convicted.

Alex Stone of Missouri said young people are looking for a leader to fill Kirk's shoes, though his memory remains.

"Since Charlie's assassination, people have been lost," he said. "People have been looking for a voice or a leader to lead them in the right direction, and so we need people who are going to stand up and rise up and say, 'this is what is good, this is what is true, this what is beautiful.' And 'this is wrong, and here's what we should do in the face of it.'"
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Democratic socialist backed by Bernie Sanders ousts Providence, Rhode Island mayor
summary: Rhode Island Rep. David Morales, 27, defeated Providence Mayor Brett Smiley by 8 points after campaigning on rent stabilization and housing justice.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani says Rhode Island State Rep. David Morales’ Providence mayoral primary victory as evidence voters support rent stabilization policies.

Rhode Island State Rep. David Morales, a 27-year-old democratic socialist endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., defeated Providence Mayor Brett Smiley in the Democratic primary Wednesday night, ousting the incumbent after one term.
If Morales wins the general election, he will be Providence's youngest mayor in history.

"Few believed that a 27-year-old democratic socialist could ever, few believed that we could ever take on big money, corporate real estate interests and endless attack ads – and we took them on and we won," Morales said in his victory speech, delivered partly in Spanish, after winning by 5 points (52.5%-47.5%).
Smiley, 47, who faced his heaviest media scrutiny over his handling of the Brown University shooting last December, served just one term.
