Morales will face Republican nominee Dave Talan, 77, in November. Republicans hold no seats on the Providence City Council, and Democrats make up a majority of registered voters in the city. Former Vice President Kamala Harris beat President Donald Trump in the city by 51 points in 2024.

"The voters of Providence made their choice, and they chose David Morales as our next mayor in the Democratic primary," Smiley said in his concession speech after calling Morales. "While I’m not happy with that outcome, I’m so happy and proud of the campaign that we ran."

The contest was part of a broader series of Democratic primary battles between progressive challengers and more established incumbents. title: Presidential flip? GOP insider predicts Trump change of mind on key AI policy ahead of midterms
summary: Trump ally Amy Kremer predicts President Donald Trump will shift on AI data centers after hearing from Americans on the midterm campaign trail.
story: Amy Kremer, a Republican National Committee member and chairwoman of "Humans First," is calling on President Donald Trump to reconsider his AI data centers position.

EXCLUSIVE: A GOP insider making the conservative case for regulating artificial intelligence development predicts President Donald Trump’s full-throated support for data center expansion will soon change after he hears from the American people on the midterm campaign trail.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Amy Kremer, a close Trump ally, Republican National Committee member and founder of "Humans First," warned that the voice of the average American is being left out of the ongoing AI data center debate. She believes that is about to change as the president prepares to hit the campaign trail in support of Republicans ahead of the midterms this fall.
Right now, Kremer asserted that Trump is "only hearing one side of the story from big tech."

"He's getting ready to go out on the campaign trail, and I think he's going to hear more from the American people on the data center side of things. And I hope he does," she said, adding, "I know the president, and his heart, and he would not like the way the Americans are being treated."
MAGA BEGINS TO CRACK AS 2026 GOP ROSTER BACKS AWAY FROM TRUMP'S TECH VISION

President Donald Trump has said any governor or local government official should want to welcome the construction of AI data centers. Meanwhile, voices are growing, including within the GOP, in opposition to the current data center development landscape. (Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images; Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Kremer was pivotal in founding the modern Tea Party movement and through the years established several pro-Trump political action committees, including the "Great America PAC," the first and largest grassroots organization founded in 2016 to support then-candidate Trump.

Now, she is the chairwoman of "Humans First," a political group calling for an "America First approach to AI" that it says would keep the U.S. ahead of China while protecting American families, communities and jobs.
She said that while Trump has made it clear that he wants America to lead on AI development, she believes that innovation and safety are "not mutually exclusive."

"I love the president. He has been an amazing president. I know he wants us to lead the world in technology and innovation, and I support him in that," she said, while noting, "There's this narrative out there that [with] innovation, you have to forego safety, and it's just not accurate. It's not true."
TEA PARTY FOUNDER LAUNCHES NATIONWIDE 'DATA CENTER REVOLT' AGAINST AI DATA CENTER EXPANSION

Protestors hold up "Stop data centers" signs, on the day of U.S. President Donald Trump's speech at the General Motors Proving Ground, in Milford, Michigan, U.S. July 27, 2026. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)

As the GOP gathers in Dallas for its first midterm convention, Humans First unveiled a new data center policy outline that it is urging the president and Republicans in Congress and state legislatures to adopt. The plan, obtained exclusively by Fox News Digital, calls for greater local control over data center development and rejects the use of eminent domain for land seizures.

The plan opposes federal and state "efforts to strip communities of that authority," including through a federal data center moratorium, which many opponents of AI development have called for. Instead, the plan calls for local communities to be given the ability to welcome or reject new data center developments through zoning and land-use processes.
Additionally, the plan rejects what it describes as "blank-check tax breaks" and subsidies and states that "any incentives must be transparent and tied to enforceable benefits for the community."

The plan calls for full transparency on data center development, stating that "before approval, communities deserve to know the project's end user, electricity demand, water use, land requirements, infrastructure costs, tax incentives, permanent jobs and environmental impacts."

It also calls for protection for ratepayers so that families and small businesses do not pay higher electric bills. Instead, it states that data centers should pay the full cost of the power generation, transmission, grid upgrades and infrastructure they require.
TRUMP SAYS GOVERNORS, MAYORS SHOULD WELCOME AI DATA CENTERS NATIONWIDE

President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, July 15, 2025. Trump will announce $70 billion in artificial intelligence and energy investments in Pennsylvania on Tuesday, the latest push from the White House to speed up development of the emerging technology. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Two other provisions address some of the most controversial aspects of AI data center development: local water usage and development on farmland, which the plan refers to as a "strategic American resource that should be protected."
The way Kremer put it? She posited that "there are more regulations on a hot dog that you buy on a street corner in New York City than there are on these big tech companies with this technology."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"We are not anti-AI, we're not anti-technology, and we're not anti-data centers," she explained. "What we are is we want the American people to have a seat at the table and a voice in this conversation."

"We can lead on innovation, we absolutely can," she said. "But that doesn't mean that it has to be on the backs of the American taxpayers."
Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: House panel to probe foreign ‘Trojan horses’ as Singham scrutiny widens
summary: House lawmakers will examine alleged foreign malign influence operations, including campaigns tied to China, Cuba and U.S. data centers.
story: Bitcoin Policy Institute research chief details alleged foreign influence targeting US data centers ahead of testimony before the House Foreign Affairs Committee on "Trojan horses" undermining the U.S.

FIRST ON FOX: Congressional scrutiny of foreign influence operations in the United States is widening, with a powerful panel of lawmakers set to hold a hearing next week examining how nonprofits and activist networks serve as potential "Trojan horses" for foreign adversaries.

Fox News Digital has learned the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia has scheduled an open hearing for Tuesday titled "Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America."

"This is a critically important topic right now because the vectors for foreign influence in our public discourse are greater than they've ever been before, in large part because of social media," Sam Lyman, head of research at the Bitcoin Policy Institute and one of the hearing's planned witnesses, told Fox News Digital.

"Social media acts as a gain-of-function for mind viruses that are incubated overseas and oftentimes find their way over to the United States," said Lyman, a former senior advisor and speechwriter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Medea Benjamin (right) and Olivia DiNucci (center) of CodePink protest against the U.S. war in Iran. (Fox News Digital)

The planned hearing, which takes its name from the mythological horse Greek soldiers hid inside of to infiltrate the fortified city of Troy, is expected to include a scrutiny of influence from China and Cuba to the Islamic Republic of Iran and pro-Palestinian groups. It marks an expansion of congressional scrutiny of foreign influence beyond the tax and financial questions already being pursued by the House Ways and Means Committee, which has subpoenaed three nonprofits in a network funded by Neville Roy Singham, an American-born communist tech tycoon now based in Shanghai.
Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation who is scheduled to testify as a witness, told Fox News Digital the threat is real.

"Adversaries and outright enemies of the United States such as China and Cuba, shadowy non-government organizations surreptitiously implanting Islamism – and even friendlier countries such as Mexico, which tries to use its diaspora populations for lobbying – take advantage of the open nature of our society to infiltrate and influence America."
Evidence of foreign influence abounds throughout society, he said.

"They do it in the K-12 educational system that instructs our entire population, the institutions of higher education that produce our leaders, the government agencies that make up our government, the lobbying firms that write far too many of our laws, the museums that exist to transmit our heritage to future generations, etc.," Gonzalez said.

The Senate Judiciary Committee, House Oversight Committee and the House Select Committee on China have also investigated the issue of malign foreign influence. Singham hasn't responded to repeated requests for comment.

The Foreign Affairs Subcommittee, which oversees the State Department's Office of Public Diplomacy, now promises to ask the larger national-security question behind those financial investigations: whether America's open political system and nonprofit sector are being exploited as Trojan horses by foreign governments seeking to influence American politics, public opinion and strategic policy from within. Earlier this year, the Office of Public Diplomacy, led by Undersecretary Sarah Rodgers, issued the subcommittee a report about foreign "vectors" of influence in the U.S.

In March, Fox News Digital published a five-part investigation that mapped 223 transactions totaling $591 million across five continents from 2017 through 2025 through 67 core organizations in the Singham network that act like an inner hub for a constellation of an estimated 2,000 groups worldwide, pushing pro-China, anti-American propaganda, including the communist Party for Socialism and Liberation.

The investigation documented how Singham directly poured $285 million into an activist network of six pro-China, pro-communist nonprofit organizations, starting in 2017 – Breakthrough BT Media Inc., CodePink Women for Peace, Justice and Education Fund Inc., People's Forum Inc., People's Support Foundation Ltd. and Tricontinenental Ltd.

As Fox News Digital first reported in June, the Justice Department is investigating alleged financial crimes connected to Singham and the nonprofit organizations he funded, with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York opening a grand jury investigation into Singham's money. Singham and the nonprofits have denied taking direction from the Chinese government, and neither Singham nor the organizations have been charged with crimes.

Rep. Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., chairs the South and Central Asia subcommittee, while Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif., serves as ranking member. Republican members include Reps. James Moylan of Guam, Jefferson Shreve of Indiana, Thomas Kean Jr. of New Jersey, Scott Perry of Pennsylvania, Tim Burchett of Tennessee, Keith Self of Texas and Michael Baumgartner of Washington. Democratic members include Reps. Ami Bera of California, Kweisi Mfume of Maryland, Pramila Jayapal of Washington, George Latimer of New York and Julie Johnson of Texas.
HOUSE COMMITTEE PASSES FOREIGN FUNDING TRANSPARENCY ACT TO EXPOSE FOREIGN DONATIONS TO NONPROFITS

The hearing puts the investigation under the umbrella of House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., whose committee has made confronting the Chinese Communist Party and strengthening U.S. defenses against Beijing a central focus. Earlier this year, Mast joined lawmakers from both parties in pressing the Trump administration to tighten export controls aimed at restricting China's access to advanced semiconductor manufacturing technology.

The three scheduled witnesses invited by Republican lawmakers to testify at the hearing bring together three different fronts in the emerging foreign-influence investigation: Cuba's influence infrastructure inside the United States, the Chinese Communist Party's broader political and technological strategy and campaigns by the Singham network targeting America's artificial-intelligence and data-center buildout.
DOJ, TREASURY INVESTIGATE NONPROFITS AND LEADERS ALLEGEDLY COORDINATING WITH CUBA IN INFLUENCE CAMPAIGN
Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga of Michigan arrives at a campaign rally for now-President Donald Trump, on Nov. 1, 2024 in Portage, Michigan. (Bill Huizenga campaign)

Gonzalez is expected to speak on Cuba's alleged influence network in the United States. "Cuba is 100% operating a foreign influence operation in the U.S.," Gonzalez told Fox News Digital earlier this year, describing the communist island as "ground zero for anti-American revolutionary organizing in the Western Hemisphere."
Gonzalez said investigators should determine whether American organizations crossed the line between constitutionally protected activism and political activity coordinated by a foreign government.
INSIDE CUBA’S FOREIGN INFLUENCE CAMPAIGN: FROM THE '60S VENCEREMOS BRIGADE TO A CALIFORNIA UNION HALL
Democratic Socialists of America member Hasan Piker and CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans of CodePink meet in Cuba, as part of "United Front" to support the communist regime. (CodePink via Storyful)

A Fox News Digital investigation identified an ecosystem of U.S. organizations supporting Cuba that overlaps significantly with the Singham network. CodePink, the People's Forum, BreakThrough News, Tricontinental, the ANSWER Coalition and the Party for Socialism and Liberation have all been key players supporting the Communist Party of Cuba and developed close relationships with Cuba and its state institutions. Gonzalez has written specifically about that intersection.

A second witness, Jamestown Foundation senior fellow Matthew Johnson, brings expertise on the Chinese Communist Party. Johnson specializes in China's elite politics, strategic thinking, technology policy and the party-state's control over China's financial sector and private economy. His research has examined the relationship between CCP ideology, propaganda, political control and China's technology strategy.
FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS
Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., questioned a State Department official who said the Biden administration was trying to make maps "more gay." (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The third witness, Lyman, has investigated another front of the same battle: the campaign against America's AI and data-center infrastructure. Lyman co-authored research identifying the Singham network, and particularly the Party for Socialism and Liberation, as a significant force in protests against data centers around the country. His research identified 21 campaigns across 14 states and calculated that about $23.6 billion in proposed AI and data-center investment had been delayed, reduced or blocked in campaigns in which the Party for Socialism and Liberation was a significant mobilizing force.

The research described a broader information environment in which Chinese state media criticized the environmental and economic effects of American data centers while Beijing subsidized the expansion of its own AI infrastructure. Lyman has argued that legitimate debate over AI safety, energy use and data-center construction should be insulated from influence by geopolitical competitors seeking an advantage over the United States.

House Ways and Means Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., has described the organizations as part of a "foreign-aligned influence network" and is investigating whether some tax-exempt groups are functioning as agents of foreign interests. His committee recently issued subpoenas to the People's Forum, Tricontinental and BreakThrough BT Media after months of seeking records about their funding, foreign contacts and relationships with Singham. The organizations refused to produce documents in response to the subpoenas, saying they were the targets of a "witch hunt."

title: 9/11 Museum unveils exhibition for generation too young to remember the attacks: 'Called everybody to lead'
summary: The 9/11 Memorial and Museum unveils a new exhibition featuring artifacts and firsthand accounts showing how the attacks inspired a generation of service.
story: 9/11 Memorial and Museum President and CEO Elizabeth L. Hillman told Fox News Digital how the museum is helping younger generations understand the lasting impact of the terrorist attacks.

The 9/11 Memorial and Museum is marking the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks by unveiling a new exhibition exploring the legacy of service inspired by that day and preserving its history for the next generation.
In Their Honor: 25 Years of 9/11 Inspired Service highlights how 9/11 inspired thousands of Americans to serve their communities and country in the years that followed.

"So many people who visit the museum or who are interested in learning about 9/11 are too young to remember themselves, and one of the stories that they don't necessarily realize when they start to encounter the history of 9/11 is how much it changed the arc of people's lives," 9/11 Memorial and Museum President and CEO Elizabeth L. Hillman told Fox News Digital.

The exhibition features artifacts, interactive displays, and firsthand accounts from those who turned the tragedy into a lifetime of service, including military members, first responders, volunteers, educators and victims' families.
AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS
A boy points towards the center of the reflecting pool at the National September 11 Memorial Museum in New York on Sunday, Sept. 11, 2022. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Hillman said the exhibition's "signature artifact" is Feathers of the Phoenix , a 15-foot papier-mâché sculpture created by children who lost loved ones on 9/11 while attending America's Camp.

"The reason I think that's the best artifact to talk about the entire exhibition is that those young people have grown up, and the exhibition is about what they decided to do in the wake of that loss they suffered on 9/11," she said.

Outside the exhibition, the museum also offers a free digital learning experience with a 35-minute film featuring six personal stories. One story follows brothers James and Patrick Dowdell, whose firefighter father was killed responding to the Sept. 11 attacks, inspiring James to join the Fire Department of New York and Patrick to serve in the U.S. Army.
"I think that first-person storytelling is the way to reach young people," Hillman said.
MASSIVE PIECE OF 9/11 HISTORY MAKES STUNNING 10,500-MILE JOURNEY ACROSS AMERICA

With more children growing up with no memory of 9/11, Hillman said the museum tailors its educational resources by age and recommends tools like "Sesame Street's" post-9/11 episodes to help families discuss the attacks.
"There are age-appropriate materials that change over time for what students are ready to understand," she said.
Hillman said the museum is preparing the next generation to carry forward the lessons.

"We need to reach the people who are becoming teachers, who are becoming firefighters, police officers, members of the Armed Forces, and help them understand what it was to come together after 9/11 and develop a response to a catastrophe that we did not anticipate," she said.
WHERE TUNNEL TO TOWERS' STEEL ACROSS AMERICA TOUR WILL STOP AHEAD OF 9/11
Two flags flutter on a fence in front of Lower Manhattan and One World Trade Center at the Tear Drop 9/11 Memorial at sunset on June 13, 2026, in Bayonne, New Jersey. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)
Twenty-five years later, Hillman said the museum's mission is more important than ever.
"It really called everybody to lead," she said. "I think that's different now than what it has been at previous points in time when we were closer to the attacks and not 25 years away."

The exhibition opens to the public on Sept. 12.
Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: America's reddest state chases billion-dollar boom as others sour on massive emerging industry
summary: Wyoming's vast land, affordable energy and fiber optic corridors could lure billions in data center investment as other states add new taxes.
story: Tax Foundation Senior Fellow Jared Walczak says Wyoming’s abundant land, affordable energy and high-capacity fiber could give the state an edge as others consider new taxes on booming data centers.

As Americans weigh the costs and benefits of massive data centers emerging in their towns to fuel the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, the country's reddest state could be poised to capitalize on billions of dollars in investment that other states are increasingly reluctant to welcome.

With wide-open spaces, abundant energy and a business-friendly environment, Wyoming has many of the ingredients tech companies are looking for as they race to expand their AI infrastructure in the U.S.
The opportunity comes as the rapid buildout of data centers has sparked political fights across the country over their enormous electricity demands, water use and tax treatment.

As some states and communities consider new taxes, restrictions or even moratoriums on data center construction, Wyoming has a chance to position itself as an alternative. Supporters argue the projects could bring billions of dollars onto local tax rolls and potentially ease the burden on homeowners.
THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS

Virginia has long been the nation’s data center hub, while Wyoming is emerging as a potential destination for the next wave of AI infrastructure investment. (Lexi Critchett/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
And Wyoming already checks many of the boxes data center developers are looking for.

"Data centers need a few things. They need land, they need affordable energy, they need to avoid natural disasters, and, of course, they need regulatory approval," Jared Walczak, vice president of state projects at the Tax Foundation, told Fox News Digital.
The Cowboy State also already has high-capacity fiber running along major interstate corridors, Walczak said, giving developers another key piece of infrastructure.
"If more states start imposing discriminatory taxes just on data centers, then places like Wyoming, at least as long as they don't do likewise, can become even more attractive," he said.
ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM

As states weigh the costs and benefits of data center development, Wyoming could stand to attract billions in AI investment with its abundant land, energy and favorable business environment. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/Contributor/AFP/Getty Images)
Wyoming is wrestling with some of the same questions confronting communities elsewhere.

Cheyenne officials rejected a proposed one-year moratorium on new data centers in May following public debate over electricity rates, water use and other concerns. Wyoming lawmakers have also considered reclassifying data centers as industrial property, a move that would subject them to a higher property tax assessment rate.
ELECTION WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS FOREIGN ACTORS ARE SPENDING BILLIONS TO TURN AMERICANS AGAINST AI
But Walczak argues that attracting the facilities could deliver a significant payoff for Wyoming homeowners.

"You have potentially billions of dollars worth of taxable property coming into a couple hundred acres," he said. "And that's the sort of increase in the tax base that can allow significant property tax relief for every other payer in the jurisdiction."
Wyoming is emerging as a potential hub for AI data centers as tech companies search for locations with ample land and access to affordable energy. (George Rose/Getty Images)
"Wyoming's been having a lot of conversations about lowering property taxes," Walczak added. "This is a great way to do that."
He pointed to Loudoun County, Virginia, the country’s largest data center market, as an example of how that tax base can benefit residents.

"Data centers provide about 45% of all local tax revenue to Loudoun County," Walczak said, adding that the average homeowner would pay an estimated $5,800 more annually in property taxes without the industry.
Wyoming’s abundant land and energy could make the Cowboy State an increasingly attractive destination for billions of dollars in AI data center investment. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The economic upside comes with a broader debate over who pays for the infrastructure needed to serve the power-hungry facilities.
Walczak said data centers can avoid pushing those costs onto residents if operators pay for the additional generation and transmission capacity they require.
For Wyoming, that leaves policymakers facing the same question confronting states nationwide as they look to capture a piece of the AI investment boom without leaving residents to shoulder the costs.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: GOP firebrand says he's 'not going to apologize' after flipping script on Dems' latest woke trend
summary: Rep. Brandon Gill's fiery land acknowledgement at the Republican convention flipped the Democratic tradition on its head, drawing roars from the Texas crowd.
story: Rep. Brandon Gill spoke with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Texas.
DALLAS – Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, generated another viral moment on Wednesday during his speech at the Republican midterm convention — and he says he’s not sorry.

Gill opened his remarks with a land acknowledgment, a growing trend among Democratic politicians to begin speeches by noting the Native American tribes who historically lived on the land their events are on.

"I'd like to acknowledge that we stand here today in the great state of Texas and the United States of America is the ancestral homeland of great American patriots, pioneers and explorers who put down roots, fight for freedom all over the globe and bled and died to build the greatest civilization ever known to man," Gill said, the Republican crowd roaring in response.
GOP'S FRESHMAN FIREBRAND GOES VIRAL TARGETING 'UTTERLY INTELLECTUALLY INDEFENSIBLE' DEI POLICIES
U.S. Rep. Brandon Gill speaks on stage on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center on September 9, 2026, in Dallas, Texas. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
He told Fox News Digital afterward that it was his way of fighting back against Democrats’ way of viewing the United States.

"Listen, you see Democrats all the time wanting to begin their conventions or their gatherings by acknowledging, making some bizarre land acknowledgment that we live on stolen land, and they essentially just want to apologize for our country," Gill said.
WOKE STUNT GOES HORRIBLY WRONG AS MICHIGAN DEMS OPEN CONVENTION WITH BRUTAL ‘LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT’
The American Airlines Center, as preparations are underway for the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, U.S., September 7, 2026. (Jessica Koscielniak, Reuters)

"I think most Americans believe, rightfully so, that we live in the greatest country that's ever existed, and I'm not going to apologize for it…certainly most Americans don't want their elected officials apologizing for it either."
An official with Michigan’s Democratic Party spurred ridicule on the right after her attempt at a land acknowledgment ended up with her bungling the names of the tribes she was trying to honor.
Brandon Gill mocks ‘land acknowledgments’ with patriotic twist at Texas convention. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Land acknowledgments were also made in Corpus Christi, Texas, where state Democrats met for their nominating convention.

title: Trump puts himself back on the ballot: 5 takeaways from GOP midterm convention night one
summary: President Donald Trump unveiled a $5,000 dividend for every American adult at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, with one major spending caveat.
story: The president is claiming that he will disburse over $1 trillion in payments to citizens if Republicans retain control of Congress.

DALLAS – Facing a difficult political environment as Republicans fight to hold their congressional majorities, President Donald Trump used his address at the first-ever GOP midterm convention to unveil an unusual offer: a $5,000 dividend for every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate.

With less than two months until the midterm elections — and early voting just weeks away — Trump and Republican leaders on the first night of the two-day convention used their speeches to showcase policy wins and paint Democratic Party politicians as far-left radicals.

Facing energized Democrats and stiff political headwinds, Trump and Republicans are using the gathering at the American Airlines Center in Dallas to motivate the party's MAGA base and boost turnout in key races that will determine control of Congress.
"I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," the president urged, as he rallied his supporters.
FOX NEWS LIVE UPDATES FROM THE REPUBLICAN MIDTERM COVENTION

President Donald Trump speaks on stage on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center on Sept. 9, 2026, in Dallas, Texas. Trump headlined the Republican National Committee's first-ever midterm convention to highlight his administration's achievements and rally support for GOP candidates ahead of the November elections. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
Here are five takeaways from night one at what has been described by Republican leaders as a "Trumpapalooza."

Nearly an hour into his address, Trump unveiled what he described as "the best part of the speech," direct payments to the Americans funded by tariff revenues if Republicans retain control of Congress.

"If the Republicans win the ​House of Representatives and the United States Senate,⁠ both of them," Trump announced, "because of our ​tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a ​dividend to every ‌adult citizen in the United States of  America for $5,000."
The president didn't reveal any other details, other than to add, "The only caveat I have is ​that the dividend that we're making must be spent in the ‌United States of America."
Democrats quickly pounced on the president's proposal.

"Donald Trump and Republicans are once again offering empty promises to Americans," Democratic National Committee (DNC) Rapid Response Director Kendall Witmer claimed in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Amid persistent inflation, a new surge in fuel prices due to a flare-up in the ongoing war with Iran, and a deepening trade war with neighboring Canada, public opinion polls indicate Trump's approval ratings on the economy remain underwater.
But the president painted an optimistic picture of better times ahead.
Trump touted, "I’m bringing the prices down, way, way down." He also said that "oil will be going down as soon as we win the war with Iran," which he said "is taking place right now."
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

President Donald Trump greets attendees as he walks on stage on the first day of the Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 9, 2026. Trump headlined the Republican National Committee's first-ever midterm convention as he aimed to highlight his administration's achievements and rally support for GOP candidates ahead of the November elections. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Trump also showcased the tax cuts passed last year along party lines by the GOP-controlled Congress.
"The largest tax cuts in the history of the country," he highlighted. "We gave you no tax on tips, no tax on overtime and no tax on Social Security."
He also pointed to "the largest prescription drug price cuts in history... that alone should win the midterms."

While Trump touted "tremendous economic success," public opinion polls paint a very different picture, with the president's approval rating on his handling of the economy well into negative territory. Inflation was a key issue that helped boost Trump and the GOP to sweeping election victories in 2024. But Democrats say affordability has been the issue that fueled their ballot box victories and overperformances since Trump returned to the White House.
The DNC, which remains in debt and decided against holding a similar convention, is more than happy to focus on the economy.

"The only people reaping the benefits of Trump’s economy are himself, his family, and his ultrarich elite donors. Meanwhile, working families get nothing except sky-high receipts at the grocery store and the pump, unaffordable healthcare premiums, and wages that aren’t keeping up with inflation," the DNC's Witmer charged.

Midterm elections are often a referendum on the party in power, but Republicans aim to use the convention to draw a contrast as they spotlight Democrats' leftward lurch in this year's primaries and tie the party to far-left and socialist proposals.
"These people are radical left communists," Trump claimed, as he referred to Democrats.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
"Crazed lunatics and radicals," he added.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in his speech from the convention podium, argued: "the radical left is relentless in their pursuit to remake America, in the image of every socialist hellscape of the last century."

And Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming, the number three Republican in the chamber, charged that "Democrats north, south, east and west are running on this radical roadmap. They sound like an anti-American hate group."
Hours before the confab kicked off, Democrats presented their prebuttal.

"Voters can see through the BS that Republicans are spewing," Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois told reporters at a DNC counterprogramming news conference across the street from the convention hall.
"This bizarre Republican midterm convention here can't paper over the fact that Republicans have done nothing to earn your vote," Pritzker said.

Following Trump's speech, which lasted nearly two hours, DNC Chair Ken Martin argued, "The biggest liability in American politics right now is Donald Trump — and he just proved it. Republicans now have to spin his disastrous, rambling speech when it’s clear that this bizarre dog-and-pony show is being held to placate Trump’s fragile ego."
Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, a centrist Democrat known for bashing his party's left flank, made a surprise pre-recorded video appearance at the GOP convention.
As he introduced Pennsylvania's other U.S. senator, Republican David McCormick, Fetterman explained his appearance.

"Why am I here talking to you today? Because. Well, I'm a commonsense Democrat. I'm always going to stand with America. I'm always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life," the senator said. "Dave McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done, and he's going to fight for Pennsylvania. I'm proud to count him as my friend right back over my shoulder."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fetterman, who is a strong supporter of Israel, has increasingly railed against fellow Democrats who have criticized Israeli leaders over their ongoing war against Hamas in Gaza. Fetterman has said he has "no plans" to leave the Democratic Party. But he added if Democrats officially became the "anti-Israel party," count him out.

In a statement released after his appearance, Fetterman emphasized, "I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party — and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on."
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Ex-NFL cheerleader battles former gubernatorial aide in tight GOP primary race
summary: Elaine Pelino and Aaron Guckian are locked in a Rhode Island Republican primary too close to call as the GOP eyes a historically blue state.
story: Attorney Matt Belinsky and The Federalist's Brianna Lyman discuss an Axios report detailing Democratic midterm campaign strategies. The panel also reacts to Steve Hilton's viral comments on Joe Rogan's podcast regarding Los Angeles' decline and high gas prices under Democratic policies.

Elaine Pelino, a former NFL cheerleader and publisher pitching herself as the party-line choice, and Aaron Guckian, a former aide to former Gov. Donald Carcieri and a more centrist candidate are locked in a GOP primary that remained too close to call by early Thursday morning.
The race centered on experience and qualifications as Republicans hope they have found a candidate to win over a historically Democratic-leaning state.
SENATE REPUBLICAN PUSHES OVERHAUL TO CUT RED TAPE AND SPEED UP AMERICAN ENERGY PROJECTS
Aaron Guckian, left, pictured alongside Elaine Pelino, right. (Guckian for Governor; Jared Siskin/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
In the last election, Daniel McKee, the then-Democratic candidate and current governor of Rhode Island, beat out Republican challenger Ashley Kalus in a 57.9% to 38.9% victory.

Among other priorities in her campaign, Pelino promised to champion merit-based hiring, support law enforcement, immigration law and school choice. "This is what I’m going to do. I’m learning. Everything is a learning [curve] because I’m not a lifetime politician. I’m here because I love Rhode Island. And I want them to have a great life. I want them to live in a prosperous and safe place. We should get all the illegals out of here," Pelino said at a candidate forum.
DEM INCUMBENT BECOMES FIRST SITTING GOVERNOR TO LOSE PRIMARY SINCE 2018
Rhode Island Governor Donald Carcieri speaks to the media February 22, 2003, in West Warwick, Rhode Island. (Douglas McFadd/Getty Images)

Before her time in politics, Pelino had a wide range of experience, working as a model, in media and even as a cheerleader for the Houston Oilers, the football team that would eventually become the NFL’s Tennessee Titans. Later, in 2011, she founded Tigress magazine, which published 12 issues.

For his part, Guckian took a far more policy-centric approach, committing to overhaul Rhode Island’s permitting, improve service delivery and tighten use of the state’s revenue. He argued that the state’s budget growth had "gone too far."

"The state budget increased from $9.3 billion in 2019 to more than $14 billion between 2024 and 2026, nearly 50% growth in five years, even as federal COVID relief dollars are expiring," Guckian said on his campaign website.
"Rhode Island made a critical mistake. We built permanent commitments on temporary federal money."
SELF-FUNDED CEO CLAIMS GOP NOMINATION TO CHALLENGE MASSACHUSETTS DEMOCRAT’S SECOND-TERM BID
Aerial view of Rhode Island State Capitol in Providence, Rhode Island. (Visions of America/Joseph Sohm/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Once one of them has secured the primary, Pelino or Guckian will face an uphill battle in the Nov. 3 general election.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Trump makes stunning first-of-its-kind cash promise in bid to rally GOP voters at Dallas midterm convention
summary: President Donald Trump promised a $5,000 "Trump dividend" to every adult citizen if Republicans keep Congress at the GOP midterm convention.
story: President Donald Trump has renewed his promise to hold rallies for 35 Republicans running in tough House and Senate races.

DALLAS — President Donald Trump delivered the keynote speech on day one of the GOP's inaugural midterm convention, alternating between touting his successes in office and rallying thousands of supporters for Republican candidates ahead of November's general election before making a promise to American voters.
In a stunning move, Trump made a promise unheard of in the history of American politics — offering a cash prize should Republicans keep control of Congress.

"I can make this promise to you, and here is my promise," he said. "If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them, because of our economic — tremendous economic success like in history, we've never had anything like what's happening. But because of our tremendous strength and success economically — I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000. Very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to its shareholders."
TRUMP'S UNUSUAL ROLE AT MIDTERM CONVENTION REVEALED AS SCHEDULE GOES PUBLIC
President Donald Trump speaks on stage on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 9, 2026. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
"It will be called the 'Trump dividend,'" he added.

Trump opened the speech by grading his own performance since taking office for a second time in January 2025, saying he's "doing a great job." He quickly shifted to addressing the historical challenge that incumbent parties rarely retain control of Congress in midterm elections.
JOHNSON DOWNPLAYS GOP'S MIDTERM WOES AS DEMOCRATS EYE HOUSE TAKEOVER: 'I AM VERY BULLISH'

"But I say, why is it that no matter how well you're doing, we see not a president — Democrat or Republican — almost never wins the midterms?' said Trump. "We've got to change that because we have something going that's so good we can't let that string be broken. So I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot, just one more time."
During his effort to rally GOP voters to help Republicans hang onto the House and Senate, Trump made sure to give credit to Republicans on Capitol Hill for their work in passing his agenda.
MILLIONS TAP TRUMP TAX CUTS THIS FILING SEASON AS REFUNDS TOP $3,400

"Our Republican Congress puts thousands of dollars into the pockets of working families with the largest tax cuts in the history of our country," he said. "So we had the largest in history. We gave you no tax on tips, no tax on overtime and no tax on Social Security for our great seniors."
He said his administration's efforts on critical issues will be crushed if the GOP loses majorities in either or both chambers of Congress.
TRUMP ADMIN MARKS 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH ZERO BORDER RELEASES AS APPREHENSIONS PLUNGE 94%
"Because if we lose, you're going to lose your border," he said. "You're going to lose your tax cuts. You're going to lose your safety and security. You're going to lose your wealth."

President Donald Trump greets attendees as he walks on stage on the first day of the Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 9, 2026. Trump headlined the Republican National Committee's first-ever midterm convention as he aimed to highlight his administration's achievements and rally support for GOP candidates ahead of the November elections. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Fox News polling shows Trump is underwater with voters on the economy, cost of living and inflation. Sixty-five percent of voters disapprove of his handling of the economy. The president also defended the military conflict in Iran, saying he has received criticism over rising gas prices tied to the conflict but arguing that "I'm right," because Iran was one month away from securing a nuclear weapon. Inflation has risen from 2.4% to 3.4% since the war began in February, while gas prices have also increased.
RECORD GAS PRICES SQUEEZE AMERICANS AS SUMMER TRAVEL SEASON ENDS, MIDTERMS LOOM AND IRAN WAR WAGES ON
Republicans who spoke to Fox News Digital on day one of the convention weren't concerned with Trump's economic policies.

"I believe that Trump is doing the right thing," one RNC attendee told Fox News Digital. "The tariffs are bringing a lot of money back, you know, correcting the national debt. And that's gonna improve everything across the board."

"I feel like as soon as we bring this conflict in Iran to a close, we'll start seeing the full effects of President Trump and the greatness that he's done as far as the economy, the great thing of tariffs, and some of the products of the Trump economy in the golden age," said Jacquez Jones of Texas.
Later, Trump shifted his sights to Texas' high-profile U.S. Senate race between Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democrat state Rep. James Talarico.

"We have to elect Ken Paxton," he said, segueing into border security, a top issue under both Trump administrations. "Together, we're going to continue to have — we have the strongest borders now in the history of our country."
'FAKE' MODERATE TALARICO'S TEXAS SURGE TESTS PAXTON IN FIGHT TO HOLD CRUCIAL GOP SENATE SEAT

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is shown during the Texas GOP convention in the George R. Brown Convention Center in Houston Friday, June 12, 2026. (Melissa Phillip/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
"We have the lowest level of illegal immigration ever recorded in our country," he said, adding that zero illegal immigrants have entered the country through Texas in 16 months.

"And therefore zero have been admitted into Texas, where they used to be running around, running rampant, killing people, destroying many houses and farms, and ruining property values and creating havoc all over the state of Texas," he said.
During the speech, he also took aim at Democratic Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina.
LONGTIME GOP AIDE DEFECTS TO DEM RISING STAR AS TEXAS SENATE BATTLE FOR CORNYN'S SEAT HEATS UP

He also touted what he described as foreign policy wins. After the arrest of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Trump boasted about "the biggest oil deal" ever, which he said might be "the biggest deal in the history of our country."
"Sixty-five billion barrels are ours," Trump said. "And you know what they say, it is lifetime 500 years."
Later, Trump transitioned to slamming the GOP's far-left opponents.

"In this election, the Democrats have nominated the most extreme and dangerous group of candidates for the House and Senate ever to seek office," he said. "These people are radical left communists. Many of them. Not all of them, but many of them in state after state. The Democrat establishment has been overthrown and replaced by crazed lunatics and radicals. They call themselves Democrat socialists. But actually they're communists. They're not socialists. They're long beyond socialists."
Members of the Democratic Socialists of America gather outside a Trump-owned building on May Day, May 1, 2019, in New York City. (Getty Images)
He noted the DSA has proposed abolishing prisons, ICE, Border Patrol, the U.S. Senate and the presidency.
That message was one Alex Stone of Kansas City, Missouri, hoped for earlier in the day.

"Tell the truth about who they are, what they believe and what they plan on doing," he told Fox News Digital when asked what Trump's message to Americans should be. "Democratic Socialists of America with El-Sayed in Michigan, in particular, these people want to destroy people like myself. They want to destroy people like President Trump and many of the other people here. If they get into power, what is going to happen to us?"

The president said he's prepared for stiff opposition from those opponents.

title: Fetterman teases where his true loyalty lies after surprise appearance at GOP convention
summary: Senate Democrat John Fetterman drew a hard line after introducing Dave McCormick at the Republican National Committee's midterm convention.
story: Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., calls himself a "commonsense Democrat," rejects socialism and praises Republican Sen. Dave McCormick in a video appearance at the RNC Midterm Convention in Dallas.
DALLAS — A rogue Senate Democrat toying with the idea of leaving his party drew a hard line in the sand after making a surprise appearance at the GOP’s Trump-centric convention.

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., has been welcomed with open arms by Republicans to join the party after he floated leaving his own caucus and spurred further speculation that he would jump ship after dropping a video introducing his colleague, Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention on Wednesday.

But in a statement to Fox News Digital, the progressive-turned-centrist said that he wasn’t turning his back on the Democratic Party, even as the knives have come out to cut him loose from the Senate.
DEM SENATOR DELIVERS SURPRISE VIDEO AT REPUBLICAN CONVENTION BACKING MCCORMICK
Senator John Fetterman, D-Pa., left, pictured alongside Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., right. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images; Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

"My remarks introduced Dave McCormick as a great American and friend. We are in different parties, but we are both Team PA," Fetterman said. "We have delivered hundreds of millions of dollars back to Pennsylvania, fought for improved transportation and affordable housing, and the Steel Way of Life."
"I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party — and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on," he continued.

Fetterman started his career in the Senate after besting Dr. Mehmet Oz in a tight race for power in 2022, where he clinched a historically thin Democratic majority in 2022 running on a progressive platform.
TOP REPUBLICAN NAMES WHO HE SAYS IS REALLY LEADING DEMOCRATS — AND IT'S NOT SCHUMER OR JEFFRIES
But since then, he has become a thorn in Democrats’ side and challenged the direction of the party.

Earlier this year, Fetterman warned that if Democrats became more entrenched in anti-Israel policy positions, he would exit the party and has taken jabs at the party’s direction during this midterm election cycle as far-left progressives, like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, have emerged as standard-bearers.

Fetterman has routinely bucked Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and his colleagues on a handful of key issues, like President Donald Trump’s war in Iran or voting with Republicans to end the marathon government shutdown last Fall.
FETTERMAN FACES DEM REVOLT AS BOMBSHELL REPORT FUELS PUSH TO OUST HIM: 'DISGRACE'

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks during a Senate Republicans press conference at the U.S. Capitol on June 2, 2026, flanked by Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., and Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W. Va. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc)

His latest edict followed a bombshell report that alleged through leaked texts with his aides that the maverick Democrat would often brush off duties of his office, like meeting with paralyzed veterans or charging that a three-hour funeral service for slain police officers was a "non-starter."

And Republicans would gladly welcome him into the fold. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said in July that he and others in the Senate GOP have "had conversations with him in the past … about the challenges he faces in his caucus."

"And, you know, there are many of us who I think would welcome the opportunity to have him join the Republican conference," Thune said.
But for now, Fetterman is staying put even if Democrats flip the Senate in November.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: EXCLUSIVE: 25 years after 9/11, ICE says more than 2K known or suspected terrorists have been deported
summary: ICE arrested over 2,150 known or suspected terrorists and deported more than 2,000 since Trump took office, DHS says ahead of the 9/11 anniversary.
story: Border czar Tom Homan slams calls from progressives to abolish the agency as border enforcement actions reach historic levels. Homan highlights recent record-breaking arrests and deportations, emphasizing that seventy percent of those detained are convicted criminals. He also reveals ICE's critical role in rescuing over one hundred and fifty thousand smuggled children, warning of the dangerous consequences of dismantling the agency.

EXCLUSIVE: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has deported more than 2,000 known or suspected terrorists from the U.S. since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) tells Fox News Digital, as the nation prepares to mark 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks.
DHS said ICE arrested more than 2,150 known or suspected terrorists between Jan. 20, 2025, and Sept. 9, 2026, and deported 2,015 during that period.

"As we reflect on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, the brave men and women of ICE continue to carry out their duty to protect the homeland and keep the American people safe," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in the department’s announcement.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, along with other federal law enforcement agencies, attend a pre-enforcement meeting in Chicago. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)
Mullin said ICE had arrested more than 2,100 known or suspected terrorists and deported more than 2,000, adding that the anniversary underscored the department’s commitment to "eternal vigilance."
DHS pointed to several recent cases involving alleged terrorists and members of designated foreign terrorist organizations.
WHITE HOUSE UFC TERROR PLOT 'RINGLEADER' IS A MEXICAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT, DHS CONFIRMS
ICE agents conduct a multi-agency targeted enforcement operation in Chicago. (Christopher Dilts / Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)

In June, federal authorities arrested Abraham Hermosillo Alvarez, a Mexican national DHS described as the suspected ringleader of an alleged mass-casualty plot targeting UFC Freedom 250 at the White House.
DHS said Alvarez overstayed a visitor visa that expired in 2001 and later received DACA status in 2014. ICE lodged a detainer following his arrest.

Days earlier, ICE Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) arrested Felipe Linares De Oliveira Dell Aquilla, a Brazilian national DHS identified as a former commander of two designated foreign terrorist organizations.
Authorities said they recovered a handgun, cash and multiple electronic devices after a vehicle and foot pursuit in North Carolina.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SAYS FEDERAL AUTHORITIES HAVE ARRESTED MORE THAN 10,000 SUSPECTED GANG MEMBERS
ICE conducts an immigration operation in New York City. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images, File)
DHS said Aquilla was wanted in Brazil on criminal association and extortion charges and was allegedly holding his wife against her will while preparing to flee to Mexico.
ICE lodged a detainer after his arrest, while investigators pursued additional firearm and kidnapping charges.
Four Venezuelan members of Tren de Aragua also pleaded guilty in May to charges stemming from a 2024 Bronx shooting that killed two people.
DHS said all four had entered the United States illegally between 2022 and 2023.
REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS
Flowers left by mourners at the 9/11 Memorial in New York City. (Getty Images)
The announcement comes as the nation prepares to mark 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people in New York City, at the Pentagon and in Pennsylvania.

The attacks prompted the largest overhaul of the nation's homeland security apparatus in decades, including the creation of DHS in 2002 and ICE the following year.

Friday's anniversary will commemorate the victims of the attacks and the first responders who rushed into danger, while marking a quarter-century of U.S. efforts to prevent another large-scale terrorist attack on American soil.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Talarico says he 'missed the mark' as he backtracks on controversial woke statements
summary: James Talarico now backs banning transgender surgeries for minors and opposing trans athletes in girls' sports as the Texas Senate race heats up.
story: Democrat James Talarico reversed several of his most controversial takes as a critical Senate race tightens in Texas.

In a Fox News exclusive interview, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico came out in favor of banning gender surgery for minors and opposed transgender-identifying men competing in women’s sports.
Talarico also backtracked on several of his more controversial claims, including saying there are six genders and that "God is nonbinary."

This comes as the Texas Senate race, which is surprisingly close according to recent Fox News polling, enters its final months. The race is considered critical to both parties' chances of securing a Senate majority. Talarico is facing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican who has faced controversies of his own. A Republican loss in Texas would significantly impact President Donald Trump's ability to implement his agenda.
Fox News spoke with Talarico at a food drive campaign event in Dallas on Tuesday. Talarico’s event took place as the first-ever GOP midterm convention kicked off just miles away in downtown Dallas.
TALARICO CAMPAIGNS WITH SURGEON WHO OPERATED ON TRANSGENDER MINORS: ‘WOLF IN SHEEP’S CLOTHING’

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a campaign rally at the Cailloux Theater on Aug. 31, 2026, in Kerrville, Texas. Talarico is campaigning across the state in a close race against Republican candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
Asked whether he would vote as a U.S. senator in favor of a national ban on gender surgery for minors, Talarico answered, "Absolutely."
He said, "I've been consistent on this issue," explaining his opposition to a Texas bill to ban transgender surgeries on minors by saying the measure "was overly broad."

"If you go back and check, I voted for a major amendment to limit the bill to banning surgeries for minors," he said. "As a lawmaker, my job is to try to sift through everything the bill does. And sometimes there's stuff in it that's really harmful, and I have no choice but to oppose the bill as a whole."

"It's why I try to use amendments, to narrow the focus of the bill so that it does exactly what we intend it to do," he continued. "It's what I tried to do with that piece of legislation, and unfortunately, the amendment I supported was unsuccessful."

In 2023, as a member of the Texas House of Representatives, Talarico voted against a state bill titled SB 14, which prohibited certain gender surgery, puberty blockers and certain hormone treatments for minors. There were 18 amendments to the bill proposed by Democrats, all of which Talarico voted in favor and all of which ultimately failed.

In the same interview, Talarico acknowledged that men in women’s sports is a significant issue in Texas. He said, "I oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness."

"Every sport has to be safe and fair. As a former public school teacher, I care a lot about our student athletes. I care a lot about our students. And so, I will oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it risks safety or fairness," he said.
Talarico’s comments mark a shift from his earlier position as a Texas state lawmaker.

In 2021, while serving on the Texas House Public Education Committee, he opposed SB 29, which sought to require public-school athletes to compete based on the biological sex listed on their birth certificate, calling the issue a "manufactured problem." Later that year, he voted against HB 25, which enacted similar restrictions into Texas law.
JAMES TALARICO ADMITS PAST COMMENTS 'MISSED THE MARK' WHEN CONFRONTED ON CLAIMS LIKE GOD IS 'NON-BINARY'

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks to volunteers at a "Love Thy Neighbor" Statewide Grocery Drive on September 9, 2026, in Dallas, Texas. Talarico continues campaigning across the state in a close race with Republican candidate, state Attorney General Ken Paxton ahead of the November 3 general elections. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

He also addressed perhaps his most controversial statement, which he made in 2021, while opposing a Texas bill to keep men out of women’s sports. Talarico said on the state House floor that "God is both masculine and feminine and everything in between. God is non-binary."

"I was being provocative with that statement. I get that," Talarico admitted, explaining, "What I was trying to say is that you can't use human categories to define God, and that's not controversial theologically. In fact, the late Charlie Kirk, the late Pope Benedict all said the same thing."
Talarico continued, claiming "these comments are being clipped out of context to try to distract from Ken Paxton's career of corruption."

"You mentioned [Paxton] being acquitted in the state Senate. That was after two of his billionaire megadonors gave the lieutenant governor a $3 million check to buy his acquittal," Talarico said. "So, Ken Paxton is the most corrupt politician in Texas, and he's gonna try to clip some of my comments, including comments where I was being a little provocative in order to try to distract from that career."
Fox News Digital reached out to the Paxton campaign for a response.
LONGTIME GOP AIDE DEFECTS TO DEM RISING STAR AS TEXAS SENATE BATTLE FOR CORNYN'S SEAT HEATS UP
Regarding his past comment about there being more than two genders, Talarico said he does not currently believe there are six sexes.

"I've missed the mark on some of my past statements. I will be the first to admit it," he said. "What I meant is that there are two sexes, and then there's a small percentage of people with genetic abnormalities."

"Obviously didn't say it correctly. There are not six sexes. There are two, and I think the reason that politicians in that convention center across the street want to talk about six sexes is because they don't want to talk about $6 diesel," he said.
Though he walked back these controversies, Talarico did not hold back on his criticism of the Supreme Court, which he described as "infected" with corruption, saying it "needs to be overhauled."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is urging the Republican Party to start spending now in the ballyhooed Senate race in the largest red state. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

He said that if elected, "You're going to expect that I will vote for overhaul to the Supreme Court. That will include binding codes of conduct for our justices. It'll include term limits, and I am open to a discussion about expanding the number of justices."
Following these controversies, Talarico pledged to keep his message focused on affordability for the remainder of the campaign.

"Everywhere I go across the state of Texas, people are struggling to survive in this economy. They are struggling to afford the basics: groceries, gas, utilities, healthcare. And that's what I'm going to be focused on from now until Election Day."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

On the topic of affordability, Talarico said that "we should not have a state income tax" in Texas. This is despite Talarico previously voting against a measure to permanently ban a state income tax, which he suggested was redundant and an example of "government waste at its worst."
The measure was ultimately passed by the Texas Legislature and approved by Texas voters in November 2019.

title: George W Bush recalls moment with Derek Jeter before nerve-wracking pitch at Yankee Stadium after 9/11
summary: Former President George W. Bush recalls throwing the ceremonial first pitch at Yankee Stadium weeks after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
story: O'Hara's Restaurant and Pub serves as a historic sanctuary for first responders near Ground Zero. Steve Doocy reports live from the venue alongside former NYPD Chief of Department John Chell to reflect on the legacy of 9/11.

Former President George W. Bush recalled Wednesday a lighthearted moment he shared with New York Yankees shortstop Derek Jeter before throwing out a ceremonial first pitch at Yankee Stadium just weeks after 9/11.
Bush told the story alongside Condoleezza Rice, his national security advisor at the time of the attacks, during a reunification event at the George W. Bush Presidential Center in Dallas, Texas.
During the World Series in October 2001, Bush said he was feeling the pressure of leading the nation through a fragile moment when Jeter told him before the game, "Don’t bounce it, they’ll boo you."
As the audience chuckled at the joke, Bush recalled feeling the raw emotions inside the NYC stadium as he walked to the mound at center field.
GEORGE BUSH WELCOMES TOP OFFICIALS TO HIS HOME STATE FOR 9/11 REMEMBRANCE ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF ATTACKS
Former President George W. Bush speaks during a 9/11 remembrance event at the George W. Bush Presidential Center in Dallas, Texas. (Pool)
"I looked at the catcher, he looked really tiny, and the ball felt really heavy," Bush said.
While scanning the faces in the crowd, Bush said he could imagine people thinking, "You can knock down our buildings, but you d--- sure not going to touch our soul."
AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS

President George W. Bush throws the ceremonial first pitch prior to Game Three of the 2001 World Series between the Arizona Diamondbacks and the New York Yankees at Yankee Stadium on Oct. 30, 2001 in Bronx, New York. (Rich Pilling/MLB via Getty Images)
Bush recalled throwing the ball, which made it over the plate, and described the moment as "memorable."
"I mean, it was an amazing feeling," he said.

A view of the World Trade Center rubble is seen in this file photo from early September 2001 shortly after the 9/11 terrorist attacks in New York City. (Jane Tyska / Digital First Media / East Bay Times via Getty Images)

This coming Friday will mark the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, when al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four commercial airplanes in a coordinated attack against the United States.

Two of the flights struck New York City’s Twin Towers at the World Trade Center, sending both buildings crashing down and causing mass casualties. A third flight struck the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., while the fourth crashed in a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
Nearly 3,000 people died in the terror attacks, including hundreds of firefighters and police officers.

title: Floating solar panels could save cities millions. Is your town next?
summary: Lima, Ohio, has installed 3,120 floating solar panels on its Twin Lakes Reservoir, projecting nearly $10 million in electricity cost savings.
story: Fox News host Will Cain discusses Cowboy Space Corporation’s plans to launch solar-powered data centers into orbit by 2028 as demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure grows. Cain explains how the technology could use solar energy to power AI chips in space.

What if your town could build a solar farm without giving up acres of valuable land? Lima, Ohio, is trying something different. The city has completed a 2-megawatt solar array that floats on the Twin Lakes Reservoir, its primary drinking water source.

More than 3,000 solar panels now sit on the water and feed electricity to the nearby water treatment plant. The city projects the system will save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over its lifetime. That kind of savings could get the attention of cities far beyond Ohio.
So, could floating solar panels eventually show up on a reservoir near you? Here's how the technology works, why cities are interested and what it could mean for your community.

WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE
An Ohio city is using floating solar panels on its drinking water reservoir to power its water treatment plant and cut millions in projected energy costs. (D3Energy)
Ohio puts 3,120 solar panels on a drinking water reservoir

Lima officially celebrated the completion of its Twin Lakes Floating Solar Project on Aug. 12. The final system includes 3,120 solar panels spread across about 3.6 acres of water, according to developer D3Energy. The 2-megawatt array sits on Lima's primary drinking water reservoir. That reservoir serves roughly 35,000 residents.

Next door, the city's water treatment plant processes about 14 million gallons of water each day. It also consumes more electricity than any other city facility. That makes the plant an obvious place to look for energy savings. Lima projects the floating solar system will save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over its lifetime. Earlier city estimates put first-year savings at roughly $200,000. For a city utility, that is serious money. Actual lifetime savings will depend on factors including future electricity prices and how the system performs over time.
How floating solar panels work
Instead of attaching panels to racks planted in the ground, engineers mount them on floating platforms. Anchors and mooring lines keep the array in position.

Lima uses Ciel & Terre's Hydrelio floating system. Its anchoring setup connects to the banks and reservoir bottom. The design also allows the array to move as water levels change. The project uses bifacial solar panels, which can capture light on both sides.

Electricity travels from the array to eight inverters onshore. From there, the electricity helps power the water treatment plant. The result looks a bit like a traditional solar farm that traded grass for water.
Why cities may want solar panels floating on water

Here is where the idea gets particularly interesting. Land costs money. It also competes with housing, businesses, agriculture and other development. Reservoirs already occupy space. Lima's floating array covers about four acres.

A land-based system producing the same amount of electricity would reportedly need at least 10 acres. That could make floating solar attractive to cities with limited open space. The panels can also sit near the facilities that need the electricity. In Lima, the water treatment plant sits right beside the reservoir. That reduces the need to find a distant solar site and then figure out how to move the electricity where the city needs it.

Researchers have also studied whether floating solar can help reduce evaporation by shading portions of the water surface. Of course, every reservoir comes with different conditions. Water depth, changing levels and recreational use can affect whether a project makes sense. Federal researchers also consider existing dam operations when evaluating potential sites.
LAWMAKERS TARGET ENERGY AFFORDABILITY THROUGH SWEEPING PERMITTING OVERHAUL IN NEW HOUSE BILL
Floating solar could help cities generate clean energy without using valuable land, but questions remain about long-term costs and water safety. (D3Energy)
What about putting solar panels on drinking water?

This was one of my first questions. These panels are floating on the same reservoir that provides drinking water to about 35,000 people. Lima's system uses Ciel & Terre Hydrelio floats made from high-density polyethylene, or HDPE.

Ciel & Terre says its floating system complies with the BS 6920:2000 standard for nonmetallic materials that come into contact with water intended for human consumption. Still, communities considering floating solar have more to evaluate than whether the structure can float safely.

The National Renewable Energy Laboratory has examined environmental and regulatory questions surrounding floating solar. Its research notes that projects can affect water bodies differently depending on the location. That means a system that works well on one reservoir may require a different design somewhere else.
The project cost millions before it could save millions

There is another number worth paying attention to. The Lima project cost about $5.3 million. Federal support played a substantial role in making the numbers work. The city received a $2.4 million Department of Energy grant. Combined with almost $900,000 in federal direct-pay tax credits, that support helped offset roughly half of the project's cost.

Those incentives covered a significant share of the upfront expense. That context is important when another city looks at Lima's projected $10 million in savings. A town considering floating solar would need to look at construction costs, financing and expected electricity production. Available incentives could change the calculation as well.

Lima began considering the project years before crews put panels on the water. City Council approved moving forward with the project in 2023. Construction began in 2025 before the system came online this August.
Could floating solar panels spread across America?

Lima may look unusual today, but floating solar has substantial room to grow. Ohio already has more than one project. D3Energy and ARP Solar completed a 1.5-megawatt floating array for Del-Co Water in Delaware, Ohio, in 2024. A 6-megawatt system in Monroeville is expected to come online before the end of 2026.

The bigger opportunity stretches far beyond Ohio. National Renewable Energy Laboratory researchers studied federally owned or regulated reservoirs across the U.S. They estimated those reservoirs have technical potential for 861 to 1,042 gigawatts of floating solar capacity.
That figure represents technical potential rather than a prediction that thousands of reservoirs will soon disappear under solar panels. Plenty of locations would never make sense.

Still, the scale helps explain why energy developers and local governments are taking a closer look at water. CyberGuy has covered this idea before on a much larger scale. India's Omkareshwar project showed how enormous floating solar installations can become. We have also seen developers rethink the shape of solar installations on land. One Texas company is building vertical solar towers designed to produce more power from a smaller footprint.
AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING
Cities across the U.S. are exploring floating solar as a way to reduce utility costs while making use of existing reservoirs. (D3Energy)
Will floating solar panels lower your utility bill?

Here is the part I would keep an eye on. Lima expects to save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over the project's lifetime. But that does not mean residents will suddenly see a cheaper water bill. The city could use those savings in different ways. Lower energy costs could help cover other expenses, pay for infrastructure upgrades or ease pressure on future rate increases.

So, if a floating solar project comes to your town, there is one question worth asking: Will any of those savings eventually make their way back to you? That answer could determine how much this technology really helps the people paying the bills.
What this means to you

You probably do not spend much time thinking about how much electricity your local water plant consumes. Yet you ultimately help pay for that electricity through taxes, utility rates or both. Floating solar gives cities another way to attack that expense without buying a huge parcel of land.

It also raises questions you should ask before cheering on a project. How much will it cost? How much electricity will it realistically generate? What happens to the savings? You should also ask what testing and monitoring will protect the water supply. Those answers will tell you whether a floating solar project makes financial sense for your community.
Kurt's key takeaways

What I like about Lima's floating solar project is how practical the idea feels. The city already owns the reservoir, and its water treatment plant right next door uses a huge amount of electricity. So instead of finding another piece of land for solar panels, Lima put them on the water. Then there is the projected $10 million in savings. That certainly gets my attention. I want to see whether those savings hold up over time and, more importantly, whether residents eventually benefit from them. Lima also gives other cities something real to look at. We are seeing communities experiment with new ways to generate and store energy, from floating solar to massive battery projects. And who knows? The next solar project in your town may end up floating right on the water.

Would you be comfortable with thousands of solar panels floating on your town's drinking water reservoir if officials said the project could save millions, or would you need to see more long-term evidence first? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.
