title: Lindsay Clancy fixation and alleged plot to poison husband emerge as accused mom claims psychosis
summary: Corie A. Walsh's defense team claims a psychotic episode led to her son's death, but prosecutors allege she also had a plot to poison her husband.
story: Chicago-Kent College of Law professor Richard S. Kling breaks down why a mental illness diagnosis alone does not determine criminal responsibility.

An Illinois mother accused of strangling her 2-year-old son was suffering a "psychotic episode" when the child was killed, her high-profile defense attorney says, even as prosecutors allege she was plotting to poison her husband.

The competing accounts come as Corie A. Walsh's attorneys accuse jail officials of failing to provide her prescribed psychiatric medication after hospital doctors recommended she receive around-the-clock psychiatric care upon her discharge, according to the defense.

The sharply different portrayals of Walsh's mental state underscore a central legal question likely to shape the case: whether evidence of severe mental illness can satisfy Illinois' legal standard for insanity.
ILLINOIS MOTHER CHARGED WITH MURDER IN DEATH OF 2-YEAR-OLD SON IN CASE DRAWING COMPARISONS TO LINDSAY CLANCY
Andrea Lyon, a prominent defense lawyer who previously served on Casey Anthony's legal team, said in a statement to Fox News Digital this week that Walsh's actions were driven by mental illness.

Corie A. Walsh, 38, in a booking photo provided by law enforcement. Prosecutors are asking a judge to deny her pretrial release following the death of her 2-year-old son. (Will County Detention Facility)

"This is a tragedy for the Walsh family, all of whom are mourning the loss of this child," Lyon said. "It is also a tragedy in that Corie herself was experiencing a psychotic episode at the time this happened."
MOM ‘VERY INVESTED’ IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE HIRES CASEY ANTHONY ATTORNEY AFTER ALLEGEDLY KILLING SON: DOCS
While Lyon described Walsh as experiencing a psychotic episode, legal experts say a psychiatric diagnosis alone does not determine whether someone meets Illinois' legal standard for insanity.

"The definition of insanity is, as a result of a mental defect or disability, that you're unable to appreciate the criminality of your conduct," Richard S. Kling, a clinical professor at Chicago-Kent College of Law and former Cook County public defender who has handled insanity cases, told Fox News Digital.
ACCUSED NC KILLER MOM PLANS INSANITY DEFENSE — AS RETIRED JUDGE SAYS MORE MAY FOLLOW LINDSAY CLANCY STRATEGY
Corie Walsh, right, poses with her husband and children inside a church. Walsh faces three counts of first-degree murder in the death of her 2-year-old son, Barrett. (CREDIT: Facebook/ Corie Walsh)

Kling said psychiatrists first determine whether someone meets the criteria for a recognized mental illness before courts consider whether that illness prevented the person from appreciating the criminality of their conduct. He also said defendants who pursue an insanity defense must present evidence they were legally insane at the time of the alleged offense. Illinois also recognizes a separate verdict of guilty but mentally ill, distinct from a finding of not guilty by reason of insanity.
But behind the scenes, a battle over Walsh's mental health care is unfolding.

Following her arrest, Walsh was treated at Silver Cross Hospital for self-inflicted wounds to her wrists and thighs. According to her defense team, hospital doctors recommended she receive 24/7 psychiatric care upon her discharge.
Corie Walsh, top left, pictured with her husband and children wearing matching holiday pajamas on a couch. (CREDIT: Facebook/ Corie Walsh)
However, Walsh's attorneys said she is not receiving her prescribed medication inside the Will County Adult Detention Facility.
The Will County Sheriff's Office, which oversees the jail, did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment regarding Walsh's medical treatment.
The defense's account differs sharply from prosecutors' allegations.
LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE SCORES ‘EXTREMELY HELPFUL’ PSYCHOSIS CONCESSION AS EXPERT FLAGS NEXT HURDLE
Along with three counts of first-degree murder, prosecutors also allege Walsh was planning to poison her husband Michael Walsh, before her son's death.

Further details regarding the alleged poisoning plot – including how far along the plan was or what substance was involved – were not immediately disclosed in court. Michael Walsh was traveling out of state when the couple's son was killed and flew home that evening. He has not responded to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Speaking generally and not about Corie Walsh's case specifically, Kling said evidence that a defendant planned or attempted to conceal a crime can become relevant in an insanity case because prosecutors may argue it shows the defendant understood the criminality of the conduct.
Walsh allegedly told police she killed the toddler because she believed he was the "devil," a petition seeking to deny her pretrial release states.
Defendant Lindsay Clancy watches jurors enter the courtroom during her murder trial on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)

Witnesses also told investigators Walsh had recently grown "very invested" in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, a Massachusetts mother who was charged with murdering her three children during an alleged bout of postpartum psychosis.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Walsh allegedly texted friends about the Clancy case as late as 12:30 p.m. on the day of her son's killing.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
"It is our hope that through a thorough presentation and investigation of the facts, that all of us will come to see this heartbreak for what it is," Lyon said.
SEND US A TIP
The competing claims have prompted a deeper investigative look into Walsh's background.
GOT A TIP?

Kling said a documented history of mental illness, psychiatric treatment and medication can become critical evidence in an insanity case because psychiatrists often examine a person's mental state before and after an alleged crime to help evaluate their condition at the time of the offense.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Fox News Digital has reached out to multiple immediate family members, in-laws and former neighbors to determine whether there were prior warning signs, isolation or documented mental health struggles leading up to the holiday weekend.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Additionally, Fox News Digital has filed public records requests with local police departments seeking years of 911 dispatch logs and wellness checks connected to Walsh's current and former residences.

Because of the victim's age, the three first-degree murder counts carry a potential sentencing range of 60 to 100 years in prison, to be served at 100% upon conviction.

title: FBI arrests suspect accused of paying LA homeless to forge signatures using registered voters' identities
summary: James Brass allegedly ran a ballot harvesting scheme on Los Angeles' Skid Row, paying homeless people to sign petitions using stolen voter identities.
story: The Department of Justice warns of widespread voter fraud in California after a woman pleaded guilty to paying homeless people to register to vote and sign ballot petitions. Officials highlight how lax state laws facilitate such activity, impacting state and federal elections.

A California man was arrested early Thursday amid allegations that he and two others paid homeless people living in Los Angeles' Skid Row neighborhood to sign petitions using the stolen identities of registered voters in an effort to qualify ballot initiatives for local elections.

James Brass, 47, a.k.a. "Lord," was taken into federal custody in Victorville, 85 miles northeast of Los Angeles, the Justice Department said. Brass and the other two defendants — Courtney Price, 49, of Jacksonville, Florida, and Jateisha Herron, 33, of Boron, California — are charged with conspiracy to commit identity fraud in furtherance of a state felony.
Brass and Price are additionally charged with identity fraud in furtherance of a state felony.
TRUMP ELECTION FRAUD CRACKDOWN LANDS FIRST ARREST, PUTTING LONGTIME CRITICS IN WHITE HOUSE CROSSHAIRS
A view of a homeless encampment on Skid Row on Sept. 23, 2021 in Los Angeles. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
"Securing American elections from criminal interference is of the utmost importance to the FBI," Director Kash Patel wrote on X. "If you mess with our elections, the FBI will find you."
Brass allegedly orchestrated the ballot harvesting scheme through the management of a team of signature collectors, as well as collecting signatures himself, federal prosecutors said.
EX-NEW JERSEY MAYOR, HER HUSBAND CHARGED FOR USING FAKE BALLOT SIGNATURES AFTER SHE PLEADED GUILTY TO DUI

James Brass is accused of running a scheme in which homeless people in Los Angeles' Skid Row were paid to sign petitions to qualify ballot initiatives with the stolen identities of registered California voters. (Getty Images; Justice Department)
Price and Herron were employed by Brass, authorities said.

From February through August, the trio allegedly gathered the identities of voters from a database and handed the information to homeless people on Skid Row, a neighborhood in downtown Los Angeles that contains one of the largest concentrations of homeless people in the United States.
FORMER DEM MAYORAL CANDIDATE ADMITS FORGING VOTER REGISTRATION APPLICATIONS
Tents and encampments remain visible near the Skid Row Care Campus, a taxpayer-funded facility that provides healthcare, housing assistance and harm-reduction services. (Fox 11 Los Angeles)
FBI RAIDS SOROS-BACKED VOTER GROUP’S HEADQUARTERS IN REPORTED FRAUD PROBE
The homeless participants were allegedly paid to sign petitions in the names of the voters.

After the petitions were signed, Brass and Herron signed declarations at the bottom of the petitions, declaring that they personally witnessed the named registered voters sign the petitions and that each signature was, to the best of their knowledge, "the genuine signature of the person whose name it purports to be," federal prosecutors said.
The bogus petitions were turned in by Brass and Herron to petition coordinators. In total, authorities claim Brass was paid $41,600 from one petition management company.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said the alleged conduct "undermines the confidence voters have in our election systems," adding his office "will vigorously investigate and charge anyone involved in corrupting our elections."
All three defendants face up to five years in prison per count if convicted. Brass is expected to appear in court Thursday.

title: 20-year-old Michigan man killed by possible lightning strike in Florida

A 20-year-old Michigan man who had moved to Central Florida just days earlier to begin the Disney College Program was killed in an apparent lightning strike while on a walking path, authorities and his family said.
Matthew Eric Jenkins of Shelby Township, Michigan, was found unresponsive Tuesday evening on a walking path behind a hotel in Celebration, according to the Osceola County Sheriff's Office.
Jenkins' father told WESH-TV his son had moved to Central Florida last week to begin the internship program at Walt Disney World.
AMERICAN TOURIST KILLED BY LIGHTNING WHILE HIKING SICILY'S MOUNT ETNA
Deputies were called to the path in the 700 block of Bloom Street at about 6:25 p.m. Investigators said lightning had struck nearby. (FOX35 Orlando WOFL)
Deputies were called to the path in the 700 block of Bloom Street at about 6:25 p.m. Investigators said lightning had struck nearby.
Spyro Betz, who had been walking nearby before reaching his car, told FOX35 Orlando he heard a powerful crack of lightning.
"I heard the big crack of lightning that was like right overhead," Betz said.
He initially thought it had struck a building.

Matthew Eric Jenkins of Shelby Township, Mich., was found unresponsive Tuesday evening on a walking path behind a hotel in Celebration, according to the Osceola County Sheriff's Office. (FOX35 Orlando WOFL)
"When I heard the lightning strike, I expected it hit the building or something like that or hit the hotel. I didn't expect it to hit a person," Betz said.
Felipe Costa told WESH-TV he ran toward the path after hearing the lightning and found Jenkins on the ground.
LIGHTNING STRIKE TURNS 100-FOOT DINOSAUR INTO RAGING FIREBALL, STUNNING ONLOOKERS
"As soon as I heard that, I started running, and I came over here [where it happened]. That's when I saw the man," Costa said.
A woman joined Costa and began performing CPR while they waited for first responders.
The sheriff's office said detectives are awaiting the medical examiner's determination of Jenkins' official cause of death. (FOX35 Orlando WOFL)
Jenkins was taken to AdventHealth Celebration, where he was pronounced dead.

title: Pilot rescued after World War II-era plane crashes at Pennsylvania airport
summary: The World War II-era plane had been airborne just nine minutes before crashing at Heritage Field Airport in Pennsylvania, causing a fuel leak on site.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A World War II-era plane crashed while attempting to land at a Pennsylvania airport Wednesday evening, trapping the pilot inside the overturned aircraft before police and an airport employee freed him, authorities said.
Limerick Township police responded to Heritage Field Airport around 7:17 p.m. and found the small aircraft upside down on the runway with the pilot, its only occupant, trapped inside.
An airport employee and officers freed the pilot from his parachute and pulled him from the plane, police said.
FIERY SAN DIEGO PLANE CRASH KILLS 2
Police and an airport employee pulled a trapped pilot to safety following the crash of a WWII-era aircraft on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (FOX29 Philadelphia WTXF)

"We got reports the pilot was trapped in the plane. On our arrival, they were pulling him out. So there was no extrication needed by the fire department," Limerick Township Fire Chief Ken Shuler told FOX29 Philadelphia.
The pilot was conscious and able to stand but had visible cuts, police said. He was treated at the scene by Freedom Valley Medical Rescue and taken to a hospital.
The pilot was transported to Reading Trauma Center and was alert and talking after the crash, according to FOX29. No further update on his condition was available.
The pilot was the only occupant aboard the WWII-era plane when it crashed at Heritage Field Airport on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (FOX29 Philadelphia WTXF)
The single-engine plane had taken off from Pottstown and was headed to Quakertown, the station reported, citing Limerick Township officials. It had been in the air for about nine minutes.
FATAL AIR AMBULANCE CRASH EXPOSES GROWING GPS DANGER FACING US FLIGHTS
The crash caused a fuel leak, according to the outlet, and firefighters remained at the airport to address the spill and watch for a possible fire.

Heritage Field Airport, formerly Pottstown Municipal Airport, serves private and recreational aircraft. The airport remained closed Wednesday night while crews handled the fuel leak and removed the plane.
It was unclear what caused the crash at Heritage Field Airport on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (FOX29 Philadelphia WTXF)
Police said they notified the Federal Aviation Administration's Eastern Region Operations Center after the crash.

title: 9/11 hero Welles Crowther's firehouse president reveals what shaped the 'man in the red bandana'
summary: Welles Crowther's volunteer firehouse shaped the hero who saved 18 lives on 9/11. Its president reveals how training and community forged the legend.
story: David "Trevor" Gottlieb, the president of Empire Hook and Ladder Company No. 1 in Upper Nyack, New York, explains how his volunteer firehouse helped shape the heroism of Welles Crowther, also known as 9/11 heroic "Man in the Red Bandana."

When President Donald Trump awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously to Welles Crowther for his heroism during the 9/11 terrorist attack during a Tuesday ceremony, Crowther's mother Alison specifically mentioned the Upper Nyack, New York, volunteer firehouse where Welles got his training.

"Welles... would not have been able to do what he did as effectively on 9/11 if it had not been for the training and experience he gained as a member of Empire Hook and Ladder Company Number One of Upper Nyack," she said.
Crowther, as Empire Hook and Ladder Company Number One president David "Trevor" Gottlieb explained to Fox News Digital, was forged in the volunteer firehouse's traditions of community and sacrifice.
FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP’S 9/11 TRIBUTE TO FEATURE MASSIVE PIECE OF GROUND ZERO HISTORY AT WHITE HOUSE
"I joined in '88, he was five years younger than me so probably '93 is when he first started," Gottlieb told Fox News Digital.
Welles Crowther at Empire Hook and Ladder Company No. 1 in Upper Nyack, New York. (Robert McGreevy/Fox News)

"I was still away in college. I came back and worked with him from '93 on. Volunteer fire service is usually multi-generational, and Welles' father, Jefferson, was an ex-captain. He was our treasurer, just, you know, part of the fabric of the company. Kid's been coming down here since he could walk," Gottlieb said.

In the 25 years since the terrorist attacks on 9/11, Crowther's story has become something of a legend. Known as the "man in the red bandana," Crowther carried a red bandana on his wallet while working as a stockbroker in the South Tower. When the attack struck, he immediately leapt to action, helping usher people to safety as the building burned around him.

"Welles Crowther was in the towers. He was working for a trading firm that day. And he assisted with the rescue of at least 18, I think was the final count they got. Eighteen civilians that he helped lead to safety and ultimately lost his life doing that," Gottlieb said.

"I think what Welles' impression he left upon us was anything's possible. And when you're faced with, you know, 108 floors and the chaos and the destruction all around you, when you sit back and rely on your training, on how you were brought up, I think that makes your job much easier," he continued.
Plaque commemorating Welles Crowther's 9/11 sacrifice outside Empire Hook and Ladder Company No. 1 in Upper Nyack, New York. (Robert McGreevy/Fox News)
Gottlieb credited Crowther's instinct to help people without hesitation to his upbringing at Empire Hook and Ladder.

"This fire company is stocked with great people. We have five generations, some of the families go back in this company. And it's great to see the pride, the dedication, commitment to a community that exists when you have such a special place like this," he said.
Empire Hook and Ladder Company No. 1 President David "Trevor" Gottlieb points to the original charter for the firehouse on Sept. 9, 2026. (Robert McGreevy/Fox News)

"I would lay my life down for any one of them. And I think they would do the same for me," Gottlieb said of his firehouse family. "That's something that's kind of instilled in when you join here. And it's perfected throughout years and multi-generations of that behavior," he continued.
9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD'
Crowther's ultimate sacrifice was indicative not only of his upbringing in Empire Hook and Ladder, but of the spirit that inhabits all volunteer firefighters, Gottlieb argued.
Empire Hook and Ladder Company No.1 in Upper Nyack, New York on Sept. 9, 2026. (Robert McGreevy/Fox News)

"When you look at what happened that day, somebody made the decision to not run. They made the decision to stay and help. And they didn't ask if you're a Republican, a Democrat, a Muslim, a Jew, a Catholic," he told Fox News Digital.

title: Lindsay Clancy's attorney asks judge to acquit her outright, ending case and barring a retrial
summary: A fellow juror reveals the lone holdout in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial used an exercise band and water bottle to reenact the strangulation.
story: The latest move by Lindsay Clancy's defense to have her declared not guilty before a retrial can take place is routine but unlikely to succeed, according to a retired Massachusetts judge who is following the case.
Reporter's note: If you were a member of the jury who would like to speak out, please contact me at Adam.Sabes@fox.com.

Lindsay Clancy's attorney is asking a judge to acquit her after a mistrial was declared on Friday, arguing the trial evidence was legally insufficient to prove she was criminally responsible for killing her children.

Clancy, 36, faced three counts of first-degree murder in connection with the slayings of her children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — who were discovered strangled at the family's home in January 2023. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Friday after jurors could not agree on a unanimous verdict, with the panel split 11-1.

"The argument by Mr. Reddington is not based on the holdout juror — it is that the evidence was insufficient to support a finding that the defendant, Ms. Clancy, was criminally responsible," says retired Massachusetts Judge Jack Lu, who breaks down the filing below.

The motion, filed by defense attorney Kevin Reddington on Thursday, asked Sullivan to enter a finding of not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility on each charge. He wants the motion to be heard at a hearing on Sept. 29.
LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT

Lindsay Clancy looks at jurors as Judge Sullivan asks them to start deliberations for a sixth day during her murder trial on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Pool Photo by Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger)
"A hung jury is not a verdict; jeopardy does not terminate on a hung jury, and a mistrial ordinarily permits retrial," Reddington conceded in the filing.

However, he argued that 11 of the 12 jurors "applied the reasonable doubt standard" and concluded that the prosecutors hadn't proven Clancy was criminally responsible. The holdout, the filing suggests and other jurors have alleged, allegedly ignored his own doubts and insisted on a guilty verdict.
In particular, Reddington targeted the prosecution's witnesses.

"Taken at their strongest, these show that Ms. Clancy could perform familiar tasks and act in sequence," he wrote of the Commonwealth's rebuttal experts. "They do not show that she could appreciated wrongfulness or conform her donut to the law. That is the element. Nothing else counts."
Prosecutors short-circuited their own case when the Commonwealth's forensic experts agreed that Clancy had a serious mental illness on the day she strangled her kids, Reddington argued.
Read the filing:

"The treating clinicians who saw Ms. Clancy in the weeks before January 24 testified that she presented with postpartum depression and anxiety and that they did not observe psychosis; that testimony bears on which illness she had, not on whether she had one, and depression and anxiety of the severity that led to psychiatric admission are themselves a mental disease or defect," Reddington wrote. "No rational jury could find beyond a reasonable doubt that she had no mental disease or defect when the Commonwealth's own proof established that she did."
Reddington cited Rule 25 under the Massachusetts Rules of Criminal Procedure, which Lu said governs motions like the one filed Thursday.

"This translates to the defendant moving for a court-ordered not guilty claiming that the defendant is entitled to a not guilty as a matter of law," he told Fox News Digital. "In this case it is based on the claim that the prosecution witnesses were insufficient to prove that the defendant was criminally responsible."
Such filings are routine, he said, but seldom prevail. In his own time on the bench, he said he could not remember granting one.

Lindsay Clancy was indicted on three counts each of murder in the 2023 deaths of her 5-year-old daughter Cora, 3-year-old son Dawson and 7-month-old son Callan. She pleaded not guilty to the charges. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)
"I cannot remember ever seeing one of these motions acted on," Lu said. "Mr. Reddington is asking to wipe the entire case out and that is a big ask."
What the other jurors are saying:
Nick Dargie, 25, told ABC News that the lone holdout juror at one point attempted to mimic the way Clancy killed her three kids with an exercise band and water bottle.
"He took the exercise band out of the bag, grabbed an empty water bottle and tied the band around the water bottle and pulled it," Dargie said. "I was just so shocked that he did that."
Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)
WHAT IS A TUEY-RODRIGUEZ CHARGE? JUDGE GIVES INSTRUCTION TO DEADLOCKED LINDSAY CLANCY JURY
"I was shocked, it didn‘t make any sense to me. Like, we‘re not in here to play detective or it‘s not a game of Clue. like, this is serious. I asked him why," he added.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
Dargie said the holdout juror refused to explain how witness testimony helped prove his stance.
SEND US A TIP

"There was several times I would ask him to show us evidence or, you know, describe a witness testimony that helped to prove what he was saying, and ... he couldn't," Dargie said. "There wasn't a single piece of evidence or witness testimony that he used to prove why he was thinking the way he was, which is why we ultimately sent in that note."

Kevin J. Reddington addresses the media as he arrives at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. Reddington is representing Lindsay Clancy on murder charges for the deaths of her three children. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)
LINDSAY CLANCY'S LAWYER REVEALS POST-MISTRIAL STRATEGY AS RETRIAL LOOMS
He was referring to the note sent by the jury foreperson, who reported that one juror was refusing to follow the court's instructions on reasonable doubt.

After several jurors came forward about what went on in the deliberation room, Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, told "CBS Mornings" Wednesday that he would be filing a new motion to dismiss based on double jeopardy.

"I would defend that person's right to be a holdout for a month," Reddington said. "That's what the system is based on, but when the forelady indicated clearly and unequivocally in the jury question that this person had doubt, reasonable doubt as we know now, and just refused to listen to the judge's instruction on the law, that's when I was upset."

title: Salvation Army responder opens up on 9/11 cancer battle, phone call that changed his life
summary: Salvation Army responder Ken Tregellas battled stage 4 cancer after months at Ground Zero but says he wouldn't have changed a thing about serving.
story: Fox News senior correspondent Eric Shawn reports on NYPD Detective Jillian Suarez carrying on the legacy of her father, officer Ramon Suarez, who was killed while rescuing people during the September 11th attacks.
Twenty-five years later, the grief of Sept. 11 remains with Salvation Army responder Ken Tregellas, and so does his conviction that his experience was worth the sacrifice.
"My kids had asked me over the years, ‘Dad, knowing you'd get cancer, would you still have served?’ And I told them, ‘I wouldn't have changed a thing. It was an honor,’" he said.

During this year's anniversary, Tregellas is looking back on the decision that took him from his family in Wisconsin to Ground Zero, where he spent months caring for people searching for answers about their loved ones.

It started as a typical Tuesday morning. Tregellas was getting his twins ready for school when he saw the North Tower had been struck. Like millions of Americans, he was confused. It wasn't until United Flight 175 struck the second tower that he knew America was under attack.
SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POSSIBLE LINK BETWEEN 9/11 AND ACCELERATED AGING
Twenty-five years after 9/11, Salvation Army responder Ken Tregellas reflects on months spent caring for recovery workers and families searching for loved ones. (Ken Tregellas)
Within a few hours, his phone rang, a call that would change the course of his life.

Tregellas previously operated The Salvation Army's emergency assistance programs in underserved communities. So when he was asked to be the Red Zone coordinator at Ground Zero, he knew he needed to deploy.
When flights opened back up, Tregellas flew from Wisconsin to New York City. Only four other passengers were on board.
"I'd never been to New York in my life, so I really didn't have, other than pictures and movies, I didn't have anything to compare it to," he said.
Tregellas could not have known that his first glimpse of New York would come under such unimaginable circumstances.

Walking into the Red Zone in Lower Manhattan, he encountered a scene unlike anything he had ever witnessed. Smoke continued to rise from the twisted shards of metal, while the remains of the World Trade Center smoldered in a massive pile.
"I was still pretty shocked that there was still fire burning," Tregellas said. "I mean, the piles where the two main towers were, were still burning every time they were picking up debris."
Ken Tregellas helped lead Salvation Army relief efforts at Ground Zero before later developing cancer linked to his exposure after the attacks. (Ken Tregellas)
Working at Ground Zero
As the Red Zone coordinator, Tregellas was responsible for overseeing all of The Salvation Army's efforts on the ground.
"Our job was really to take care of the people that were looking for bodies at that point," Tregellas said. "It was more of a recovery effort."

Six tents were set up at the site, including makeshift cafeterias and sleeping areas that quickly became a refuge for workers. Weary responders arrived with boots melted by the intense heat of the metal. They could replace their shoes, grab a meal, rest and talk with others about what they had witnessed at the pile.

The Salvation Army provided more than food, clothing and shelter. Beyond basic necessities, workers received counseling and other forms of spiritual relief to make the grueling work at Ground Zero somewhat manageable. Tregellas emphasized that the organization's mission went beyond meeting physical needs. It was also there to provide emotional and spiritual care.
9/11 VICTIM'S IDENTITY EMERGES NEARLY 25 YEARS LATER AFTER DNA BREAKTHROUGH CRACKS MYSTERY

Prayer was offered around the clock to anyone who wanted it. Tregellas said one of the most striking parts of the experience was the diversity of people who came to the site including families who traveled from around the world searching for answers about their loved ones.

"There were people coming from all over the world to look at the site and try to understand why they weren't hearing anything about loved ones," Tregellas said. "You had to listen. You were dealing with interpreters. It was a whole different thing than I think most of us had ever dealt with before."

At Ground Zero, Tregellas said, the work extended far beyond recovery. The Salvation Army was caring for people in the middle of unimaginable loss, providing a meal, a place to rest, a prayer or simply someone willing to listen.
Responders work to clear rubble at Ground Zero in New York City on Oct. 8, 2001. (Ken Tregellas)
The weight of recovery
Although he had worked for The Salvation Army for almost 32 years and witnessed many heartbreaking moments, the weight of what Tregellas witnessed at Ground Zero followed him home.

After seeing the scale of the loss in New York, he found himself struggling to process other disasters the way he once had. Returning to disaster sites, such as floods, where people had lost their homes and belongings, he found himself comparing those losses to the lives lost on Sept. 11.
"Seeing the depth of tragedy of New York, so much loss of life, and just how large and devastating it was, I really had a hard time on the empathy part," Tregellas said.

He knew the loss of a home, furniture or clothing was devastating to the people experiencing it. But privately, he found himself thinking about how different those losses were from what he had witnessed in New York.

"I was thinking in my head, ‘that's just stuff, you didn't lose your life," he said. "And I compared everything in my life, even my children I would tell them, doesn't compare to the loss of life. I had a really hard time getting over that."
Lingering effect of 9/11
Cancer certifications have risen from 3,204 in 2015 to 57,044 this year between workers, Twin Tower survivors, and Manhattan residents, The New York Post reports.
Ten years after Sept. 11, Tregellas became a part of those statistics.
When Tregellas was having trouble eating and swallowing, he went to the doctor, not thinking much of it and unaware that his sacrifice helping others at Ground Zero would come at a cost.
During the visit, doctors found cancer in his tonsils.
"I hadn't really dealt with cancer at all. And then as they started to look at it and it showed up in a couple other places," he said.
FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE
Smoke rises from debris at Ground Zero on Oct. 8, 2001. Tregellas recalls his surprise at seeing fire was still burning in the rubble of the Twin Towers. (Ken Tregellas)
He was then diagnosed with stage 4 mantle B-cell lymphoma, and the treatment was intense.
"It was probably eight months of chemotherapy and long stays in the hospital, and it was a very rare cancer."

According to the Victims Compensation Fund, cancer has become one of the lingering health consequences of 9/11, as responders and survivors continue to face illnesses linked to their exposure at Ground Zero.

There were more than 69 reported types of cancer, with non-melanoma skin cancer being the most common, with more than 18,400 cases among responders and survivors, while lymphoma, on the rarer side, accounted for around 2,500 cases among responders and survivors.
The 9/11 VCF was able to assist him with his treatment.
"I went through a bunch of chemotherapies. I had a stem cell transplant that was, they said, my best chance to survive."
About a year after completing that first treatment, the cancer came back in his other tonsil.
"I thought we were just going to do the same thing again, which I wasn't excited about, but I was thinking, ‘Well, it worked once, it can work again,’" he said.
Doctors thought that would be too harsh on his body, so they put him on ibrutinib, a drug used to treat certain blood cancers and one he’d be on until this year.
"And boy, I was on that drug till February of this year, and it put me back in remission, I never had any cancer since," he said.
Tregellas says he would return to Ground Zero after 9/11, even knowing it would later lead to a cancer diagnosis. (Ken Tregellas)
Keeping the memory alive
Today, Tregellas spends part of his time speaking, often to students, about what he witnessed on 9/11. For many of them, the attacks are something they have only learned about in history books.
When speaking to Fox News, he got emotional. He took a beat with a heavy sigh that held weight as if sharing his experiences with younger generations brought him back in time to those moments.
Tregellas knows he and others on the ground will never forget. But feels it’s vital to bring it to the forefront so the younger generations know, so they can remember.
"That's where we bring it back," Tregella said. "It's an important part of history. And yeah, it united us. I think it still does at times."
This week, on the 25th anniversary, he says most of all he looks forward to the shared solidarity.

"It's a week of, ‘we did it,’ this is how we did it and let's look back and learn that together we can do a whole bunch," Tregellas said. "And yeah, I'm proud to be a part of that."

title: Amazon cargo pilot repeatedly warned aircraft was 'too fast' before deadly Miami crash, NTSB says
summary: The National Transportation Safety Board says one pilot warned the other was "too fast" for nearly two minutes before the Amazon cargo plane crash.
story: The NTSB said the thrust reversers and speed brakes did not deploy when an Amazon cargo jet overran the runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, according to available data.

One of the pilots of the Amazon cargo plane that crashed in Miami last weekend, killing five people on the ground, repeatedly warned the other pilot the aircraft was "too fast" during the final approach and after touchdown, according to newly released information from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).
The pilots have been identified as Capt. Joseph Carroll, 55, and First Officer Jaime Felipe Silva Molina, 37, both of cargo airline 21 Air.
The NTSB did not identify which pilot was making the warnings or which pilot was receiving them as they approached Miami International Airport on Sunday.
The warnings continued for nearly two minutes, but the receiving pilot never gave "a consistent verbal response" to them, according to the NTSB's summary of the cockpit voice recorder.

A parking lot filled with Tesla Cybercabs is seen in the foreground as the nose of a Prime Air cargo plane rests on the ground on Sept. 7, 2026, after the aircraft overran the runway and struck cars the previous day at Miami International Airport in Miami, Florida. (CHANDAN KHANNA / AFP via Getty Images)
AMAZON CARGO JET PILOT REPORTEDLY TOLD WIFE, 'MY CAREER IS OVER' SHORTLY AFTER DEADLY CRASH

Information from the flight data recorder shows the plane made an unstable approach in strong winds. After touchdown, the pilots briefly tried to take off again by advancing the throttles and releasing the brakes before abandoning the maneuver about four seconds later.
The cockpit voice recorder also captured a series of automated warnings, including repeated "sink rate" and "too low terrain" alerts, as the aircraft descended toward the runway.
FlightRadar24 data indicates the Amazon plane first touched down nearly 5,000 feet into the airport's 9,360-foot Runway 30, leaving it with less than half the remaining runway to stop.
Officials inspect an Amazon cargo plane two days after it overshot a runway at Miami International Airport on Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, in Miami. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)
VICTIMS IDENTIFIED IN FATAL AMAZON CARGO JET CRASH AT MIAMI AIRPORT

The plane touched down awkwardly before the pilots briefly attempted a go-around, then resumed braking, according to the NTSB. The Boeing 767 then barreled about 1,300 feet beyond the end of the runway and struck a van, killing the five people inside.
The five people killed in the van were part of a crew that cleaned planes at the airport, NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy said Tuesday.
A crushed vehicle is seen after an Amazon cargo plane crashed off the runway at Miami International Airport in Miami on Sept. 6, 2026. (Al Diaz/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Five others were injured, including two who were in critical condition as of Tuesday. The pilots, who were injured as well, were treated and released before speaking with investigators on Wednesday, according to The Associated Press.
The full transcript of the cockpit conversation has not yet been released as the investigation continues.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Charlie Kirk assassination: New UVU president says it will continue to 'host the frays,' embrace free speech
summary: UVU's new president revealed his two daughters were just yards from Charlie Kirk's assassination and vowed to continue fostering free speech on campus.
story: "We don't jump in the fray, but we host the fray," Utah Valley University's new president Dr. Jon Anderson tells Fox News Digital as the campus prepares to mark one year since Charlie Kirk's murder. (Credit: Alec Thornock for Fox News Digital)

PROVO, Utah — A year after Charlie Kirk was assassinated in the central courtyard at Utah Valley University, school officials will close campus for the day — as the school's new president revealed his own daughters were at the scene and vowed to continue to foster free speech in higher education.

Dr. Jon Anderson, who joined UVU just before the start of the fall 2026 semester, was in his prior role as president of Pennsylvania Western University when Kirk was shot and killed on Sept. 10, 2025, but his family has roots in Utah, he told Fox News Digital in a sitdown interview.
His wife called him to break the news, he said.
JUDGE IN ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON'S CASE EXPLAINS WHY DEATH PENALTY REMAINS ON TABLE IN WRITTEN ORDER
Charlie Kirk speaks at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025 in Orem, Utah, shortly before his assassination. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)
"I had two daughters and a son-in-law. They were about 10 yards from the assassination when it happened," he said. "And so I knew that our future would be tied to it in one way or the other."

"When the opportunity came up to come home — this is the place that I'm from — and help this institution move forward and heal, it's something I leaned into immediately," he told Fox News Digital. "I wanted to be here to help in any way that I could, and I have found since coming here, this place is so resilient. Its people are gritty, they're ready to move forward, and they're to learn from everything that we can learn from that day."
ERIKA KIRK REFLECTS ON FIRST YEAR OF GRIEF AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION IN NYT ESSAY
UVU students pause to reflect as they gaze over the spot where Charlie Kirk was assassinated, Orem, Utah, Wednesday, Sept. 17, 2025. (Matthew Finn/Fox News)
With students, faculty and other campus staff dealing with Kirk's assassination in their own ways, Anderson said the campus will be closed on Sept. 10, the one-year mark.

"I think one thing all of us at UVU have learned is that traumatic events, sometimes there's an initial reaction and sometimes there is a delayed reaction, and it's important for us to be very empathetic with each other as everyone goes through the healing process in their own way," he added.
ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION
UVU students pause to reflect as they gaze over the spot where Charlie Kirk was assassinated, Orem, Utah, Wednesday, Sept. 17, 2025. (Matthew Finn/Fox News)
Although the school is not hosting an official event, he said Turning Point USA plans to hold its own memorial on campus.
"We want people to have their own space to heal in their own way," he said. "TPUSA is using some space on campus to hold their event here, and we are supportive and reflective of that."
HOW CHARLIE KIRK INSPIRED HIS MENTOR'S FIGHT TO DEFEND REALITY

Kirk was a founder of TPUSA and was speaking at an event sponsored by its UVU chapter at the heart of campus when he was killed. The group will hold its memorial at UVU's UCCU Center at 6:30 p.m. MT on Sept. 10.

A memorial honoring conservative influencer Charlie Kirk has steadily grown outside Utah Valley University's campus in the wake of his assassination on Wednesday, Sept. 10, 2025. (Fox News Digital/Deirdre Heavey)
As for plans for a potential permanent memorial, Anderson said work is underway from a group including board members and students.

"They're sorting through lots of voices, getting people to the table to talk through what that might look like, looking at other institutions, what they have done," he said. "I can't guarantee that it's going to be anytime soon, but I can tell you if and when that happens, it will be thoughtfully done and well placed."
INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES

Many locals and students returning to campus on Monday, Sept. 15, 2025, stopped by a memorial at Utah Valley University to pay their respects to conservative influencer Charlie Kirk. (Fox News Digital/Deirdre Heavey)
While the public university is "politically neutral and apolitical," Anderson said it's important to provide a space to share varied viewpoints for the students' benefit.

"We don't jump in the fray, but we host the frays," he said.

"We allow people to come in and focus on civil dialogue, engaging in new and good ideas, and that's where we hope to excel," he continued. "A place that anyone can come with any idea, have a place for open, honest, violence-free debate, and that's what our future is, and that is what institutions of higher education are, when they are at their best."

title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer reveals post-mistrial strategy as retrial looms
summary: Lindsay Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington reveals his strategy after the mistrial, urging prosecutors to pursue treatment instead of prison while appealing to President Donald Trump.
story: Defense attorney Kevin Reddington discusses the next legal steps following the mistrial, says he'll appeal if necessary and responds to criticism over his comments about the lone holdout juror.

Kevin Reddington is laying out an aggressive, multipronged strategy to keep Lindsay Clancy from facing another jury — and, ultimately, from going to prison — as prosecutors weigh whether to retry the Massachusetts mother after last week's mistrial.

In his first interview with Fox News since the jury deadlocked after seven weeks of testimony, Clancy's attorney detailed his plans to challenge any retrial in court, push prosecutors to reduce the charges, seek a bench trial instead of a jury trial and argue for psychiatric treatment rather than incarceration.
A Norfolk Superior Court jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict last week, prompting Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial.
Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity to charges stemming from the 2023 deaths of her three children. Prosecutors have not yet announced whether they will retry the case.
LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR WHO BACKED THE DEFENSE ALSO PUBLICLY CHEERED KAREN READ'S ACQUITTAL
Kevin J. Reddington addresses the media outside of Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., on Thursday, September 3, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

Reddington said his first priority is arguing later this month that a retrial would violate Clancy's constitutional protection against double jeopardy because the mistrial was declared over the defense's objection. If that effort fails, he said he hopes Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz will reduce the charges to second-degree murder, so Clancy could waive her right to a jury trial and instead have her case decided by a judge.

"I would like to see Tim reduce it to a second degree... and fashion something where Lindsay gets the mental, physical help that she needs rather than criminal prosecution, because I would not ever, ever in a million years have that woman go to Framingham State Prison," Reddington said.
He said he would seek a sentence centered on probation and mandatory psychiatric treatment in a secure facility rather than incarceration.
LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT

Kevin Reddington, defense attorney for Lindsay Clancy, and Lindsay Clancy look on as Judge William Sullivan (out of frame) instructs the jury to continue deliberating, during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on September 4, 2026. (Greg Derr / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
Reddington also stood by his criticism of the lone holdout juror, rejecting accusations that his post-trial remarks amounted to intimidation.

"I was angry because of his refusal to follow the law," Reddington told Fox News. "That's what I was angry about. That's why I felt that the other jurors, after their seven-week sacrifice, were robbed. That's why I felt for Lindsay, because she deserved to have the verdict that she was entitled to."
He added that he would have defended the juror's right to hold firm if he had simply disagreed with the other 11 jurors on the merits of the case.

"If this guy just said, 'look, I think the government proved their case, and I'm not bending,' I would be the first person to defend his right to do that because that's the jury system," Reddington insisted.
Reddington also renewed his call for President Donald Trump to weigh in, saying he hopes the president will personally urge Cruz not to pursue another trial.
"I'd like the president to pick up the phone and speak with Tim Cruz," Reddington said.
"If you do that, that'd be great. I mean, they're both Republicans."
Reddington argued such a conversation would not be improper because the decision over whether to retry Clancy rests with the district attorney, calling it "an executive decision."

Despite repeatedly criticizing Cruz in the days following the mistrial, Reddington also offered a pair of rare public concessions, saying he regretted accusing the district attorney of not knowing the names of Clancy's three children and boasting that he had "crushed" him at trial.
"I had no right to accuse the man of not knowing the names of those kids and I regret that," Reddington said.

Reddington also said he "probably should have used a different set of words" after declaring he had "crushed" Cruz, adding that he should have simply said he believed the defense presented the stronger case while emphasizing that the burden of proof rested with the prosecution.
Lyndsay Clancy's defense lawyer, Kevin Reddington, arrives at Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., Thursday, September 3, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The comments mark one of Reddington's first public acknowledgments that he went too far in some of his post-trial remarks, even as he continues to press for a resolution that prioritizes treatment over incarceration.

title: Brooklyn teachers who witnessed 9/11 as children reveal what they want the next generation to remember
summary: A Brooklyn principal watched a twin towers collapse from a school roof, not knowing her FDNY firefighter brother was underneath the rubble that day.
story: Educators at St. Patrick Catholic Academy in Brooklyn who saw blackened skies and frightened classrooms on Sept. 11 share the lessons they now pass on to their students who know the attacks only as history.

When Americans mark 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks on Friday, Kathleen Palladino will remember the day through the eyes of a New York City 6-year-old who did not yet understand what she was seeing.
Palladino was a kindergartner in Brooklyn when classmates suddenly began being called over the school PA system to go home.
Eventually, her mother arrived to collect Palladino and her older sister, and as they walked home, the little girl looked toward Manhattan.
"It was like a dividing line," Palladino recently told Fox News Digital. "From the bridge backwards was just blackness."
REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS
A view of the rubble of the World Trade Center and the Winter Garden in New York City in 2001, shortly after the 9/11 terrorist attacks. (MediaNews Group via Getty Images, File)
The other side of the afternoon sky remained clear and blue.
"Mommy, why is the sky black?" Palladino remembers asking. "She just kept squeezing my hand, and we just kept going," she said.

A quarter-century later, Palladino teaches nursery school at St. Patrick Catholic Academy in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, where her 3-year-old students were born more than two decades after the attacks that shaped their teacher's childhood.
She is one of several educators at the school whose memories of 9/11 stretch back to their own school days.
As the nation remembers Friday, they are teaching children about an event that remains deeply personal to them but that their students know only as history.
AS AMERICAN PRIDE HITS A 25-YEAR LOW, A NEW 9/11 EDUCATION PLATFORM URGES THE NATION TO NEVER FORGET
A boy points towards the center of the reflecting pool at the National September 11 Memorial Museum in New York City. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)

Their principal, Kathy Curatolo, carries an even more personal connection — she watched one of the towers collapse from a school roof that morning, unaware her youngest brother, 31-year-old FDNY firefighter Robert Curatolo, was underneath it.
For Palladino's young students, the lessons begin simply.
"I don't go into the events of 9/11," she said. "They are too young, and the scope of what happened is just beyond their understanding right now."
Instead, she teaches them what they can do when someone is hurting.
"Can we clean up our toys without being asked? Can we go give them a hug?" she said. "Anything to show the ones that we love that we're here for them."
MASSIVE PIECE OF 9/11 HISTORY MAKES STUNNING 10,500-MILE JOURNEY ACROSS AMERICA

FDNY Firefighter Robert Curatolo was killed at the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001, after surviving the first tower collapse and returning to help others, according to his sister, Kathy Curatolo. (Courtesy Kathy Curatolo)
For fourth-grade teacher Elizabeth Giacchino, 9/11 begins in her memory with a ringing telephone.
Giacchino was a sixth grader at Our Lady of Guadalupe School in Brooklyn when her teacher answered a call and told the class something had happened involving the Twin Towers.
"So many of my classmates around me just started screaming and crying because they had family members that were working in the city," she said.
Outside the window, Giacchino could see smoke. Parents began arriving, but Giacchino and her older sister remained because their mother worked at the school.
"All I wanted to do was just be with my family at that time," she said.
I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES
Flowers are left by mourners at the 9/11 Memorial, offering gifts to remember those killed in the 9/11 terrorist attacks in New York City. (Getty Images, File)
Years later, after becoming a teacher herself, another memory took on new meaning. Giacchino remembered how calm her own teacher had remained while children cried around her.

"I don't even know if she was feeling some type of way or if there was any personal situation she was going through, because all she thought about was us," Giacchino said. "So that's what I always make sure to do with my students too."
Nikki Fregara, now a third-grade teacher at St. Patrick, was a high school senior when a phone call interrupted her first class of the day, history.
"I hate to tell you all this, but I'm afraid that the Twin Towers got hit," she remembers her teacher saying.
The students went to the window.
"We saw the smoke," Fregara said.
NYPD CHIEF: 9/11 HEROES’ LEGACY LIVES ON IN EVERY GENERATION OF OFFICERS
New York City Firefighter Gerard McGibbon, of Engine 283 in Brownsville, Brooklyn, prays after the World Trade Center buildings collapsed Sept. 11, 2001. (Mario Tama/Getty Images, File)

She remembers crying and screaming in the hallway and students gathering in the auditorium around a small box television to watch the news. Fregara worried about her father, whose work took him to buildings around the city, and her sister and brother-in-law, who worked nearby.
Today, she steers her third-graders away from the graphic details and toward the first responders who ran toward danger.
"Helping others is so important, especially when they are in need," Fregara said.
Her message to them is simple: "Never forget to be an everyday hero."
For Curatolo, however, the hero she tells students about was her younger brother.
Curatolo was headed to a principals' meeting on Sept. 11, 2001, when she heard on the radio that a plane had struck the World Trade Center.
At the meeting, she and the other principals watched the second plane strike on TV before returning to their schools.
9/11 VICTIM'S IDENTITY EMERGES NEARLY 25 YEARS LATER AFTER DNA BREAKTHROUGH CRACKS MYSTERY
American flags flutter on a fence in front of Lower Manhattan and One World Trade Center at the Tear Drop 9/11 Memorial at sunset in Bayonne, N.J. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images, File)
Curatolo had four brothers, three firefighters and a police officer, and her mother initially called with reassuring news: all four were OK.
Curatolo turned her attention to her students and eventually went onto the school roof.
"I saw the second tower fall, not realizing that tower killed my brother," she said.
Robert Curatolo had been an FDNY firefighter for six years and was assigned to Ladder 16 in Manhattan.

Kathy said Robert had just gotten off duty when the attacks began and headed toward the World Trade Center with two other firefighters in a police car. One survived, allowing the family to later learn some of what Robert did that morning.
AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS

Robert Curatolo, the youngest of eight siblings, is pictured with his brothers and sisters as children. His sister Kathy Curatolo now shares his story with students 25 years after the 9/11 terrorist attacks. (Courtesy Kathy Curatolo)
Robert began directing dazed people away from falling debris, Kathy said. When the first building collapsed, he was in a walkway between the towers. Curatolo survived and then returned to the rubble.

Kathy said her family learned that Robert pulled a man with two broken legs through the debris and into the street. When the second tower collapsed, Robert dove beneath a fire truck, she said, but it could not withstand the collapse.
People have asked Kathy why he didn't leave after surviving once. "That's not who he was," she said. "That's not how we were raised."

Yet that is not the only Robert she wants her students to know. The youngest of eight siblings, Robert was funny, easygoing and athletic. He loved movies and traveling and was, Kathy remembers, almost always late.
"So he actually ended up at the Trade Center on time, where we're like, the only thing you ever got to on time," she said.

Olga Colon, 65, blows a kiss as she finds the name of her brother, Carlos Rey Lillo, a paramedic killed when the South Tower collapsed, at the south reflecting pool during the annual 9/11 Commemoration Ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum in New York City. (Adam Gray/Getty Images, File)
Robert had married at Disney World just three weeks before 9/11. The wedding was the last time Kathy saw him, though she spoke to him by phone the day before he died.
"I want them to know that Robert was — he was a regular kid growing up just like them," she said.
Curatolo remembers realizing around the 10th anniversary that students increasingly had no memory of 9/11.
"These kids have no idea what I'm talking about unless they learn it from us in school or their parents who had experienced something," she said.
Today, she said, children accustomed to smartphones and instantaneous communication are astonished to learn survivors sometimes couldn't contact their families.
She tells them about grounded planes, postponed baseball games and packed churches and remembers that after the attacks, "people were kinder to each other."
Families visit the South Memorial Pool during 10th anniversary ceremonies at the World Trade Center site in New York City. (Robert Deutsch/Pool via Reuters, File)
Twenty-five years later, Curatolo said she also wants students to understand that remembering tragedy does not mean allowing it to define a life.

"My brother is always with me, but I don't let 9/11 define me," she said. "You can survive a tragedy and still live a good life because the people who were lost don't want you to stop living your life."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Her family continues to honor Robert through a scholarship foundation, charitable work and support for Tunnel to Towers.
Kathy still counts him among the eight Curatolo siblings.
"There are eight of us," she said. "Four live in Florida, three live on Staten Island, and one's in heaven."
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Teen boater found clinging to capsized vessel after 3 go missing; 2 bodies recovered

title: US forces obliterate suspected 'narco-terrorist' vessel in lethal Eastern Pacific strike, killing 3
summary: A U.S. military strike destroyed a suspected drug-smuggling vessel in the Eastern Pacific, killing three alleged narco-terrorists, officials said.
story: SOUTHCOM carried out a lethal strike on a go-fast boat along a known trafficking route. Chief Gen. Francis L. Donovan says Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere will "hunt, disrupt, and defeat" cartel networks.
A suspected drug-smuggling vessel was wiped out in a lethal U.S. military strike Wednesday in the Eastern Pacific, killing three alleged "narco-terrorists" aboard, according to the Department of War.
Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere carried out the Sept. 9 strike under the direction of U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) after intelligence allegedly tied the vessel to drug trafficking.
"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking," the department said in a post on X. "The operation killed three narco-terrorists."
WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES
The operation marked the latest U.S. attack on suspected cartel vessels accused of moving deadly narcotics along known trafficking routes off the coast of Latin America.

It came less than two weeks after the Pentagon released newly unclassified images to Fox News Digital showing suspected drug boats speeding across open water, including one vessel loaded with what appeared to be bundles of narcotics.

The images, dated Oct. 27, Oct. 29 and Dec. 4, 2025, offered a rare look at suspected smugglers under U.S. military surveillance as the Trump administration intensified its campaign against cartel networks.

Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson accompanied the release with a deadly warning for traffickers who threaten American communities.

"Nearly one year after the first strike, the message to narco-terrorists remains unchanged: if you traffic deadly illicit narcotics and threaten the American people, we will hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you," Wilson told Fox News Digital at the time.
The Pentagon said Operation Southern Spear had carried out 67 strikes as of late August, beginning with the first operation on Sept. 2, 2025.

Wilson said the campaign had disrupted trafficking networks, forced smugglers to change their tactics and removed "dangerous narcoterrorists."

"Operation Southern Spear has disrupted trafficking networks, forced trafficker adaptations, removed dangerous narcoterrorists, and demonstrated that the United States will use every lawful tool available to defend our Homeland and protect our communities," Wilson said.
One of the most recent strikes came Aug. 25, when U.S. Southern Command said four alleged drug smugglers were killed aboard a fast boat operating along known trafficking routes in the Caribbean.
"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking," SOUTHCOM said at the time.
US FORCES SINK NARCO-REFUELING STATION LINKED TO ECUADORIAN CARTEL IN PACIFIC: SOUTHCOM
The operation was carried out by Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere under the direction of Gen. Francis L. Donovan.
"Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere continues executing precise, lethal operations against the cartels," Donovan said. "We will hunt, disrupt, and defeat these narco-terrorist networks."
"SOUTHCOM is resolved to neutralizing cartel terror and violence throughout the region and into the U.S. homeland," he added.
Days before that Caribbean strike, the U.S. military said two people were killed in an attack on a vessel in the Eastern Pacific. It was the first reported strike in more than two months.
US MILITARY KILLS THREE 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' IN LATEST LETHAL STRIKE ON VESSEL IN THE EASTERN PACIFIC
Department of War Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during a news briefing at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C. (Oliver Contreras / AFP via Getty Images, File)

President Donald Trump has described the fight as an "armed conflict" with cartels in Latin America and argued the attacks are necessary to stop drugs from reaching American communities and fueling fatal overdoses.
The administration is also pursuing agreements with allied nations that could extend the campaign onto land in several Latin American countries.

A Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) special agent who investigated child exploitation cases has been indicted on rape, incest and multiple child sex abuse charges involving a juvenile girl in Alabama, authorities said.

A Baldwin County grand jury indicted Kent Blacklidge, 43, on charges of first-degree rape, second-degree rape, first-degree sodomy, second-degree sodomy, two counts of first-degree sexual abuse, two counts of second-degree sexual abuse and incest, according to the Spanish Fort Police Department.
Police said investigators opened the case Jan. 11 after receiving a report alleging the sexual abuse of a juvenile female.

Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall said his office is prosecuting the case after the Baldwin County District Attorney's Office recused itself because Blacklidge is a witness in other cases it handles.

Marshall said the allegations are especially troubling because Blacklidge's duties with HSI included investigating child exploitation cases and helping educate the public about crimes against children.

title: Surrogate who refused abortion takes fight to Supreme Court as baby's life hangs in balance
summary: Surrogate McKenna West asks the Supreme Court to block a California ruling that left her unable to advocate for a newborn with a rare heart defect.
story: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton discusses a case on ‘The Will Cain Show’ about a surrogate who gave birth in Texas to a baby with a heart defect after the biological parents requested an abortion.

A surrogate who defied a California couple’s demand to abort their baby after a devastating heart diagnosis is taking her fight to the U.S. Supreme Court, arguing a lower court ruling has left her powerless to advocate for the medically fragile newborn.

Attorneys for Alaska cardiac nurse McKenna West filed an emergency application Wednesday, asking Justice Elena Kagan to temporarily block a Los Angeles court ruling that declared the California couple the baby’s legal parents.
Kagan handles emergency matters arising from the 9th Circuit, which includes California. She has not ruled on the request.
SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION
Surrogate mother McKenna West, who fled to Texas after her baby's birth parents allegedly asked her to abort the child. (Live Action)
West carried the child under a surrogacy agreement with California couple Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed, who call the baby Rumi. West calls him Gabriel.
The baby was born in Texas Aug. 12 with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, or HLHS, a rare condition in which the left side of the heart is severely underdeveloped.
KAGAN RECALLS LINDSEY GRAHAM'S VOTE THAT HELPED SEAL HER SUPREME COURT CONFIRMATION

The legal war began after the condition was detected during a 20-week ultrasound. West alleges Gilkar and Ahmed asked her to terminate the pregnancy under a provision in their surrogacy agreement covering serious fetal abnormalities.
West refused, telling the surrogacy agency she could not abort "this precious baby" after feeling him move and learning treatment was available, according to the filing.
She offered to raise the child herself or arrange an adoption if the couple no longer wanted him, while allowing them to walk away from any further financial obligations.
Her attorneys allege West was then warned that continuing the pregnancy could expose her to more than $250,000 in financial penalties.
CONSERVATIVE GROUPS SAY JUSTICE KAGAN CANNOT BE IMPARTIAL IN UPCOMING SUPREME COURT CLIMATE LITIGATION
McKenna West, center, arrives at a Dallas court hearing over the custody dispute. (LM Otero/AP Photo)

Gilkar and Ahmed later turned to a California court to establish their legal rights as the baby’s parents. West argued the case belonged in Alaska under the surrogacy agreement and said she appeared in California solely to challenge the court’s jurisdiction.

The Los Angeles Superior Court determined that West had effectively consented to its authority by submitting a 147-page filing that addressed the "substance of the issues," according to the application.
West’s lawyers said most of those pages were exhibits supporting her jurisdictional challenge and that she had repeatedly refused to argue the underlying case.
"Any reasonable view of consent would recognize that ‘no’ does not mean ‘yes,’" they wrote.
West also claims she was never properly served. Her filing says a FedEx package containing the court papers was delivered to her babysitter, who allegedly was not told what was inside.
The California court declared Gilkar and Ahmed the baby’s legal parents June 22, and West failed to persuade three state courts to put the ruling on hold.
SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION
McKenna West, left, appears with attorneys at Dallas family court amid a custody dispute with the intended parents of the baby she carried. (LM Otero/AP Photo)
The judge acknowledged during the California proceedings that the dispute "[m]ay be a question of life and death" for the unborn child, according to West’s application.
The fight then moved to Texas, where West traveled so the baby could be delivered at a hospital equipped to treat his condition.
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secured an emergency order before the birth, directing the hospital to provide life-saving care and preventing the child from being removed from the state.

West previously said she had only about one minute with the newborn while his umbilical cord was still attached before he was taken from her. A court order later barred her from seeing or holding him.

The baby underwent the first of three anticipated open-heart surgeries Aug. 17. He was later returned to a breathing tube after his condition declined, according to court filings previously reviewed by Fox News Digital.
Gilkar said during a hearing last month in Dallas that the couple had remained at their son’s bedside and accused West of trying to take him.
"He’s our child," Gilkar said, according to The Associated Press. "He’s the love of our lives."
She also told the court the newborn was "suffering a lot" as he struggled to breathe, choked on tubes and required a blood transfusion following surgery, according to the AP.
West has said she would abandon her custody effort if a court determined the intended parents were committed to providing the child with life-saving care.
But on Sept. 2, a Texas judge upheld the California ruling and removed West from the case. Paxton has also stepped away from the legal fight.
HHS WARNS TEXAS HOSPITALS AGAINST DENYING LIFE-SAVING CARE TO NEWBORN WITH DISABILITY
McKenna West, center, walks with her legal team at a Dallas family court hearing in the legal fight over a critically ill newborn. (LM Otero/AP Photo)

West’s attorneys argue she is now barred from receiving information about the baby or defending the order requiring his continued treatment. They allege Gilkar and Ahmed are challenging that medical care order.
The couple previously agreed to the baby’s first surgery and said they would approve life-saving care if doctors determined he was a candidate.

West is now asking the Supreme Court to temporarily block the California ruling, which could give her a path back into the Texas case. Her attorneys argue the dispute raises a broader constitutional question over whether challenging a court’s authority can itself be treated as accepting that authority.
McKenna West arrives for a Dallas court hearing in the surrogate custody dispute. (LM Otero/AP Photo)

Her lawyers stressed that temporarily blocking the ruling would not decide who the baby’s legal parents are or direct doctors to provide a particular course of treatment. Instead, it could allow West to ask the Texas court to bring her back into the case.
Without Supreme Court intervention, her attorneys warned, West will remain shut out of decisions and updates about the baby’s condition as the appeals process plays out.
"Unless this Court provides relief from that judgment, M.W. will have no access to information about Baby G.’s condition," West’s attorneys wrote.

They argued that a victory later could come too late to protect the child.
"Relief later in Texas proceedings may only restore her right to protect a child that has already passed," the filing states.

title: Manhattan prostitute pleads guilty to killing 3 men with fentanyl-laced drugs in robbery scheme

A Manhattan prostitute who killed three johns when she fed them fentanyl-laced drugs to rob them pleaded guilty Tuesday.

Tabitha Bundrick, 39, admitted to giving her customers the powerful synthetic opioid between April 2023 and February 2024 and then taking their personal belongings, including their cell phones, sneakers, money and watches, the Manhattan District Attorney's Office said.

"The defendant knowingly killed three people by providing them fentanyl-laced drugs," said District Attorney Alvin Bragg. "As they lay unconscious, she robbed her victims and left them to die. In several instances, the victims’ bodies were found by their friends or family members."

Fentanyl pills  (Getty Images)

Bundrick's crimes began on April 30, 2023, when she met Mario Paullan, 42, and his friend on the street and offered to sell them soap. She then offered to have sex with them for money and took them to an apartment she broke into, prosecutors said.

The third incident occurred on Feb. 25, 2024, when Abrihan Fernandez, 34, died in his apartment. Bundrick was caught entering and exiting the Upper Manhattan apartment several times with large bags.

title: Mamdani, NYPD give security update ahead of Jewish High Holy Days, 9/11 25th anniversary
summary: Zohran Mamdani and Jessica Tisch announced an increased NYPD presence at synagogues across New York City as antisemitic hate crimes rise ahead of holy days.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York Police Department Commissioner Jessica Tisch explain the expanded security measures the city will take ahead of the Jewish High Holy Days and the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York Police Department (NYPD) Commissioner Jessica Tisch revealed increased security measures ahead of September's Jewish High Holy Days and ceremonies to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

During a press conference Wednesday, Mamdani discouraged the public from traversing through lower Manhattan on Friday. The city will be closing streets around Ground Zero with dignitaries, including Vice President JD Vance, slated to attend a commemoration of the 25th anniversary of 9/11.
The mayor also expressed sympathy to Jewish New Yorkers who have experienced an uptick in antisemitic hate crimes in recent years.

"I want to speak directly to our Jewish New Yorkers now," Mamdani said. "Your safety during these sacred days is of the utmost importance to our administration, and we will work tirelessly to ensure that you can observe the holiday securely. There will be an increased NYPD presence outside of synagogues across the five boroughs, as well as other Jewish religious and cultural locations."
MAN CHARGED WITH ASSAULT, HATE CRIMES AFTER ALLEGEDLY DISRUPTING SHABBAT SERVICES AT NYC SYNAGOGUE

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch announce a new memorial honoring victims of 9/11 inside 1 Police Plaza, New York, N.Y., Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (Cristina Matuozzi/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)
Mamdani said there were no specific or credible threats to any New Yorkers but maintained that the city will remain vigilant ahead of the weekend's events.
Tisch echoed Mamdani's message that there were no specific threats, adding that hate crimes, and antisemitic hate crimes in particular, are on the rise.
ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE ESCALATES AS DEADLY WEAPON ATTACKS SURGE IN 2025: REPORT

"Even as shootings and murders have fallen to historic lows, hate crimes are moving in the wrong direction through the first eight months of this year. Confirmed hate crimes citywide are up 16%, and antisemitic hate crimes are up 9%. And once again, more than half of all confirmed hate crimes in New York City have targeted Jewish New Yorkers, even though Jews make up only about 10% of this city's population. Those numbers are deeply disturbing," Tisch said.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch announce a new memorial honoring victims of 9/11 inside 1 Police Plaza, New York, N.Y., Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (Cristina Matuozzi/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)

She pointed to specific incidents, including the July stabbing of Moshe Grunhaus, a 50-year-old Jewish man wearing a kippah who was attacked with a screwdriver outside The Jewish Center in Manhattan's Upper West Side.
SUSPECT ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY YELLING ‘ALLAHU AKBAR,' STABBING 2 MEN IN NYC ATTACK
She also revealed that intelligence officers have disrupted multiple plotted attacks on Jews in New York in recent years.
Members of the NYPD’s Counterterrorism Unit stand guard outside the Jewish Museum in New York City, May 22, 2025.  (Kevin C. Downs for Fox News Digital)

"Since October 7th, our intelligence community has also tracked threats and disrupted plots directed at Jewish institutions here in New York, including alleged plans for attacks against a Manhattan synagogue and a Jewish center in Brooklyn," Tisch said.
Tisch assured New York's Jews that they can rely on the NYPD to protect them.
