He told “Good Morning America” on Thursday about his frustrations with the holdout juror, who has yet to be publicly identified.
“I think we felt defeated,” Dargie said about the case’s conclusion. “We spent seven weeks on this trial, almost two months of, you know, all of our lives dedicated to it.”

He is among at least five jurors — and the first male — who have spoken out about the case and what happened inside the deliberation room at Plymouth Superior Court last week. After more than 38 hours, the jurors could not reach a unanimous decision, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial after they deadlocked three times.
Add to Google
Add to Google

On Thursday, defense attorney Kevin Reddington filed a renewed motion to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility on each of the three charges, arguing that the prosecution did not prove, beyond a reasonable doubt, that Clancy was not in psychosis at the time of the killings.

Dargie told “Good Morning America” that toward the end of deliberations, the holdout juror would not engage in discussions with others or provide evidence that supported his reasoning, instead choosing to scroll on his phone.

Ultimately, Dargie said, he confronted the holdout juror after the man mimicked the killings, tying an exercise band entered into evidence around an empty water bottle and pulling it tight. Dargie said he is not sure why the man did that.
“I was shocked. It didn’t make any sense to me,” Dargie said. “We’re not in here to play detective or it’s not a game of Clue. This is serious.”

Throughout the trial, Clancy’s defense attorney argued that she was in a state of psychosis when she strangled the children with exercise bands and therefore was not aware of what she was doing. The prosecution, however, argued she was not actually experiencing postpartum psychosis and planned the killings ahead of time.

Three women on the jury told NBC Boston that the 11 jurors agreed to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. The holdout wanted to convict, they revealed, but admitted he expressed doubt in the prosecution’s case.
“It was definitely frustrating, mainly frustrating when [the holdout juror] explicitly said, ‘You know, I don’t know if the prosecution or the defense proved their case,’” Dargie told “GMA.”
Reddington in the motion also pointed to the fact that in this case, every juror except one — who did not apply the reasonable-doubt standard — came to that same conclusion.

“No rational jury could find beyond a reasonable doubt that she had no mental disease or defect when the Commonwealth’s own proof established that she did,” the motion said, noting the 11-1 jury split.
And at first, Dargie said, a number of jurors thought Clancy was guilty of the crimes, and at times the jury’s votes differed day to day.

A female juror who spoke with CBS Boston anonymously said many people on the jury were initially “firm in their beliefs,” and that she was one of the people who, at first, agreed with the holdout and thought Clancy was guilty.

She explained how there was so much “gray area” and doubt in the case, and that ultimately, she switched her tune because she thinks Clancy is mentally unwell and that she’d get better help in a state mental health facility than in prison.

Dargie told “GMA” that “once we laid out all of the evidence and how we saw it, that really brought everyone kind of on the same page, except for this one juror.” The female juror chalked it up to one person being unable to let go of their convictions.

When that one juror didn’t agree with the group, Dargie said, he asked him to show evidence that “helped to prove what he was saying, but he couldn’t.” That’s what led the jury foreperson to send a note to the judge about the holdout during deliberations, explaining that he wasn’t meeting the burden of reasonable doubt the prosecution must overcome.
Dargie acknowledged that it’s fair for someone to have a differing opinion, but said this particular juror would not engage and could not “find something to support his view.”
Now, prosecutors must decide whether they want to retry Clancy. The next hearing for the case is scheduled for Sept. 29.

Dargie, who was serving in the military overseas, said he’s “haunted” by the case. Specifically, he said, the recording of the 911 call made by Clancy’s then-husband, Patrick Clancy, when he found the dead children that night is seared into his memory. The recording was played in court and was not released to the public.
“I’ve never heard something like that, like a scream like that, come out of someone’s mouth,” Dargie said of the recording. “It’s horrifying.”
The anonymous female juror told CBS Boston that she will “never be the same after that 911 call.”
Dargie also rejected online conspiracy theories that Patrick Clancy was actually the one who carried out the killings, noting that if anyone had heard the 911 calls, they would change their mind.
“I think if they tried the trial again the way they did, I think nine times out of 10, I think the jury would come back with not guilty by reason of insanity, no doubt,” Dargie said.

title: Oil prices surge to $107 for the first time since May as bond yields jump
summary: The price of oil surged again, with Brent crude surpassing $107 per barrel for the first time since May as markets brace for a long U.S. war with Iran.
story: The price of oil surged again Thursday, with Brent crude surpassing $107 per barrel for the first time since May and U.S. crude oil jumping above $100 per barrel, also its highest level since mid-May.

A primary driver of the move in oil prices was President Donald Trump’s comment Wednesday night that he is not looking for a deal with Iran. Trump also said that he did not expect oil prices to fall until “right after” the November midterm elections, despite having said for months that the war would be over quickly.
“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump told reporters Wednesday afternoon. “They’re going to be tumbling down, and we’ll get them down.”
Commodities experts warned earlier this week that oil prices as measured by Brent could rise to $120 or even as high as $150 per barrel if the stalemate with Iran continues to drag on.

Trump’s suggestion that the war would continue for many more months also puts global crude oil stockpiles in focus. Earlier this year, dozens of nations agreed to release 400 million barrels in order to keep a lid on prices in the early months of the war.
The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since the 1980s.
Additionally, Saudi Arabia informed OPEC that its crude oil output plunged to the lowest level since 1990 last month due to renewed hostilities with Iran, according to a report from Bloomberg News.
NBC News was not immediately able to confirm that report.
“The move reflects a market still pricing in persistent geopolitical risk, with Persian Gulf tensions showing no credible path to de‑escalation,” analysts at ING said Thursday.

As a result of those rising prices, the national average gas price rose another 5 cents overnight to $4.27. Diesel fuel, which powers everything from farms to trucking to trains, rose 3 cents overnight to $5.97.

Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury bonds continued to sell off, driving their yields higher. The 10-year Treasury yield, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates, especially for mortgages, touched 4.93%, its highest level since 2023.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.07% Thursday, according to Mortgage News Daily. This is the highest rate since May 2025.
The 30-year Treasury yield spiked to 5.35%, its highest level since 2007.
The move in Treasury yields was driven mostly by the soaring price of energy, which has triggered renewed fears of an inflation crisis.

title: Spice Girls fans feel duped after social media tease wasn’t for tour, but a music re-release
summary: Spice Girls fans are telling you what they want — what they really, really want — and it’s a tour that they aren’t getting any time soon.
story: Spice Girls fans are telling you what they want — what they really, really want — and it’s a tour that they aren’t getting any time soon.

The disbanded girl group excited their followers on Wednesday with a social media post teasing a big announcement for the following day. A short clip posted to Instagram showed an issue of “The Stage” magazine left on a set of stairs before zooming into a clasified advertisement seeking Spice Girls Fans who are a “superfan, a collector, a music lover.”
“No sheet music required but you will need a vinyl or cd player,” the ad said.
Fans immediately jumped to speculation on what it could be, with many hoping for a possible reunion.
“If it’s a world tour, I’m selling my house to buy tix,” one Instagram commenter wrote.
Another wrote, “please say it’s @spherevegas,” referring to the popular Las Vegas venue where the Backstreet Boys are currently in residency.
But some should have slowed it down and read the sign.

On Thursday, the Spice Girls account announced a re-release of “all the singles” with b-sides and surprises “from the vault” on CD and vinyl. A previously unreleased demo of a song called “Do You Think About Me” was also made available on streaming services Thursday.

The full collection will release in November and ranges in price from $128.99 to $380.99, according to the band’s website. The re-release is meant to honor the 30th anniversary of their single “Wannabe,” the hit that changed the trajectory of their lives.
It was a blow to the ‘90s band’s most loyal fans, who were ready to promise they would be there in the stands.
“Negotiating with my husband on my price cap for Spice Girls tickets today was for NOTHING,” one woman wrote in the comments.
“Guys we want two things- Spice World on streaming platforms and a tour with the full line-up,” another Instagram user wrote. “Please make it happen.”
“I hear the millennial sigh of devastation from across the world,” one person said.
Spice Girls drop a cryptic video spurring reunion rumors

The Spice Girls have been asked repeatedly about a tour in recent years in interviews, but it appears that a reunion performance with all five original members is a pipe dream. There was a small tour across the U.K. and Ireland in 2019 that didn’t feature Victoria Beckham, aka Posh Spice.

Beckham expressed her excitement to go watch her former bandmates even if she wasn’t going to be on stage. The fashion mogul has said in the last year that she hasn’t performed in years and doesn’t feel that she is the strongest singer or dancer.
She told Andy Cohen on his radio show in October that she didn’t think she could even make a world tour work with the demands of her business.

“Before I was in the Spice Girls, I was so self-conscious and they made me feel that I was good enough, but being on stage, I realized as fun as it is, you know, it’s not ultimately what I want to do anymore,” Beckham said.
Melanie Brown, or Scary Spice as she’s known to fans, reiterated that a tour was not happening in an interview with Hello! magazine published in April.
“I’m 50. You can’t be nagging everyone to go on tour if they don’t want to,” Brown said. “I laid that to rest when I turned 50.”
But the women are still close friends.

All but Beckham were in attendance for Melanie Chisholm’s wedding earlier this year. And though she couldn’t be there for Sporty Spice on her big day, Beckham designed the singer’s wedding dress, according to Vogue.

All five women were together earlier this year, according to social media. Beckham’s youngest son posted a video on Instagram in February of the Spice Girls singing their song “Viva Forever” around a dinner table while he played guitar for him. The video has been watched more than 13 million times.
“Love you all,” Beckham wrote in her son’s comment section.

title: Rick Springfield recalls killing a man in Vietnam while he was there performing for troops
summary: Rocker Rick Springfield recalled this week how, as a teenager, he performed for U.S. forces in Vietnam and killed a Viet Cong attacker — haunting him to this day, that he “was responsible for the end of a life.”
story: Rocker Rick Springfield recalled this week how, as a teenager, he performed for U.S. forces in Vietnam and killed a Viet Cong attacker — haunting him to this day, that he “was responsible for the end of a life.”

The Australian singer-songwriter became an ‘80s superstar with his megahit “Jessie’s Girl,” but in 1968 he was an unknown 17-year-old musician who had traveled to Southeast Asia to entertain American troops at the height of the Vietnam War.

Springfield, 77, recounted that harrowing experience on an episode of the “Joe Rogan Experience” posted on Tuesday. He said he was staying at a U.S. Navy encampment in the Marble Mountains near Da Nang in when they suddenly came under attack.

“We met these guys, and we really got along well, and we stayed overnight with them, and we all got in the bunkers, in the perimeter bunkers, and I stayed in the radio shack,” he recalled. “And we got attacked, and I’m throwing mortars down the freaking tube of the radio shack.”
In the heat of the moment, Springfield said he was haphazardly loading a launcher and “could have easily lost a hand.”

“It was like the movies,” he told Rogan. “They said, ‘Hey, you want to throw some mortars down the tube?’ And it was John Wayne time, you know. I mean, as a young kid, I didn’t really understand what I was doing.”
But what began like a scene from an action film gave way to the cold, hard realities of war.
“I’d thrown a mortar down and it had hit somebody, and they came in the next day and said, ‘Hey, you got one! You got one!’” Springfield said.
“That’s really the one thing I brought back with me that I couldn’t really find a place for that to land,” he said, saying that it feels like it happened to “another guy” in  “another place.”
Rogan asked, “How long did that sit with you for?” and Springfield said the experience has never left him.

“I think it’s still there,” Springfield replied. “It’s hard for me to face that I was responsible for the end of a life, even though it’s distant and it’s war and I didn’t really have anything to do with it and didn’t really know what I was doing.”
Springfield also vividly recalled how unpopular the war was with the Americans fighting it in Vietnam.
“All the ones I met were, ‘Dude, I don’t know why we’re here. I don’t know what I’m doing here,’” Springfield remembered.

title: Nicolás Maduro’s wife seeks home detention ahead of trial citing ‘serious’ heart condition
summary: The wife of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Cilia Flores, asked a federal judge late Wednesday to release her from jail pending trial, citing a “serious” heart condition.
story: The wife of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Cilia Flores, asked a federal judge late Wednesday to release her from jail pending trial, citing a “serious” heart condition.

In the filing, Flores’ attorney Mark Donnelly said she “deserves the opportunity to await her trial while on home confinement” in order to recover from a recommended cardiac catheterization, which could lead to more invasive heart procedures.

“Prior to the United States’ military invasion of Venezuela, Ms. Flores de Maduro was physically healthy and took no ongoing medication, other than a monthly injection to help control her mitral valve prolapse,” Donnelly said.

Now, Flores is prescribed multiple medications, including one to take in the event of a potential heart attack, while continuing to grapple with the medical recommendations that she undergo testing and surgery, he said.
Donnelly said Flores has not received her monthly injection for her mitral valve prolapse since her incarceration.

Flores, 69, and Maduro, 63, have been held at a Brooklyn jail since U.S. forces captured the couple at their Caracas home in a nighttime raid and brought them to New York to face criminal charges in January.
The couple was federally charged with conspiracy to import cocaine, along with possession of machine guns and destructive devices. Maduro is also charged with a narco-terrorism conspiracy.

In the indictment, prosecutors in Manhattan alleged that Maduro and his co-conspirators have, “for decades, partnered with some of the most violent and prolific drug traffickers and narco-terrorists in the world, and relied on corrupt officials throughout the region, to distribute tons of cocaine to the United States.”
Maduro and Flores have pleaded not guilty to all counts and are scheduled to go to trial in June. They face potential life sentences if a jury finds them guilty.
Last week, they asked a federal judge to dismiss the drug trafficking indictment, arguing they are immune from prosecution as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.

If Flores were released ahead of trial, her attorney recommended placing her under home detention with GPS location monitoring, 24-hour armed surveillance, surrender of all travel documents, and a third-party custodian approved by pretrial services and the court.
Donnelly said the Trump administration is aware of his client’s request but opposes her release.

“Despite the ongoing efforts of the MDC staff, a detention center lacks the conditions needed for such a recovery. Her reticence to undergo cardiac exploration and surgery only to return to the conditions which have contributed to the deterioration of her health is reasonable,” he said.
Flores has lost more than 25 pounds and two molars and sleeps no more than three to four hours per day, according to Donnelly.

On July 29, Flores experienced “a significant, 30-minute episode of intense pressure in her chest along with feeling a lack of oxygen” and “suffers from lingering light-headedness, dizziness, and shortness of breath,” the filing stated.

Flores’ legal team, in consultation with outside medical experts, believes she may have suffered a minor heart attack during the July episode. However, because lab tests were not taken or documented in her medical records at the time, the extent of her condition remains unclear, Donnelly said.
A spokesperson for the Southern District of New York declined to comment.

title: Florida attorney general sues Netflix over ‘bait-and-switch’ on privacy for kids
summary: Florida’s attorney general filed a sweeping lawsuit against Netflix, accusing the streaming giant of misleading consumers about its data collection practices.
story: Florida’s attorney general filed a sweeping lawsuit Wednesday against Netflix, accusing the Hollywood streaming giant of misleading consumers about its data collection practices and exposing kids to “addictive” design features.
“Netflix told Florida families they could pay a monthly fee to escape Big Tech surveillance. That was false,” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said in a statement accompanying the filing.

“Netflix collected detailed data on children and families, designed its product to keep kids watching, and then commercialized that information to launch the advertising business it promised never to build,” Uthmeier added in part.
In response to a request for comment Thursday, a Netflix spokesperson said the company “takes our members’ privacy seriously.”

“We comply with privacy and data‑protection laws everywhere we operate and have dedicated safeguards in place for kids who watch content on Netflix,” the spokesperson added. “This lawsuit lacks merit and we intend to vigorously defend the matter in court.”

Uthmeier’s suit opens another front in Florida’s legal crusade against major technology platforms. Uthmeier’s office filed suit against OpenAI in early June, accusing the artificial intelligence company of putting profit over safety. The same month, the state sued TikTok, claiming the social media application violated state child safety law.

In the 66-page suit against Netflix, Florida alleges it orchestrated a “years-long bait-and-switch.” Uthmeier’s office claims Netflix spent years marketing its subscription service as an ad-free alternative to the data-driven business models of Silicon Valley behemoths like Google and Facebook, all while assuring parents that the platform’s kids profiles were “safe.”

However, according to the Florida plaintiffs, Netflix was designing systems to collect information about how users interacted with the platform, including what they watched, clicked, paused, replayed and skipped. The state alleges Netflix used the “addictive” autoplay feature to keep adult and child users watching while logging “billions” of behavioral data points.

The streaming service introduced an ad-supported plan in November 2022 as part of a wider push to drive revenue amid slowing subscriber growth. The platform currently offers two ad-free plans, Standard and Premium, as well as a lower-priced Standard with ads plan.

“Netflix’s years-long bait-and-switch has led the company right to where it promised never to be: addicting children and families to its platform, mining those users for data, and then converting that data into lucrative intelligence for global advertising juggernauts,” Florida says in the complaint. “This is deceptive conduct that violates Florida law.”

Netflix shares a privacy statement and terms of use with members annually, according to the platform. The documents provide explanations of the company’s advertising and privacy practices, as well as members’ rights and controls. Netflix subscribers can manage their advertising preferences and turn off behavioral ads at any time, according to the service.

The service also offers parental controls that allow parents to filter content by maturity rating or block specific programming. Members can disable autoplay for episodes and trailers at any time, while parents have control over autoplay features on kids’ profiles, according to Netflix.

Florida’s suit comes four months after Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed his own complaint against Netflix, accusing the platform of “spying on” people in his state, including children, and collecting user data without consent.

“Netflix is not the ad-free and kid-friendly platform it claims to be. Instead, it has misled consumers while exploiting their private data to make billions,” said Paxton, also the state’s Republican nominee for U.S. Senate.
In a statement at the time, a Netflix spokesperson said the lawsuit “lacks merit and is based on inaccurate and distorted information.”

Florida is demanding a jury trial on its allegation that Netflix is violating the state’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act and the state’s Digital Bill of Rights. It is seeking a court ruling that would, among other things, order Netflix to “purge all data deceptively collected from Floridians.”

Uthmeier, a Republican who took office in February 2025, previously served as chief of staff to Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. DeSantis appointed Uthmeier to replace former state attorney general Ashley Moody, who resigned as attorney general to fill the U.S. Senate seat vacated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

title: Billy Joel reveals he got brain surgery because he didn’t want to lose his ‘marbles’
summary: Long Island troubadour Billy Joel revealed Tuesday that he underwent brain surgery because he didn’t want to lose his “marbles.”
story: Long Island troubadour Billy Joel revealed Tuesday that he underwent brain surgery because he didn’t want to lose his “marbles.”
Speaking on his SiriusXM channel, the 77-year-old “Piano Man” singer admitted he initially balked at going under the knife for hydrocephalus, a disorder he was diagnosed with in 2025.
“I said, ‘Well, what does that entail?’” he said he asked the doctor.
After being told that it involved having a surgeon “drill a hole through your skull” and “stick a shunt inside your brain,” Joel said “I didn’t want to do that.”

“But then I read up on it, and I realized it can help improve your balance and can help your memory,” he said. “You know, I don’t want to lose my marbles. It’s hard to tell what’s age and what’s a condition, so I agreed to do the shunt, and I had surgery, and they implanted a shunt in my brain, and it actually improved things.”

Joel did not say exactly when he had the surgery. But he was diagnosed in May 2025 with normal pressure hydrocephalus, which is a condition in which cerebrospinal fluid builds up inside of the skull and press on the brain, according to the Cleveland Clinic. The condition is often treatable and sometimes reversible.
“They used to call it water on the brain,” Joel said on his radio show.
Joel said he went to see the neurologist because he was feeling unsteady.
“I noticed that my balance was not good,” he said. “I had this sense of being on a boat, like this rocking motion. I wasn’t steady on my feet.”
Will he be returning to the stage anytime soon? Joel didn’t say on his show, and his longtime publicist did not immediately respond to an email from NBC News seeking an answer to that question.
“The doctors told me this: because of my job, which is playing rock and roll music very loud, that it was giving me something like a concussion every time I did a show,” he said.

Pounding out songs on the piano, he said, “was causing damage to my brain nerves, and I could be losing more brain cells the more shows I did. I realized that means I shouldn’t be doing this right now. I got to improve.”
So Joel said he’s been going to physical therapy and following his doctors’ advice.
“I’m doing whatever it is they tell me to do because I don’t want to lose it, you know?” he said.
And he expects to make a full recovery.
“I’m not going anywhere,” he said. “I’m here. I’m still here.”

title: Spice Girls fans feel duped after social media tease wasn’t for tour, but a music re-release
summary: Spice Girls fans are telling you what they want — what they really, really want — and it’s a tour that they aren’t getting any time soon.
story: Spice Girls fans are telling you what they want — what they really, really want — and it’s a tour that they aren’t getting any time soon.

The disbanded girl group excited their followers on Wednesday with a social media post teasing a big announcement for the following day. A short clip posted to Instagram showed an issue of “The Stage” magazine left on a set of stairs before zooming into a clasified advertisement seeking Spice Girls Fans who are a “superfan, a collector, a music lover.”
“No sheet music required but you will need a vinyl or cd player,” the ad said.
Fans immediately jumped to speculation on what it could be, with many hoping for a possible reunion.
“If it’s a world tour, I’m selling my house to buy tix,” one Instagram commenter wrote.
Another wrote, “please say it’s @spherevegas,” referring to the popular Las Vegas venue where the Backstreet Boys are currently in residency.
But some should have slowed it down and read the sign.

On Thursday, the Spice Girls account announced a re-release of “all the singles” with b-sides and surprises “from the vault” on CD and vinyl. A previously unreleased demo of a song called “Do You Think About Me” was also made available on streaming services Thursday.

The full collection will release in November and ranges in price from $128.99 to $380.99, according to the band’s website. The re-release is meant to honor the 30th anniversary of their single “Wannabe,” the hit that changed the trajectory of their lives.
It was a blow to the ‘90s band’s most loyal fans, who were ready to promise they would be there in the stands.
“Negotiating with my husband on my price cap for Spice Girls tickets today was for NOTHING,” one woman wrote in the comments.
“Guys we want two things- Spice World on streaming platforms and a tour with the full line-up,” another Instagram user wrote. “Please make it happen.”
“I hear the millennial sigh of devastation from across the world,” one person said.
Spice Girls drop a cryptic video spurring reunion rumors

The Spice Girls have been asked repeatedly about a tour in recent years in interviews, but it appears that a reunion performance with all five original members is a pipe dream. There was a small tour across the U.K. and Ireland in 2019 that didn’t feature Victoria Beckham, aka Posh Spice.

Beckham expressed her excitement to go watch her former bandmates even if she wasn’t going to be on stage. The fashion mogul has said in the last year that she hasn’t performed in years and doesn’t feel that she is the strongest singer or dancer.
She told Andy Cohen on his radio show in October that she didn’t think she could even make a world tour work with the demands of her business.

“Before I was in the Spice Girls, I was so self-conscious and they made me feel that I was good enough, but being on stage, I realized as fun as it is, you know, it’s not ultimately what I want to do anymore,” Beckham said.
Melanie Brown, or Scary Spice as she’s known to fans, reiterated that a tour was not happening in an interview with Hello! magazine published in April.
“I’m 50. You can’t be nagging everyone to go on tour if they don’t want to,” Brown said. “I laid that to rest when I turned 50.”
But the women are still close friends.

All but Beckham were in attendance for Melanie Chisholm’s wedding earlier this year. And though she couldn’t be there for Sporty Spice on her big day, Beckham designed the singer’s wedding dress, according to Vogue.

All five women were together earlier this year, according to social media. Beckham’s youngest son posted a video on Instagram in February of the Spice Girls singing their song “Viva Forever” around a dinner table while he played guitar for him. The video has been watched more than 13 million times.
“Love you all,” Beckham wrote in her son’s comment section.

title: Jimmy Kimmel says show won’t air James Talarico interview on TV, citing FCC threats
summary: Jimmy Kimmel announced on Wednesday night that his show would not air his upcoming interview with Texas’ Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico on television, citing the Trump administration’s threats against ABC.
story: Jimmy Kimmel announced on Wednesday night that his show would not air his upcoming interview with Texas’ Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico on television, citing the Trump administration’s threats against ABC.

Kimmel said that during President Donald Trump’s administration, the Federal Communications Commission “has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.”

“Out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas, who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” he said.

The interview, set for Thursday, will be posted on the YouTube channel for “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” instead, he said. Talarico, a Democratic state representative in Texas, is locked in a competitive Senate race with Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton.
The Talarico campaign and the FCC did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment. ABC Entertainment declined to comment.
FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, condemned “FCC intimidation” in a statement reacting to Kimmel’s announcement.

“No host, local affiliate, or network should have to weigh federal retaliation before booking a guest for a newsworthy interview,” Gomez said in the statement. “Any attempt to pressure broadcasters into self-censorship undermines both press freedom and the public’s right to hear from candidates in their communities seeking public office.”

Kimmel’s announcement marks the latest apparent instance in which pressure from the administration has affected content aired on an entertainment show. Stephen Colbert said in February that CBS did not air his interview with Talarico out of fear of the FCC.
Add to Google
Add to Google
“He was supposed to be here, but we were told in no uncertain terms by our network’s lawyers, who called us directly, that we could not have him on the broadcast,” Colbert said at the time.
CBS said in a February statement that “the show was provided legal guidance that the broadcast could trigger the FCC equal-time rule for two other candidates.”
Trump has publicly targeted Kimmel in the past, calling multiple times for the comedian to be fired.

About a year ago, ABC pulled Kimmel’s show following the comedian’s comments about conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated in September of last year. The show returned nearly a week later, and Kimmel said in his monologue that “it was never my intention to make light of the murder of a young man.”

The FCC, under Chairman Brendan Carr, announced in April that Disney’s eight local television stations owned and operated by ABC needed to file broadcast license renewals early. The Walt Disney Co. sued over the decision last month.

In January, the FCC issued a memo saying that late-night and daytime talk shows must adhere to the equal time rule, which requires broadcasters to offer equal opportunities to other qualified candidates who are running for the same office. The memo marked a change in the FCC’s position. Twenty years earlier, a decision found that late-night and daytime talk shows were exempt from the rule.
Trump himself was interviewed by Kimmel in 2015, when he was running for president. Kimmel recalled the interview during his Wednesday show.

“At that time, when he was the one sitting next to me, he seemed to have no problem with the idea of talk show hosts interviewing candidates,” he said. “In fact, he was very eager to come back for another interview, which he did just before he became the nominee in 2016.”
“But for some reason, and I can’t seem to figure out what that reason is, something has changed,” he said, tongue in cheek.

title: Supreme Court blocks Missouri’s attempt to use newly drawn GOP congressional map
summary: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday blocked an attempt by a Republican state official in Missouri to use a newly drawn GOP congressional map for this year’s elections.
story: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday blocked an attempt by a Republican state official in Missouri to use a newly drawn GOP congressional map for this year’s elections.
The court, in a brief order with no noted dissents, granted an emergency request brought by a group called People Not Politicians, led by activist Richard von Glahn.

The decision puts on hold a decision by Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, who ruled on Tuesday that the new map must be used, notwithstanding the Missouri Supreme Court reaching the opposite conclusion.

The swift action from the justices likely signals the end of the battle over which congressional map to use in the midterm elections this November, with the state set to use the previous map from 2022 that includes six seats currently held by Republicans and two held by Democrats.

As a result of the Supreme Court action, “my office is directing local election authorities to use the 2022 congressional map,” Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, said in a statement.
The new map sought to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic-held seats, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo.
“The law is the law, the Missouri constitution is clear, as was the Missouri Supreme Court,” von Glahn said in a statement.

Hoskins’ lawyers told the U.S. Supreme Court justices just minutes before the decision was issued that only Clark’s order is “preventing the disenfranchisement of hundreds of thousands of voters” who participated in the primary election using the new congressional map.
With little time before the November election, it is the only way that Missouri can “conduct congressional elections that comply with the federal election calendar,” they added.

The Trump administration also filed a brief backing Hoskins, saying that if the justices were to block Clark’s ruling, it would “jeopardize state officials’ ability to conduct a timely and lawful federal election.”

This is the second time the underlying fight has reached the U.S. Supreme Court. On Tuesday, Justice Brett Kavanaugh rejected a request from Hoskins seeking to block the Missouri Supreme Court ruling.
In a separate hearing on Thursday, the Missouri Supreme Court gave Hoskins a cool reception as it considers whether to hold him in contempt for defying its previous ruling.

With Hoskins appearing in person, the judges peppered his lawyer with questions about whether he would comply and use the 2022 map. They seemed dissatisfied with some of the responses, which were offered before Hoskins’ later clarifying statement.

William Seidleck, a lawyer with the Missouri Attorney General’s Office representing Hoskins, said his client would comply with the state court order requiring use of the 2022 map “unless and until” there is an intervening federal court decision. Hoskins is still “evaluating next steps,” he added.

Chief Justice Brent Powell told Hoskins not to “venture far from Jefferson City” while the court considers the contempt motion. He also pressed Hoskins to issue updated guidance to local election officials.
“We just want to make sure the law is followed,” Powell added.
Among his concerns is that if the legal fight continued, it could lead to ongoing issues after the election over whether the congressional delegation should be seated.
“We are in a precarious situation,” Powell said.
The broader clash is over a congressional map Missouri Republicans enacted in 2025, part of a nationwide redistricting push led by President Donald Trump.
The legal fight began when opponents of the new map gathered signatures in support of a state referendum that would undo the GOP-drawn map and put it on hold for the 2026 election.

But Hoskins delayed a decision on whether to include the measure on the ballot, waiting to the last minute before rejecting the plan, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to voters’ approval.

The Missouri Supreme Court, which has a majority of Republican appointees, disagreed, saying there was nothing in state law that exempted congressional maps passed by the Legislature from being vetoed by voters via the referendum process.

The federal lawsuit was filed by Rick Brattin, the Republican nominee in the district currently held by Cleaver, as well as Rep. Bob Onder, R-Mo. and two voters. Clark then ruled Tuesday that the state must use the map that people voted in during the primary.
The drama was playing out even after Tuesday’s deadline to finalize Missouri ballots ahead of this fall’s elections. First ballots are set to go out in the state on Sept. 19.

title: ‘We felt defeated’: Lindsay Clancy juror provides new details about the lone holdout
summary: A juror in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial provided new details Thursday about the lone holdout on the panel, including that he acted out the killings on a water bottle during deliberations.
story: A juror in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial provided new details Thursday about the lone holdout on the panel, including that he acted out the killings on a water bottle during deliberations.

Nick Dargie, 25, was one of the three men on the 12-person jury tasked with determining whether Clancy should be held criminally responsible for the 2023 strangulation deaths of her three young children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months old. He told “Good Morning America” on Thursday about his frustrations with the holdout juror, who has yet to be publicly identified.
“I think we felt defeated,” Dargie said about the case’s conclusion. “We spent seven weeks on this trial, almost two months of, you know, all of our lives dedicated to it.”

He is among at least five jurors — and the first male — who have spoken out about the case and what happened inside the deliberation room at Plymouth Superior Court last week. After more than 38 hours, the jurors could not reach a unanimous decision, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial after they deadlocked three times.
Add to Google
Add to Google

On Thursday, defense attorney Kevin Reddington filed a renewed motion to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility on each of the three charges, arguing that the prosecution did not prove, beyond a reasonable doubt, that Clancy was not in psychosis at the time of the killings.

Dargie told “Good Morning America” that toward the end of deliberations, the holdout juror would not engage in discussions with others or provide evidence that supported his reasoning, instead choosing to scroll on his phone.

Ultimately, Dargie said, he confronted the holdout juror after the man mimicked the killings, tying an exercise band entered into evidence around an empty water bottle and pulling it tight. Dargie said he is not sure why the man did that.
“I was shocked. It didn’t make any sense to me,” Dargie said. “We’re not in here to play detective or it’s not a game of Clue. This is serious.”

Throughout the trial, Clancy’s defense attorney argued that she was in a state of psychosis when she strangled the children with exercise bands and therefore was not aware of what she was doing. The prosecution, however, argued she was not actually experiencing postpartum psychosis and planned the killings ahead of time.

Three women on the jury told NBC Boston that the 11 jurors agreed to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. The holdout wanted to convict, they revealed, but admitted he expressed doubt in the prosecution’s case.
“It was definitely frustrating, mainly frustrating when [the holdout juror] explicitly said, ‘You know, I don’t know if the prosecution or the defense proved their case,’” Dargie told “GMA.”
Reddington in the motion also pointed to the fact that in this case, every juror except one — who did not apply the reasonable-doubt standard — came to that same conclusion.

“No rational jury could find beyond a reasonable doubt that she had no mental disease or defect when the Commonwealth’s own proof established that she did,” the motion said, noting the 11-1 jury split.
And at first, Dargie said, a number of jurors thought Clancy was guilty of the crimes, and at times the jury’s votes differed day to day.

A female juror who spoke with CBS Boston anonymously said many people on the jury were initially “firm in their beliefs,” and that she was one of the people who, at first, agreed with the holdout and thought Clancy was guilty.

She explained how there was so much “gray area” and doubt in the case, and that ultimately, she switched her tune because she thinks Clancy is mentally unwell and that she’d get better help in a state mental health facility than in prison.

Dargie told “GMA” that “once we laid out all of the evidence and how we saw it, that really brought everyone kind of on the same page, except for this one juror.” The female juror chalked it up to one person being unable to let go of their convictions.

When that one juror didn’t agree with the group, Dargie said, he asked him to show evidence that “helped to prove what he was saying, but he couldn’t.” That’s what led the jury foreperson to send a note to the judge about the holdout during deliberations, explaining that he wasn’t meeting the burden of reasonable doubt the prosecution must overcome.
Dargie acknowledged that it’s fair for someone to have a differing opinion, but said this particular juror would not engage and could not “find something to support his view.”
Now, prosecutors must decide whether they want to retry Clancy. The next hearing for the case is scheduled for Sept. 29.

Dargie, who was serving in the military overseas, said he’s “haunted” by the case. Specifically, he said, the recording of the 911 call made by Clancy’s then-husband, Patrick Clancy, when he found the dead children that night is seared into his memory. The recording was played in court and was not released to the public.
“I’ve never heard something like that, like a scream like that, come out of someone’s mouth,” Dargie said of the recording. “It’s horrifying.”
The anonymous female juror told CBS Boston that she will “never be the same after that 911 call.”
Dargie also rejected online conspiracy theories that Patrick Clancy was actually the one who carried out the killings, noting that if anyone had heard the 911 calls, they would change their mind.
“I think if they tried the trial again the way they did, I think nine times out of 10, I think the jury would come back with not guilty by reason of insanity, no doubt,” Dargie said.

title: Skeletal remains found in North Carolina nearly 50 years ago identified as 15-year-old runaway girl
summary: Human remains found nearly a half-century ago in North Carolina were identified as those of a 15-year-old Maryland girl who had run away from home months earlier, state law enforcement officials said Tuesday.
story: Human remains found nearly a half-century ago in North Carolina were identified as those of a 15-year-old Maryland girl who had run away from home months earlier, state law enforcement officials said Tuesday.
The skeletal remains were discovered on Dec. 29, 1977, in woods near a tire manufacturing plant in Wilson, 60 miles east of the state Capitol in Raleigh, State Bureau of Investigation officials said.

It took decades and multiple advances in DNA technology for law enforcement to finally put a name to the bones — they belong to 15-year-old Cindy Marcell Blizzard, “who had run away from Monkton, Maryland, in the spring of 1977,” according to an SBI statement this week.
While Blizzard’s cause of death is still unknown, state law enforcement officials are treating the matter as a possible homicide.
“Her death remains unsolved. Investigators are still looking for answers,” the SBI said.

When Blizzard’s skeleton was first found, a medical examiner could only determine that the remains were of a white female, 16 to 23, who had been dead for as little as six months and as long as two years, the SBI said.
While a cause of death has still yet to be determined, “circumstances surrounding the location and recovery of the remains raised the probability of foul play,” according to SBI officials.
DNA of the remains were first submitted to genetic data bases in 2010 with no hits, officials said.
Then, in 2024, law enforcement conducted more “advanced DNA testing” and used “forensic tools that didn’t exist in 1977,”  eventually leading to Blizzard’s identification, state officials said.

Investigators are asking for the public’s help and any tips that could be emailed to coldcases@ncsbi.gov or called in to state law enforcement at (919) 582-TIPS or the Wilson County Sheriff’s Office at (252) 237-2118.

title: Oil prices surge to $107 for the first time since May as bond yields jump
summary: The price of oil surged again, with Brent crude surpassing $107 per barrel for the first time since May as markets brace for a long U.S. war with Iran.
story: The price of oil surged again Thursday, with Brent crude surpassing $107 per barrel for the first time since May and U.S. crude oil jumping above $100 per barrel, also its highest level since mid-May.

A primary driver of the move in oil prices was President Donald Trump’s comment Wednesday night that he is not looking for a deal with Iran. Trump also said that he did not expect oil prices to fall until “right after” the November midterm elections, despite having said for months that the war would be over quickly.
“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump told reporters Wednesday afternoon. “They’re going to be tumbling down, and we’ll get them down.”
Commodities experts warned earlier this week that oil prices as measured by Brent could rise to $120 or even as high as $150 per barrel if the stalemate with Iran continues to drag on.

Trump’s suggestion that the war would continue for many more months also puts global crude oil stockpiles in focus. Earlier this year, dozens of nations agreed to release 400 million barrels in order to keep a lid on prices in the early months of the war.
The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since the 1980s.
Additionally, Saudi Arabia informed OPEC that its crude oil output plunged to the lowest level since 1990 last month due to renewed hostilities with Iran, according to a report from Bloomberg News.
NBC News was not immediately able to confirm that report.
“The move reflects a market still pricing in persistent geopolitical risk, with Persian Gulf tensions showing no credible path to de‑escalation,” analysts at ING said Thursday.

As a result of those rising prices, the national average gas price rose another 5 cents overnight to $4.27. Diesel fuel, which powers everything from farms to trucking to trains, rose 3 cents overnight to $5.97.

Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury bonds continued to sell off, driving their yields higher. The 10-year Treasury yield, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates, especially for mortgages, touched 4.93%, its highest level since 2023.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.07% Thursday, according to Mortgage News Daily. This is the highest rate since May 2025.
The 30-year Treasury yield spiked to 5.35%, its highest level since 2007.
The move in Treasury yields was driven mostly by the soaring price of energy, which has triggered renewed fears of an inflation crisis.

title: How often do you really need to wash your jeans? Here’s what experts say
summary: According to experts, you should wash your jeans every few wears — or more often if you get them really dirty. Plus, here are the best detergents for washing jeans.
story: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends on our timelines, like whether honey is good for your skin.

Taxes, death and the “can I wear this” sniff test — they’re all certainties in life. And, whether we’d like to admit it or not, we’ve all grabbed a piece of clothing off the floor (or the chair) and inhaled to see if it’s wearable. While certain pieces of clothing require washing after every use (yes, we’re also talking about lucky underwear), other items can get by with fewer spin cycles. Jeans are one of those items. You don’t need to clean them after every wear — but how often should you wash your jeans?

“Overwashing jeans can cause them to fade, lose their shape and weaken the fabric,” says Daniel Feliciano, co-founder and CEO of Clotheslyne, an on-demand laundry service. “But not washing your jeans enough can lead to bacteria buildup, odors and even skin irritation.”
So, what’s the ideal washing schedule for your denim? To answer that question, I spoke more with Feliciano and another laundry expert — plus, I got their tips on how to clean your jeans.
Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter.
How often do you really need to wash your jeans?

There is no one-size-fits-all answer on how often you should wash your jeans. If you wear your jeans to a baseball game where you may sit in something sticky or spill beer on them, the answer will be very different than if you just occasionally throw on a pair for some quick errands. That said, you can follow a general rule of thumb: “In most cases, jeans can be washed every four to five wears,” says Morgan LaLonde, a brand manager for Whirlpool Laundry. The general rule is if your jeans look or smell dirty, wash them. If not, wash them every five or so wears.

If small areas become soiled (say, you spill a bit of coffee on them) but they otherwise smell okay, you don’t necessarily need to throw them in the wash. If the stain is small enough, you can try spot-treating it, says LaLonde.
Does sticking your jeans in the freezer clean them?

Some say that rather than washing your jeans, you should put them in the freezer to clean them. It may sound like sorcery but it actually works — kind of. Freezing your jeans can make odor-inducing bacteria lie dormant, says Feliciano.

But just because your jeans may smell less funky doesn’t mean they’re clean. “Freezing them is a temporary solution — it doesn’t actually remove dirt or oils,” adds Feliciano. “A thorough washing is much more effective.”
What is the best way to wash your jeans?

Both experts recommend following the care instructions on your jeans’ tag. But generally speaking, you should use cold water and the delicate or gentle cycle of your washing machine, says Feliciano, adding that a mild or gentle detergent is best.

It’s fine to wash your denim with other items, though if they are a darker wash (think indigo or black) and new, you may want to wash them solo the first few times. The dye used on dark denim may bleed during the first few washes, so if you want to avoid the possibility of other clothes soaking up that dye, wash them on their own.

Another tip: “Turn your jeans inside out to protect against direct exposure to detergent, which could fade them more quickly or lead to faster wear and tear,” says LaLonde. Finally, if your jeans are embellished or ripped, Feliciano suggests placing them in a mesh washing bag before tossing them in your machine to protect rips from becoming larger or embellishments from falling off.
The best detergents to use on jeans

Feliciano and LaLonde both recommend sticking with a mild detergent for washing jeans. “For dark blue or black jeans, opt for detergents specifically made for dark clothing to prevent any fading,” adds Feliciano. Below are detergents that fit those requirements and that have at least a four-star average rating from 1,000 or more shoppers.
Tide Free & Gentle Liquid Laundry Detergent

This mild detergent is free of dyes and perfumes, making it a great hypoallergenic option that can clean all your laundry — including your jeans. This is my go-to detergent and I find that it does a great job at cleaning my toddler’s t-shirts, workout leggings and my favorite wide-leg jeans. The detergent is also available in pods.
Molly's Suds Liquid Laundry Detergent

If you like natural cleaning products, consider this detergent from Molly’s Suds. According to the brand, it’s mild and made with plant-derived active ingredients. The detergent comes in a handful of scents — including lavender, peppermint and unscented.
Seventh Generation EasyDose Free & Clear Laundry Detergent

Seventh Generation’s EasyDose detergent is super concentrated, so a little goes a long way. You’ll get at least 66 loads from the 23-ounce bottle, making it a great option for those who have to lug their stuff to a laundromat or apartment laundry room. The mild detergent is free of dyes and fragrances, making it gentle on materials and your skin, according to the brand.
Woolite Darks Protect Liquid Laundry Detergent

If you have dark blue or black jeans, consider washing them in this detergent from Woolite. It’s formulated specifically to maintain the color of darker clothing items and prevent fading, according to the brand. A bottle gets you through 33 loads and the cap can be used to measure your detergent.
Perwoll Renew & Repair Liquid Detergent

Like the detergent from Woolite, this option is also made specifically for dark or black clothing. Not only does this formula help prevent fading, but it can also help restore darker colors and make them look less faded, according to Perwoll. You’ll get up to 24 loads from one bottle and the cap can be used to measure what you need.
Should you put your jeans in the dryer?

Resist the urge to throw your jeans in the dryer. It might be quicker, but your jeans will hold up better if you stick to air drying them whenever possible. “Drying your jeans in a dryer can cause them to shrink, fade or cause damage to fibers,” says LaLonde. “Remove them from the washer and pull the seams taught so the jeans lay flat. Then hang them up to dry completely before wearing them.”
If you don’t have time to air dry, opt for a low- or no-heat dry cycle, and use dryer balls to keep your jeans tumbling instead of balling up, suggests LaLonde.
Frequently asked questions

If you buy light or medium wash jeans, there’s no reason to wash your jeans after buying them, according to experts. However, if you buy indigo jeans, you may want to consider a quick wash. Indigo dye may rub off on your skin, shoes or furniture if it hasn’t been washed.

Baggy jeans can generally go longer between washes than slim or skinny styles. Because the fit is looser, the fabric doesn’t sit directly against your skin the way tighter jeans do, so it absorbs less sweat, oil, and body odor over the course of a day. That means you can often get away with wearing baggy jeans five to ten times — sometimes more — before they actually need a wash.

title: Skeletal remains found in North Carolina nearly 50 years ago identified as 15-year-old runaway girl
summary: Human remains found nearly a half-century ago in North Carolina were identified as those of a 15-year-old Maryland girl who had run away from home months earlier, state law enforcement officials said Tuesday.
story: Human remains found nearly a half-century ago in North Carolina were identified as those of a 15-year-old Maryland girl who had run away from home months earlier, state law enforcement officials said Tuesday.
The skeletal remains were discovered on Dec. 29, 1977, in woods near a tire manufacturing plant in Wilson, 60 miles east of the state Capitol in Raleigh, State Bureau of Investigation officials said.

It took decades and multiple advances in DNA technology for law enforcement to finally put a name to the bones — they belong to 15-year-old Cindy Marcell Blizzard, “who had run away from Monkton, Maryland, in the spring of 1977,” according to an SBI statement this week.
While Blizzard’s cause of death is still unknown, state law enforcement officials are treating the matter as a possible homicide.
“Her death remains unsolved. Investigators are still looking for answers,” the SBI said.

When Blizzard’s skeleton was first found, a medical examiner could only determine that the remains were of a white female, 16 to 23, who had been dead for as little as six months and as long as two years, the SBI said.
While a cause of death has still yet to be determined, “circumstances surrounding the location and recovery of the remains raised the probability of foul play,” according to SBI officials.
DNA of the remains were first submitted to genetic data bases in 2010 with no hits, officials said.
Then, in 2024, law enforcement conducted more “advanced DNA testing” and used “forensic tools that didn’t exist in 1977,”  eventually leading to Blizzard’s identification, state officials said.

Investigators are asking for the public’s help and any tips that could be emailed to coldcases@ncsbi.gov or called in to state law enforcement at (919) 582-TIPS or the Wilson County Sheriff’s Office at (252) 237-2118.

title: Former lawyer who pulled gun on ex-wife in Ohio restaurant is convicted of attempted murder
summary: Prosecutors said Matthew Exton tried to carry out the “public execution” of his ex-wife.
story: A former attorney was convicted of attempted murder after officials in Ohio said he tried to carry out the “public execution” of his ex-wife in a Toledo restaurant last year.
Matthew Exton, 43, tried to shoot her, but the gun’s safety was on, and a waiter tackled him before he could try again, the Lucas County Prosecutor’s Office said in a news release Friday.
Exton was also convicted of two counts of felonious assault, with sentencing enhancements linked to all three charges, the prosecutor’s office said.
Exton was acquitted of one count of assault. He is scheduled to be sentenced later this month.

During a trial that ended last week, Exton testified that he’d worked as a prosecutor in Michigan and was licensed to practice law in Ohio. He’d handled divorce, family and bankruptcy cases, he said, but he became homeless after he split up with his wife.
The couple divorced in 2024, according to court records.
He testified that he was frustrated by how she’d handled certain aspects of their divorce when he pulled a Colt Defender on her in the downtown Toledo restaurant on April 11, 2025.
Exton saw his ex-wife and her family at the restaurant, which was having its opening night, as he left a different restaurant next door, according to the prosecutor’s office.
Exton testified that he pointed the gun to show he was serious about her following a court order. He denied trying to shoot her.
“I did not fire,” he said. “I did not hurt her. I did not try to hurt her.”
Before he pointed the gun, prosecutors said, Exton ordered a drink and had it taken to the table where his ex was sitting with her family. He spat toward them and left, the prosecutor’s office said.
He returned with a gun and headed straight for his ex, according to the release.
Video released by the prosecutor’s office showed Exton approaching the table and removing a handgun from his pocket.
His ex told authorities that he pointed the gun at her chest and pulled the trigger multiple times, according to a petition for a protection order.
“The gun made rapid ‘click’ noises as he pulled the trigger,” she wrote in a statement included in the protection order, which she filed two days after the event.
The video showed Exton pointing the Colt as his ex yelled “gun.” The waiter could be seen tackling Exton moments later.
Exton tried to fire the weapon, but the safety was still engaged. One round was in the chamber, and seven were in the magazine, the prosecutor’s office said.

“Nothing in their training and soft openings at the restaurant could have prepared the staff for what walked through that door,” Lucas County Prosecuting Attorney Julia Bates said in a statement. “The defendant did not come with the intention of having a meal. He came with anger in him and with the intention to commit a public execution of his ex-wife at the restaurant that day.”

title: Cindy Crawford Describes Meeting Son of Ex-Husband Richard Gere
summary: Nearly 40 years after Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere stepped out as one of the iconic couples of the early 1990s, their children are now starring together on the FX show “The Shards.”
story: Nearly 40 years after Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere stepped out as one of the iconic couples of the early 1990s, their children are now starring together on the FX show “The Shards.”

Homer Gere, 26, and Kaia Gerber, 25, are part of the cast of the teen serial killer drama helmed by Ryan Murphy and posed together on the cover of the September issue of Vogue. Their parents posed together for Vogue in 1992, making the latest cover shot a full-circle moment between the children of the supermodel and the actor, who divorced in 1995 after four years of marriage.

Crawford, 60, shared on TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle Sept. 10 what it’s like to see the two working together and how she first met Homer Gere, who is Richard Gere’s son with actor Carey Lowell. Gerber is the daughter of Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber.
“I had never met Homer,” Crawford said. “I met him while they were filming. He’s lovely, and Kaia enjoyed working with him.”
Crawford also expanded on how the two young actors deal with being labeled “nepo babies.”

“They’re both in the same situation,” Crawford said. “They understand it’s going to be a question they’re going to get asked, but at the same time they both work really hard and think they’re both doing a great job.”
Crawford emphasized that Gerber works hard for her modeling and acting career.
“Look, there’s pros and cons to having famous parents,” Crawford added. “And I know sometimes it feels like pressure, or she feels like, ‘Wow.’”
For example, her daughter can do a modeling shoot and commenters may bring up that her mother wore the look first.

“I’m like, ‘I know,’ because I can talk about my mom and no one knew who that was, and (Gerber) doesn’t have that anonymity,” Crawford said. “But she also understands that it does open maybe some doors.”
Gerber spoke to Vogue about what it has been like growing up in the public eye due to her mother.

“Fame was something that I was born into, so I didn’t experience what it was like to become famous,” Gerber said. “I kind of thought that my way of being raised was the most anonymous it could get under the circumstances, and then I met Homer. Like, there are no photos of him as a child online, whereas my entire childhood and teenage years are on the internet. I can only imagine. I’m 24 but … very interviewed.”
Gerber began modeling at 13 and was walking runways at 16, according to Vogue.

“I’ve only ever been a nepo baby, and I’ve only ever benefited in my career from it,” she said “But I also find myself doing it to other nepo babies, thinking, like, OK, show me why you deserve this job. I said to Homer — because the concept is daunting to him, having lived as an adult so far without that perception, whereas I sort of went through it when I wasn’t fully sentient — I said to him, ‘Homer, unfortunately with this show, it’s not like you’re just any unknown actor and people will judge you as an unknown actor.’”
Homer Gere did not begin acting professionally until appearing in a small role in the final season of HBO’s “Euphoria” earlier this year.
“I didn’t grow up in the industry at all,” he told Vogue. “I had never been on a professional set until last summer.”
He and Gerber also didn’t ignore their unique connection when they both joined the cast of “The Shards.”
“Twenty minutes into knowing each other, I was like, ‘Should we just acknowledge the fact that our parents were married?’ She was like, ‘Yeah. Cool,’” he told Vogue. “And that was it.”

title: AARP’s List of ‘Most Fabulous’ Gen X Actresses Honors Viola Davis and More Hollywood Stars
summary: Viola Davis leads AARP’s Movies for Grownups’ 25 Most Fabulous Gen X Actresses list.
story: Viola Davis is fabulous!

The Oscar winner tops AARP’s Movies for Grownups’ 25 Most Fabulous Gen X Actresses list, which “honors powerhouse female talent who continue to break barriers, command screens, and redefine what it means to be a Gen X actress in Hollywood,” according a news release.
The rankings pay homage to Generation X, which is classified as people born between roughly 1965 and 1980.

“Now, at roughly between the ages of 45 to 61, this generation of Hollywood actresses have not faded from the screen, but have built production companies, developed their own projects, and reinvented themselves behind the camera as directors, producers, and entrepreneurs fighting for equal pay and breaking stereotypes,” AARP’s Movies for Grownups said in a statement.
“They are far from slowing down and are doing the most ambitious work of their careers.”

Davis, 61, is the oldest person on the list and said in a statement connected to the honor, “My ability to overcome and to challenge and to believe in my ability is mine.” She survived a poor childhood marked by food insecurity to emerge as a critically acclaimed actor, winning a best supporting actress Academy Award for “Fences” and earning three other nominations in her career.

“When you come to Hollywood, I think women over 40, then over 50, you feel like you’ve just sort of disappeared and fallen off a cliff,” she told AARP’s Movies for Grownups. “Like you’re invisible. So, it’s nice to know that that’s not true. I feel like my value is going up. It feels fabulous.”

title: Elizabeth Acevedo Shares First Page of Novel in Verse, ‘Anger Is Only a Shadow’
summary: Elizabeth Acevedo previews the first page of her novel in verse “Anger Is Only a Shadow” and explains how it sets up the rest of her book.
story: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good story starts with a good first line. In TODAY’s “Cold Open,” authors tease their buzzy upcoming release by revealing and explaining its first line, paragraph or page.

Either because of her own lactose intolerance, or her memory of what lunch would smell like at the detention center she used to teach at, Elizabeth Acevedo knew her next novel would open with the “visceral” image of indigestion.
“Here is the most important rule of this place: Don’t drink the milk,” reads the opening line of her novel in verse “Anger Is Only a Shadow,” out Sept. 15 from HarperCollins.

The book’s narrator is a rebellious young woman named Lil, who finds herself in juvenile detention due to her “instinct for freedom,” per the novel’s premise, inspired by Acevedo’s own experience working as a teaching artist at a detention facility in Washington, D.C.
“It felt like such a visceral image to begin with, this disruption of your bodily functions in a space where that is very much monitored and very much like, not OK,” Acevedo tells TODAY.com.
The first page of the book is Lil “emphasizing the rules of this place,” both to herself and to the reader. Following the heading of, “Sunday, October 18,” it reads:

Here is the most important rule of this place: Don’t drink the milk. Trust, having the bubble guts is not the first impression you want to make. And while we’re on the subject, that’s an important rule too: don't make an impression.

Sit quiet, only slump so much in your chair, don’t look anyone in the face. Don’t avoid someone eyeing you either. And if you have to make an impression, let it be knuckle-size. Aldwin has been teaching me since I was little: know when to be brick-built, know when to be gentle. And here? Being soft don’t play here.

There are other rules you need to learn: Which YDR—youth development representative—you can joke with. When it makes sense to participate in an activity, or when it makes sense to stay your flat ass behind your door. What vent carries your voice into other units.
But the most important rule is Rule One: Don't. Drink. The. Milk.
The first page of the novel represents what Acevedo pictured her novel in verse to be. And the Lil readers meet through that introduction is the same way Acevedo found the character.

“I thought I was writing a book about a juvenile detention facility and this young woman who is in there and is kind of snarky and telling us the rules,” she says. “The first page was such a guide in her voice, really.

“Before I had plot, before I knew what the main conflict was, I was just kind of following the most irreverent character I’ve ever written,” she adds. “I knew I had a character long before I knew I had anything else.”

The rest came later, including its structure. Acevedo originally thought the novel would be entirely prose poetry, consisting of “blocky text without paragraph indentation.” In the final draft, the prose blocks, accompanied by dates, guide readers through Lil’s daily life. These entries are broken up by poems.

Acevedo first drafted a poem in Lil’s voice titled “Where I’m From.” It sparked a motif, and the character turns one writing prompt from a workshop at the detention center into a series of poems, illustrating how she’s “revising versions of herself,” Acevedo says.
When Acevedo worked as a teaching artist, she says she brought in poems.

“It’s a fraught space,” she says of her time teaching at a detention center. “You come in, and you’re like, ‘Let’s be really vulnerable in a space where you all are very reluctant to share vulnerability.’

“That tension was so visceral for me, and also ... the young women would open up in ways I had never imagined,” she adds. “It’s almost like I was constantly surprised and also fully understood like, ‘You have been looking for an opportunity for people to ask you these things.’”
But the book isn’t just about Lil’s time in the detention center. The novel also asks: “What are the stakes once you’re outside?”
“Anger Is Only a Shadow” will also follow Lil once she’s on probation, weighed down by an ankle monitor and fearing for her big brother, miles away at college.

“So many young people I know when I was a school teacher had ankle monitors, and how does that affect how you navigate your life? And what would be the thing that would lead this character, who’s very impulsive, to potentially violate the rules of the ankle monitor?” Acevedo says. “That’s when the second part of the story, a story I never thought I would write about, came forth.”
The result is “two big stories” rolled into the novel: one about juvenile detention and one about navigating a family member who has mental illness.

“I have a sibling who was diagnosed with schizophrenia when I was in the early years of my college career,” she says. “Trying to do well in my own little world of academics, while also showing up for family, and the ways in which it can be so hard to know what that person needs ... It felt like I just have so many questions about this. I don’t have answers.
“Then that felt like the challenge: Isn’t that exactly what you need to write about?” she continues.

“I’m not going to lie, I wasn’t sure,” she adds. “These are two big stories and I’m writing a very short book, I don’t think it can happen. But somehow, somehow, it felt like the two pieces were supposed to be interlocked.”

title: Harry Styles Announces 2027 Dates for ‘Together, Together’ Tour In 12 New Cities
summary: Harry Styles is adding 25 dates across 12 cities in 2027 to his “Together, Together” tour.
story: Harry Styles is adding more dates to his “Together, Together Tour.” The singer announced Sept. 10 that he will perform 25 concerts in 12 cities in 2027 that will span North America and Europe.
The new dates will begin April 2 in Phoenix, Arizona, and wrap Aug. 28 in London.

“When we decided to do the 2026 tour I knew it would be special but what you turned it into was far beyond what I could have imagined,” Styles said in an email to fans Sept. 9. “I love playing music, I love being with all of you and being a part of the love and joy you all create together every night. That’s why I wanted you to be the first to know we will be adding 2027 dates.”
In that letter to fans, Styles spoke of “what comes next” for him after touring, which led fans to speculate about its meaning.

Styles’ “Together Together Tour” launched in May with 67 shows in Amsterdam, London, São Paulo, Mexico City, New York, Melbourne and Sydney. He is in the midst of a 30-night residence at New York City’s Madison Square Garden, for what are currently his only stop in the U.S.
Tour information can be found at Styles’ website. General sale of tickets for North American dates begins Sept. 16 at 9 a.m. local time.
